Dark theme scores included; easier on the eyes in the evening follows your device's setting; Language and theme

Tip

On a phone, start with Auto (reading mode) and the Mixed lesson view: the score fills the screen when you play, and the lesson stays readable when you browse it.

Chapter 3Part I · Getting started

The app on your device

StoneKiller is the same app on a computer, a tablet or a phone, installed or opened in a browser: the same pages, the same lessons, the same functions. What changes is the room it has, the way you touch it, and what the device can do. This chapter says what changes and what stays the same, device by device.

Why take a look? Because you don't use it the same way everywhere: at the kit, with the mouse, to write a groove; at the drums, with the phone on a music stand, to play without touching it. And because a few functions depend on the device: better to know why a button is missing than to look for it. To see where each page is, go to Finding your way around the app instead; to install the app, go to Installation and devices.

At a glance

What forknowing what your device changes in the app (the menu, full screen, the gestures) and what it doesn't change.

Wherenothing to set. The layout follows the width of the screen; simple or full mode is chosen in Settings › Startup.

Key pointsit's the width that counts, not the device: up to 900 pixels, the menu moves to the bottom bar and the More panel. The installed app does a little more than a browser (hosted classes, My videos, folders).

In this chapter

  1. Width counts, not the device00
  2. The differences at a glance00
  3. On a computer00
  4. On a tablet00
  5. On a phone00
  6. The installed app or the browser00
  7. Simple or full, by device00

#Width counts, not the device

The app doesn't ask “am I on a phone?”, but “how wide is my window?”. Why: a tablet in portrait is as narrow as a large phone, and a shrunken computer window is too; so they get the same layout. To see the phone layout on your computer, narrow the window until the menu moves to the bottom. The layout changes at three widths, the same throughout the app:

Window width Where you find it What changes
over 900 px a computer, a tablet in landscape the menu stays on the left, full height; from 1100 px, the Contents can be pinned beside the page
900 px or less a phone, a tablet in portrait, a narrow window the menu moves to the bottom bar and the More panel (four tiles per row)
640 px or less a phone the pages tighten (one column, reduced bars); the More panel goes to three tiles per row

#The differences at a glance

Everything the app does works on both; the layout adapts to the width of the screen. In this guide, when a view really changes, the phone screenshot is shown next to the computer one, and asides point out the differences:

what only applies on a computer: mouse, keyboard, large screen.

what changes on a phone or tablet: touch screen, small screen.

what depends on the screen orientation.

The main differences:

  • With a finger: a long press replaces the right-click (menu of a note's variants, dragging a building block); the keyboard shortcuts disappear from the buttons.
  • The metronome shrinks to its dial (tempo, lights, pendulum, playback); its settings unfold below. When you start, it switches to full screen.
  • The menu moves to the bottom bar and the More panel (see On a phone).
  • The grid editor puts its tools in a dock at the bottom of the screen, within thumb's reach (see The grid editor).
  • The pro workshop switches to tabs (Search, Model, Composition).
  • The contents open over the page instead of being pinned next to it.

The functions that depend on the device (MIDI, class Wi-Fi, screen kept on) are in Installation and devices.

#On a computer

The computer (Windows or Mac in the installed app, any one in a browser) is the device with the most room: the menu stays on the left, from top to bottom, and the page keeps its full height for the score, the grid or the metronome.

  1. Contents: the tree of all your lessons, with a search. From 1100 px wide, the pin keeps it open beside the page (see Finding an exercise).
  2. The pages. In simple mode, as here: the home page and the categories, then All pages to unfold the full menu (see Simple or full).
  3. At the foot of the menu: My setlist, Scan a QR code, Legend, Guide, Settings and About (see The main screen).
  4. Volume and language.
  5. The page: here, the home page and its tiles.

With a mouse, hovering shows what each button does. On the keyboard, Space starts and stops playback, F1 opens the guide, Esc closes a window or leaves full screen: the full list is in Shortcuts. In the installed app, full screen for the metronome or a study makes the window itself go full screen.

With the installed app (Windows, Mac), a double-click on a StoneKiller file (a backup, lessons…) opens it; in a browser, drag the file onto the window. On Mac, the app has no access to an electronic drum kit (MIDI): to record from yours, open the .html file in Chrome, Edge or Firefox.

With the Teach edition, the computer hosts the live class (Windows, Mac) and can show the score large on a second screen (see Live classes).

#On a tablet

A tablet has no layout of its own: it takes the one of its width (see the table above). In portrait, it is that of a phone, on a wider page:

  1. The bottom bar: the home page and the first categories.
  2. More: the rest of the menu, in tiles (four per row on a tablet, three on a phone).
  3. My setlist: the round button, above the bar.
  4. The page: the home page's categories line up in as many columns as the width allows.

A tablet in portrait, or a narrow window on a computer, has the same layout as a phone: the width counts, not the device. A tablet in landscape has the menu on the left.

A large tablet, wider than 900 px even in portrait, keeps the menu on the left. For the rest, a narrow tablet works like a phone: with Auto, reading mode opens as soon as you start an exercise in portrait (in landscape, it behaves like a computer); the gestures, full screen and orientation are those of the phone (see On a phone). A Bluetooth page-turner pedal also works, in reading mode. On an Android tablet, the app installs as on a phone (see Android).

#On a phone

The phone is the one you put on the music stand to play: room is counted, a finger hides what it touches, and at the kit you don't want to touch anything. So the app changes shape there: the menu gives way to the page, full screen takes over, and the screen turns both ways.

#The bottom bar and More

On a narrow screen, the menu leaves all the room to the page, and the everyday pages move to a bar at the bottom, under your thumb.

  1. The bottom bar: the home page and the first categories. During a live class, the class's category takes the last place.
  2. More: every category, all pages, the legend, the guide and the settings.
  3. My setlist: the round button above the bar.

Your setlist stays within thumb's reach: a round button, above the bottom bar, opens it and shows how many exercises are ticked. It goes away on the Setlist page and in full screen.

  1. Contents.
  2. The home page and the categories, in large tiles.
  3. All pages: a touch unfolds them, grouped by category.
  4. My setlist, Scan a QR code, Legend, Guide, Settings, About.
  5. Volume and language.

A choice closes the panel; so does ✕, or a touch outside it.

In full mode, the bottom bar shows four pages you choose, and More all the pages, grouped by category:

  1. The bottom bar: Metronome, Lessons, Practice plan, My grooves (or the ones you choose, see At startup). During a live class, Class is added to it.
  2. More: the rest of the menu.
  1. Contents.
  2. The pages, in large tiles.
  3. The pages grouped by category (each category folds with one click).
  4. Scan a QR code, Legend, Guide, Settings, About.
  5. Volume and language.

#Narrow screen, full screen, orientation

On a phone, three things count: the room, what you can leave without touching it, and the way you hold it.

  • One column. Up to 640 px wide, the pages tighten: one column, reduced bars. The metronome and the grid editor, for example, rearrange themselves (see The differences at a glance).
  • Full screen, for playing. The metronome switches to full screen by itself when it starts: nothing scrolls, even if a stick brushes the screen, and the screen does not go to sleep (see The metronome). Reading mode shows the score alone, large; with Auto, it opens as soon as you start an exercise (see Reading mode). To leave it: the phone's back button. On Android, full screen also hides the system bars; on iPhone, it does not exist: reading mode fills the whole browser window.

In reading mode, the rotation button locks the screen in landscape when the browser allows it; otherwise the app asks you to turn the phone. The score reflows by itself, with the number of bars per line chosen for that orientation: 1 bar or ½ bar in portrait, 2 bars or 1 bar in landscape.

Sideways, the phone changes again: the bottom bar is lower (icon and name side by side), the metronome puts the lights on the left and the tempo on the right, in simple mode the home page keeps only the titles of its tiles, and in a song study the bottom bar disappears to leave all the height to the video and the tracks (it comes back when you close the study).

#With a finger

A finger is not a mouse:it hides what it touches, and there is neither hover nor right-click. A few gestures take the place of the mouse ones (the long press in place of the right-click is in The differences at a glance):

  • The metronome's tempo: slide your thumb over the number.
  • The grid editor: notes are placed cell by cell, on release; sliding scrolls the page instead of painting. A long press on a cell opens the menu of its variants (the phone vibrates a little).
  • The pro workshop's building blocks: to place one, long press, then slide (see The workshop).
  • A lesson's outline, while editing: put your finger on the ⠿ handle, then slide; the rest of the row scrolls the page as usual (see Outline and collapsing).
  • A Bluetooth page-turner pedal behaves like a keyboard: in reading mode, it changes exercise without you touching the screen.

#The installed app or the browser

StoneKiller comes in two forms: the installed app (Windows, Mac, Android) and a web page, that is, the .html file opened in a browser, or the page a phone opens when it scans a class's QR code. The pages, the lessons, the metronome, the editor: everything is there. What only the installed app does is what a browser does not allow: write to a folder without asking again, host a class for your students, create a Wi-Fi network.

  • Hosting a class (Teach). The app opens the class to your students; in a browser or an .html file, Start the class opens a demo, to try with two tabs. On the student side, only the apps find the class on their own: in a browser, type the Teacher's address, or scan the teacher's QR code (see Live classes).
  • Creating the class's Wi-Fi. The Teach app on Android only, with Android 8 or later (see A class without Wi-Fi).
  • My videos. The page that gathers the mirror's recordings, the exported videos and the Capture takes exists only in the app (see My videos). The mirror records there without asking for a folder again; in a browser, it asks for one once per launch (Chrome, Edge), or records when you stop.
  • A song's file. A study keeps a link to your audio or video file, without copying it, in the desktop app (Windows, Mac) and in Chrome or Edge; elsewhere (Firefox, Safari, phone, Android app), the file is copied to the device (see Studying a song).
  • Opening a StoneKiller file. A double-click in the installed app (Windows, Mac), “Open with” or “Share” on Android; in a browser, drag the file onto the window.
  • Keeping the screen on. The Android app does it as long as it is on screen; a browser does not.
  • An electronic drum kit (USB MIDI). It's the other way round: it works in the Windows app and in Chrome, Edge or Firefox, but not in the Mac app or the Android app (see Installation and devices).

The page a student's phone opens when it scans a class's QR code is a web page: it has neither the microphone nor MIDI, because the local network's address is not secure (see Live classes).

#Where your data goes

In the app as in a browser, your data stays on the device: no account, nothing is sent over the Internet, and nothing syncs from one device to another (see Settings, sounds and data). What changes is who keeps them:

  • the installed app keeps them for itself. Uninstalling the app may erase them; on Android, they are excluded from Google backups and from transfer to a new phone;
  • a browser keeps them for itself, on this computer: if you change browser or computer, they don't follow. Two .html files opened in the same browser may share the same data. In a private window, nothing is kept when you close it: a ⚠ warning says so;
  • a student's phone page keeps its practice plan and its log in the phone's browser, tied to the teacher's address: if that changes (another Wi-Fi), the page starts again from scratch.

In every case, the Full backup (on the My grooves page) takes everything, and Restore puts it back on another device (see Backing up and switching devices).

#Simple or full, by device

Simple or full mode does not depend on the device: it is a setting, kept separately on each device. At the first launch on a device, the welcome window asks what you're here for (see At startup: what you're here for): so you can have full mode on the computer and simple mode on the phone. What the device changes is the shape of the menu:

Computer, tablet in landscape Phone, tablet in portrait
Simple the menu on the left: the home page, the categories and All pages (folded) the bottom bar: the home page and the first categories; More: the home page, the categories and All pages
Full the menu on the left: all the pages, grouped by category the bottom bar: four pages of your choice; More: all the pages, grouped by category

The four pages of the bottom bar in full mode are chosen in Settings › Menu and home (the Bottom bar, see At startup). In simple mode, the home page fits on one screen, whatever the device (see A category's home page).

Chapter 4Part II · The basic tools

Playing an exercise

Each exercise appears in a player: the score, with the controls above it. The player does three things: it lets you hear how the exercise should sound, play it with the app at your tempo, and isolate what gives you trouble (an instrument, a bar, a tempo).

At a glance

What forlistening to an exercise, playing it with the app at your tempo, isolating what is giving you trouble.

Whereunder every exercise: in a lesson, the practice plan, My grooves.

Key points▶ to listen, − / + for the tempo, Instruments to play a part yourself, full screen to play at the kit.

In this chapter

  1. The player00
  2. Choosing your tempo00
  3. The click and the drums00
  4. Muting instruments00
  5. Sessions: practise for a set time00
  6. The Setlist00
  7. Reading mode00
  8. Variants and personal notes00
  9. The legend00

#The player

  1. Play / pause. Clicking a note in the score starts playback from that note: handy for picking up just before a hard passage. Space plays or pauses the last player you used.
  2. Tempo, in BPM (beats per minute). − and + change it by 5; you can also type a value. See Choosing your tempo.
  3. Tempos: preset values in one click, including the tempos set by the lesson.
  4. Metronome: the click. Right next to it, Drums mutes the drums so that only the click remains. See The click and the drums.
  5. Instruments: mute one or more instruments to play their part yourself. See Muting instruments.
  6. Session: timed practice, or a set number of repetitions. See Sessions: practise for a set time.
  7. Reading mode (the full-screen icon): the score alone, large. See Reading mode.
  8. The exercise actions: + Plan to work on it over time, Make a variant, your own Note, Add to a list, → Lesson (copy it into one of your lessons), Record yourself (play it and compare), Print or Print queue. The Teach edition adds → Student and, during a class, Project.

On a narrow screen (640 pixels or less), the bar tightens: Tempos, Drums, Instruments, Session and Legend move into ⋯ More settings, the actions into ⋯ Actions. The metronome and the drums stay as two small icons.

#Choosing your tempo

The tempo is your main working setting. A clean exercise at 60 BPM teaches you more than a sloppy one at 100: at a slow speed you hear your mistakes and fix them; too fast, you repeat them. The right method: start at a tempo where everything is clean, then go up in small steps.

The Tempos chips give values in one click:

  • Orig.: the tempo written in the score;
  • Start, Steady and Target, when the lesson (or your practice plan) provides them. Start is the tempo to begin at; Steady is the one you must hold easily, without mistakes, to consider the exercise learned; Target, optional, goes further, to push you;
  • common values, from 30 to 160.

You don't have to remember where you are: when the exercise is in your plan, the player starts at the tempo of your last session, and the plan raises it when you rate Good (see The practice plan).

Tip

To raise the tempo without thinking about it, use the metronome's speed-up: for example +2 BPM every 4 bars, up to your target tempo.

The player also keeps, on this device, the last tempo played for each exercise: open it again tomorrow and it starts from there. A small yellow ↺ next to the tempo shows it; a click goes back to the starting tempo (and forgets the kept tempo).

#The click and the drums

Metronome turns the click on: a short sound on each beat, with the first beat of the bar a little higher. Drums turns the exercise itself on or off.

These two buttons give the three classic steps for learning an exercise:

  1. Listen: drums and click, without playing, following the score with your eyes.
  2. Play along: drums and click, playing on top. You hear right away if you drift.
  3. Play alone: drums off, click only. This is the real check: you hold the exercise without a model.

The Alternating session moves automatically from step 2 to step 3 (see below).

#Muting instruments

Muting an instrument doesn't change the score: the app simply stops playing it. What is it for?

  • Take its place. Mute the bass drum and play it with your foot: the app keeps the hands going, and you concentrate on the foot. This is the idea of the “play-along”: the music without your part.
  • Understand a passage. Mute everything except the snare: you hear exactly where the ghost notes fall, without the hi-hat on top.
  • Build coordination. Start with the hands alone (feet muted), then the feet alone, then everything: one limb at a time is faster than everything at once.
  1. Each instrument in the exercise has its own button. One click mutes it (the button goes dark), another turns it back on.

To hear one instrument's part with nothing else, mute all the others. To keep only the click, use Drums instead.

#Sessions: practise for a set time

A session frames your work: “5 minutes on this groove” or “10 times in a row”. A fixed duration stops you from moving on too quickly; a number of repetitions makes you play to the end, even when it's hard.

  1. End: after a Duration, or after a number of Repetitions.
  2. The duration: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 or 25 minutes, or a time you type (for example 3:00).
  3. Repeat: Whole exercise plays the exercise from start to end (a bar marked ×3 in the score is played 3 times; during playback, dots next to the ×3 show which pass is playing). Each bar ×2, ×3, ×4 or ×8 repeats each bar before moving on to the next one: ideal for a long exercise that you learn piece by piece.
  4. Mode: With drums, Dry (metronome only), or Alternating (for example 2 bars with the drums, 2 without). Alternating takes you from “playing along” to “playing alone” without stopping: when the drums come back, you hear whether you kept the tempo.
  5. Start the session: the progress is shown, and at the end the app sums up the time played and the tempo.

Just above, Count-in: None, 1 bar or 2 bars of click before the first note, so you have time to pick up the sticks. The clock counts “1… 2… 3… 4…” during the count-in. The choice applies to all exercises; in the Settings you can also apply it to simple playback ▶.

In repetitions, lights count the passes, like the metronome's LEDs, so you know where you are without counting in your head: one blue light per pass (the one playing glows), one white light per ten played (11 of 23: one white and one blue). In the last ten, only the passes left remain: the second-to-last is yellow and the last red, so you see the end coming. Beyond a hundred, the tens are written in digits (124: 120 and four blue).

#The Setlist

A warm-up, a rehearsal, a class: you chain exercises that come from everywhere, and looking for them one by one breaks the flow. The Setlist is your basket: put in what you want to play, in order, then play it in one go.

To fill it, + Setlist is everywhere: on an exercise, at the top of a part or a lesson, and on a theme of the lesson book. For a part, a lesson or a theme, a window shows its exercises, all ticked: untick those that should not go in this time, rather than removing them one by one afterwards.

  1. In the Teach app: the setlist they go into: yours, the class one (see Live classes) or the next session's (see The session setlist).
  2. An exercise already in this setlist: greyed out, it does not go in a second time.
  3. Unticked: it stays in its lesson, but does not go into the setlist. All, at the top of the list, ticks or unticks everything at once.
  4. Add: the number of exercises that go in.
  1. In the Teach app: My setlist, the Class setlist (the one you project during a class) and The session.
  2. The common settings, as for a chain: Each exercise ×4 or for a duration, Repeat each bar, a Rest between two exercises, loop, Rate each exercise (see below); the Tempo as a percentage of each exercise's starting tempo, to slow everything down at once.
  3. ▶ Play the setlist chains the ticked exercises; in the ⋯ menu, Board shows them as a board. Next to it: how many exercises are ticked, and the expected duration.
  4. During a class: ◀ Previous and Next ▶ step through the ticked exercises.
  5. Unticked, an exercise stays in the list but is neither played nor projected: handy to keep it at hand without playing it today.
  6. An exercise can have its own tempo or passes (framed, marked own setting): ↺ brings it back to the common settings.
  7. ↑ and ↓ change the order; ✕ removes the exercise from the Setlist (it stays in its lesson or in My grooves).
  8. During a class: ▶ Project shows this exercise to the class.
  9. ⋯, then Print: the ticked exercises, in order, with their scores and their own settings, under the StoneKiller header, to play the setlist on paper or give it to a student.

+ Add an exercise picks one from the library; in the ⋯ menu, Clear removes everything, without deleting anything from the lessons or My grooves.

#Rate each exercise

Chaining keeps the momentum going; but after ten exercises, you no longer remember which one was sticky. With Rate each exercise, playback stops at the end of each exercise (a sound signal) and asks you right away how it went, while it's fresh. Only then come the rest between exercises, or the count-in, then the next exercise: you never answer while playing.

  1. Bad, OK, Good, Mastered: the same ratings as in the Practice plan, with the next reminder and its tempo. One click rates the exercise and starts what comes next. An exercise not yet in your Practice plan goes into it.
  2. Details: one rating per criterion (tempo, precision…), as in self-assessment.
  3. What comes next: the next exercise, after the rest or the count-in.
  4. Next without rating: carry on without rating anything.
  5. Stop the series (or Esc): nothing is rated, the series waits; in the board, ▶ resumes at the next exercise.

The same box exists in Run through (a lesson) and in the Practice bar: it's the same setting.

#The session setlist

In the Teach app, before a lesson, you gather what is planned for its students: what they have to work on, what was prepared for that lesson. The session does it for you: it is the setlist of the next session in the schedule (the one in progress, otherwise the next one), an individual or a group lesson.

  1. The session.
  2. Which one: the day, the time, the student or the group.
  3. + The planned work: what is planned for its students (prepared for this lesson, then their To work on list), without duplicates.
  4. The exercises, to play, project or print as in the other setlists.

+ Setlist, anywhere in the app, also offers the session. Once the session is over, the setlist says so: Switch to the next session starts again from the work planned for the next one.

#Reading mode

At the drums, with the phone on a stand, the controls take up room and the notes are small. Reading mode shows the score alone, large, and follows the playback. To leave: the phone's back button, Esc or ✕.

In reading mode:

  • Metronome and Drums stay within reach (the two small icons);
  • 1 bar (on a phone): how many bars per line. A whole bar reads at a glance; half a bar gives bigger notes. In portrait, the button switches between 1 bar and ½ bar; in landscape, between 2 bars and 1 bar. Your choice is remembered for each orientation (also in Settings › Display);
  • ◀ and ▶ go to the previous or next exercise without leaving full screen; “3/9” shows where you are. The keyboard arrows and a Bluetooth page-turner pedal do the same: you change exercise without letting go of the sticks;
  • if you have just played an exercise from your plan, the app first asks “Before moving on: how was it?”. One click, and your tracking is up to date; Later skips without rating. The question only comes when moving to the previous or next exercise, not when leaving with ✕ or Esc.

With Auto, starting an exercise opens reading mode directly, on a phone or on a tablet held in portrait. A tablet in landscape behaves like a computer. On a very narrow screen, the setting is in Settings › Display.

The rotate button locks the screen in landscape when the browser allows it; otherwise the app asks you to turn the phone. The score lays itself out again, with the number of bars per line chosen for that orientation.

On iPhone, full screen does not exist: reading mode fills the whole browser window.

To fix your posture, watch yourself play: the mirror shows you from several angles, and on delay.

#Variants and personal notes

  • Make a variant opens the exercise in the workshop so you can change it: an extra bass drum, another sticking… Your variant then appears under the original exercise, with the changed notes in color, so you see at a glance what changes.
  • Note adds your own text under the score: a sticking, a reminder, the name of the song where you heard this groove.

#The legend

Legend (in the menu, or in each player) explains every symbol in the score: note heads for each instrument, accents, ghost notes, flams, drags, buzzes, pad strokes. A click on a symbol plays its sound.

Scores follow the modern standard drum key: hi-hat and cymbals as crosses above the staff, snare on the third space, bass drum at the bottom. Full key, at the top of the legend, also shows the symbols that are planned but not yet available. All the symbols, with the code to type in the text notation, are in The drum key. If you are used to GrooveScribe, Settings › Display › Score engraving brings back its conventions.

Chapter 5Part II · The basic tools

The grid editor

Wherever the app lets you write rhythm (a groove in the workshop, a lesson exercise, a variant, the metronome's groove, the board of a class), it is the same grid. This chapter explains it once and for all; the other chapters refer back here.

At a glance

What forwriting or touching up a groove note by note, hearing it with every click.

WhereWorkshop › Groove editor, and wherever a score can be edited (see Where you find it).

Key pointschoose a brush, click in a cell. The score writes itself under the grid.

In this chapter

  1. Why a grid?00
  2. The editor at a glance00
  3. Placing and editing notes00
  4. Bars, subdivisions and instruments00
  5. Select, copy, shift00
  6. Grid or text00
  7. Where you find it00

#Why a grid?

The grid makes rhythm visible: each row is an instrument, each column a subdivision of the beat (a sixteenth note, a triplet eighth…). A filled cell is a stroke. You see where each stroke falls in relation to the beats, you hear it as soon as you place it, and the app writes the score for you: no need to read music to write down a groove accurately.

If you prefer the keyboard, the same score also exists as text (see Grid or text).

#The editor at a glance

What you use for every note fits in a single bar above the grid. What you use now and then (the shape of the groove, the help, the instruments) waits behind a button or under the grid: the grid keeps all the room.

  1. The everyday brushes: Normal, Accent, Ghost and the Eraser, after Undo / Redo.
  2. More: all the brushes (Flam, Drag, Buzz, Open, Closed…) and the rare strokes. When one of them is picked, the button lights up and shows its symbol. Right next to it, ⤢ unfolds them all in the toolbar, for a groove that keeps changing brushes: with their name if there is room, otherwise their symbol alone (the name shows on hover, or with a long press on a touch screen). ⤡ folds them away.
  3. Select (S): frame notes to copy or shift them (see Select, copy, shift).
  4. The pattern chip ("4/4 · Sixteenths · 1 bar · ♩ 90"): the shape of the groove at a glance; a click opens it to change it.
  5. ?: the keyboard shortcuts and how the grid works.
  6. The grid: one row per instrument, one cell per subdivision. The beats (1, 2, 3, 4) are numbered above.
  7. The subdivision of each beat: eighths, triplets, sixteenths, sextuplets… Each beat can have its own.
  8. Repeat ×N: the bar plays several times before the next one.
  9. ⋯, at the end of an instrument's name: listen to it, give it a polymeter, hide it.
  10. Under the grid: + Instrument, the sticking and the polymeter.
  11. Grid / Text: the same score, as cells or in text notation.

#On a phone

On a phone, the page's grid serves as a preview: a finger scrolls the page and the grid sideways, without ever placing a note. To write, touch the grid: the editor opens full size, on the bar you touched (see The full-size editor, by touch). The tools that remain on the page move into a dock at the bottom of the screen, under your thumb.

  1. ▶: play the groove, or stop it. Right after, Undo / Redo.
  2. Selection.
  3. Edit full size: the full-screen editor, on the bar you see.
  4. The pattern chip (its time signature) opens its settings; at the end, ? for help.

The windows of these buttons rise from the bottom of the screen. During a selection, its actions take the place of the tools in the dock.

On a tablet, the page's grid is edited with a finger: a touch places or removes a note, on release (sliding scrolls), and a long press opens the menu of its variants. Edit full size is also in its bar. Keyboard shortcuts do not appear.

#The full-size editor, by touch

On a small screen, cells the size of a fingernail are hard to touch, and the finger hesitates between placing a note and scrolling. The full-size editor settles both: it takes the whole screen, goes landscape and shows only one bar at a time, in large cells.

  1. A line above the grid reminds you of this.
  2. The page's grid: a touch opens the full-size editor on the bar touched; sliding scrolls it, sideways or with the page.
  3. Edit full size, in the dock: the full-size editor on the bar you see. On a tablet or a computer, the same button is in the grid's bar.
  1. The tools: Done (back to the page), Undo, Redo, the four brushes (normal, accent, ghost, eraser), … for the rarer strokes, and ▶ to listen.
  2. The bar in large cells: touching a cell places the brush's note, or removes it; sliding along a row places on all the cells crossed; sliding up or down scrolls the rows; a long press opens the note's variants.
  3. ◀ ▶: the previous or next bar (“Bar 2 / 4”); a bar too long for the screen is cut into parts of whole beats. While listening, the page follows the playhead.

What you do at full size is in the page's grid, and Undo still undoes it after closing. The phone's Back button closes the editor without leaving the page. If the screen does not turn, the editor stays in portrait: two beats at a time, and a line says “Turn your phone for more room.”

#Placing and editing notes

  • Choose a brush, then click in a cell: the note is placed and you hear it. A click on an existing note with the Normal brush erases it; with another brush, it takes that brush's articulation.
  • Drag to paint several cells at once. With the Eraser, drag to erase.
  • Keys 1 to 9 change brush, including those kept in More; E takes the eraser. The cursor shows the current brush.
  • To change a note without changing brush: a right-click (or Shift+click) moves to the next articulation; a held right-click opens the menu of all its variants (accent, ghost, rimshot, half-open…) and Erase the note.
  • In More, the Other… list gives the less common strokes: rimshot and half-open hi-hat.
  • A click on an instrument's name plays it (its ⋯ also offers Listen).
  • ↶ ↷ (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y) undo and redo; one dragged brush stroke counts as a single step.

Tip

In a variant, the notes that differ from the original are coloured: you see at a glance what you changed. A note put back in its place takes the original's articulation again.

#Bars, subdivisions and instruments

You rarely change the shape of a groove, but you need to see it all the time: the pattern chip sums it up, and a click opens it.

  • Time signature: 4/4, 3/4, 6/8, 7/8…
  • Grid: the subdivision of all the beats at once (eighths, sixteenths, triplets…). Then the small menu above each beat changes it for that beat only: sixteenths on beats 1 and 2, a triplet on beat 3, in the same bar.
  • Bars: − removes the last one, + adds an empty bar, Copy adds a copy of the last one: handy to write a variation in bar 2 without rewriting everything.
  • Tempo: the tempo of the groove. Clear erases all the notes (after confirmation).

A click outside, or Esc, closes the window. In the grid itself, the ×1 menu at the end of each bar makes it play from ×2 to ×16 before the next one (Repeat ×N); the score writes it with repeat bars.

Under the grid, the instruments and the sticking:

  • + Instrument: ride, bell, crash, splash, china, cowbell, tambourine, toms (up to six), second bass drum, practice pad… An empty row can be hidden with one click, or from its ⋯.
  • R L Sticking shows a sticking row (hands R / L, feet K / F); Auto sticking fills it in: alternating hands, R on the beats.
  • Polymeter repeats a figure of N cells along the whole row, which then slides over the bar; a row's ⋯ opens it straight away for that instrument. See Polyrhythms and polymeters.

#Select, copy, shift

Once the notes are placed, you often rework them in chunks: copy a beat onto the next one, move a figure by a sixteenth, move the snare part onto a tom. The selection does all that without rewriting the notes.

Take the Select tool (S) and drag in the grid to frame notes. Faster: a click on a beat (1, 2…) or a bar (M1…) in the header selects it; Shift+click extends the selection. While a selection is made, its actions take the place of the toolbar:

  1. What is selected: the number of notes and rows.
  2. Copy, Cut, Paste, Duplicate: pasting replaces the content of the frame; Duplicate copies right after. A single copied row is pasted onto the selected instrument: that is how you move the snare part onto a tom. You can also paste into another editor (from an exercise to its variation).
  3. Shift ◀ ▶ (← →, with Shift: by a whole beat): the notes move within the frame.
  4. Instrument ▲ ▼ (↑ ↓): the notes move to the instrument above or below.
  5. At the edge: what happens to the notes that leave the frame when shifting: Wrap (they come back on the other side, ideal to "rotate" a figure), Block, Cut or Extend (the frame grows).
  6. The frame: drag it elsewhere to move the notes; with Ctrl or Alt, they are copied.

Clear (Del) empties the frame; ✕ (Esc) deselects and brings the tools back. Ctrl+A selects everything.

With a finger, the selection and the frame are dragged as with a mouse; what needs a keyboard key goes through the buttons of the dock.

#Grid or text

▦ Grid / ≡ Text shows the same score in text notation: one line per instrument (H hi-hat, S snare, K bass drum…), one character per cell, - for an empty cell and | between bars.

4/4 @90 div=16
H:  x-x-x-x-x-x-x-x-
S:  ----o-------o---
K:  o-------o-------

It is handy to copy a groove into a message, paste it from another program, or type it quickly. What you change on one side shows up on the other. The character of each note (for example S: g for a ghost note on the snare) is given under each symbol in The drum key.

#Where you find it

Where What for Chapter
Workshop › Groove editor write a groove of your own, from scratch or from an exercise The workshop
Under an exercise: Make a variant change an exercise without touching the original Playing an exercise
A lesson in Detail: Edit score write or correct the exercises of your lessons Creating a lesson
Metronome, Groove mode: Edit the groove sketch a groove that plays instead of the clicks The metronome
Pro workshop: the composition compose with pieces of other grooves The workshop
Class: Compose live (Teach edition) build a groove in front of the students Live classes

In the Groove editor, your work in progress is kept automatically: it comes back when you reopen the tool. When you edit a groove that is already saved, an exercise or a variant, Save and close keeps the changes; if you close the app before that, it warns you. How to save a new groove: The workshop.

This tidy layout is the one of the Groove editor and of the lessons. The metronome, live classes, series and recording keep the full bar, with every tool laid out: they are the same tools, in the same place as before. The classic interface (Settings › Startup › Interface) keeps the full bar everywhere.

Chapter 6Part III · Practising

The lesson book

The book organizes the exercises like a method book: themes (the shelves), lessons in each theme, parts in each lesson, and exercises in each part, with their tempos, notes and variations. The app comes with lessons; you can create your own, receive some from a teacher and share them.

At a glance

What forfinding exercises, reading them in a lesson's order, and writing your own lessons.

Wherethe Lessons page; the Contents, in the menu, from any page.

Key pointstheme › lesson › part › exercise. The built-in lessons stay as they are; Duplicate to edit makes your own version.

In this chapter

  1. Browsing the book00
  2. Finding an exercise00
  3. Reading a lesson00
  4. Running through exercises00
  5. Creating a lesson00
  6. Sharing lessons00

#Browsing the book

  1. New lesson: an empty lesson, ready to fill (see Creating a lesson).
  2. ⋯: New theme (a new shelf to file lessons on), Import lessons (a .sklessons file received from a teacher or a friend) and Export my lessons.
  3. A click on a card opens the lesson.

Each lesson has an origin, which tells you what you can do with it:

Origin What you can do with it
Built-in shipped with the app. It cannot be edited, so it stays the same for everyone: you can Hide it (it can be restored at the bottom of the page) or Duplicate to edit (on its page).
Mine yours: everything can be edited.
Imported received in a file; editable like your own lessons. When the teacher sends a new version of the same file, it is updated; if you had changed it, the app asks what to keep.

View, at the top of the book, chooses the layout: Tiles (one per lesson: name, subtitle, number of exercises and progress), Compact (smaller: more lessons on screen) or List (one row per lesson). A click on a theme's name folds or unfolds it; Collapse all leaves only the themes, to find your way at a glance. A lesson's ⋯ edits it, duplicates it, moves it to another theme or up and down, exports it, prints it, hides it or deletes it.

#The 40 rudiments

Rudiments are a drummer's basic moves, like scales for a pianist: grooves and fills are made of them. The The 40 rudiments theme, built into the app, brings together the 40 International Drum Rudiments of the Percussive Arts Society (PAS), in their official order, in four lessons: Roll rudiments (1 to 15), Diddle rudiments (16 to 19), Flam rudiments (20 to 30) and Drag rudiments (31 to 40).

Each exercise is written for the pad, with the sticking above the notes (R: right, L: left), suggested tempos (start, stable, target) and a short tip. Its PAS number opens the tip: handy for finding it in a method book or a rudiment sheet. Like any other exercise, they go into the practice plan, a list or a sheet to print.

#Finding an exercise

The Contents, at the top of the menu, shows the whole book as a tree: themes, lessons, parts, exercises. It is the fastest way to reach a specific exercise, from anywhere in the app.

  1. Search: type a few letters (a name, "paradiddle", "6/8"), the tree keeps only what matches.
  2. Pin to the left: the contents stay open next to the page, to jump from one exercise to another.

The pin only exists on a wide screen (1100 pixels or more). Elsewhere, the contents open over the page and close when you tap beside them.

#Reading a lesson

  1. The lesson contents lead straight to each of its parts.

At the top of the lesson, Whole lesson to the plan adds all its exercises to the practice plan at once, and ▶ Run through plays them one after another (see below).

A lesson with many exercises and variations is easier to read as compact rows:

  1. Display: Full (one player per exercise and per variation), Mixed (exercises in full, variations as rows) or Compact (everything as rows). The choice is remembered.
  2. A click on a part title collapses or expands it. Collapse all / Expand all act on every part; collapsed parts stay collapsed on your next visit.
  3. ▶ next to a part runs it through; the printer icon prints it.
  4. A row: ▶ plays the exercise, with its name, its tempos and its notes. A click on the name opens the full card (player, notes, actions); ▾ closes it again.
  5. Variations of variations are indented under their parent variation, with the changed notes in color.

#Running through exercises

A warm-up, a rudiment routine, all the variations of a groove: Run through plays a series of exercises without you touching the app. Each exercise plays the chosen number of times, then the next one starts, at the same tempo. You keep the sticks in your hands from start to finish.

▶ Run through is at the top of a lesson, next to each part, and on an exercise that has variations (Run through with its variations).

  1. What: the whole lesson, a part, or an exercise and its variations.
  2. The list: tick what you want to play, reorder it with ↑ ↓. Auto can be replaced by a number of passes for one exercise.
  3. Each exercise: ×1 to ×50 passes (×… other number for another one), or a duration from 30 s to 10 min (other duration… for your own). Next to it: the whole exercise, or each bar 2 to 8 times before the next.
  4. Rest between: none, or 1 to 2 bars where only the click goes on, the time to read the next exercise.
  5. Start: the count-in, then the exercises in a row. Loop starts again from the top.

Next to the list, the preview plays what you ticked, the way the run-through will: the passes, the durations, the rest between. ‹ › move from one ticked exercise to the next, and a click on a name shows it. Nothing ticked: the staff stays empty and playback waits.

When it starts, the board opens full screen: one row per exercise, with its score. The one playing is highlighted, with the playhead and dots for the passes (the second-to-last yellow, the last red). The count-in shows in a ring around ▶ and in the timer, without moving anything. At the top, the usual playback bar: ▶ / ⏸, the timer, the tempo, Metronome and Drums. A click on a row jumps to it. Closing the board does not stop playback.

At the end, ★ Rate (in the board's bar) rates the whole series at once instead of exercise by exercise: see Rating a whole series. Would you rather rate each exercise right after playing it? Tick Rate each exercise: playback stops at the end of each one and asks you, before the rest and the count-in of the next (see Rate each exercise).

The choices (ticks, order, settings) are kept for each lesson. The lists in My grooves and the workshop results have the same Practice, with the same settings.

#Creating a lesson

A lesson of your own organizes your own practice or, for a teacher, prepares a class to give to the students. Everything is saved automatically.

  1. New lesson, then give it a title. The editor opens.
  2. Fill in the top of the form, then add parts and exercises:

  1. Title, subtitle, theme, author and introduction (in markdown: bold, italics, lists, links).

  2. ✦ Create with the workshop…: pick a tool (Groove editor, Ostinato, Combinations, Record, Polyrhythms, Polymeters) to create exercises directly in this part (see below).

  3. + Exercise: an empty exercise, to write in the grid (Edit score) or As text.

  4. + Part: a new part of the lesson.

  5. For each exercise, give its tempos and notes (see below). To the right of its name: ↑ ↓ to move it, the → part menu to send it to another part, Duplicate and ✕.

  6. View lesson to play it.

#The tempos of an exercise

Each exercise can set three tempos, which become one-click chips in the player and drive the practice plan of whoever works on it:

  • Start: the tempo of the notation, where to begin;
  • Steady: the tempo to hold easily, without mistakes, for the exercise to count as learned. The practice plan offers Mastered when it is reached;
  • Target (optional): beyond the steady tempo, to push those who progress fast.

You can also decide whether the metronome is on when it starts: off, for example, for an exercise to play along with a song.

#Outline and collapsing

A long lesson is quicker to reorganize in ☰ Outline than in ▤ Detail (the two buttons above the parts; the choice is remembered).

  • Detail: everything can be edited. The ▾ chevron to the left of a part or an exercise collapses it: the exercise keeps its row (name, tempos, tools) and hides its score, notes and variations.
  • Outline: one row per part and per exercise, with its Start, Steady and Target tempos and the metronome at start. Under each part title, Whole section gives all its exercises a steady tempo, a target or the metronome at once: handy to set a whole part of warm-ups to 80 BPM. Drag the ⠿ handle to change the order, also from one part to another; dropping an exercise on the title of a collapsed part files it there. ✎ opens the exercise in detail.

With a finger, put your finger on the ⠿ handle, then drag: the rest of the row scrolls the page as usual.

#Variations of variations

A variation can have its own variations, to build a progression. Example: the paradiddle; a variation with a bass drum; a sub-variation where it moves; another variation with two bass drums…

  • ↳+ on a variation creates a sub-variation from it (named "1.1", "1.2"…).
  • The ↳ menu ("derived from") attaches a variation to the exercise or to another variation.
  • Deleting a variation moves its sub-variations up one level.
  • Changed notes are colored relative to the parent variation, not to the exercise.

#Starting from an existing groove

Rather than starting from an empty grid, take a groove close to what you want. Start from an existing groove… (under each part) and Variation from another groove… (under an exercise's variations) open a visual picker:

  1. The tabs, from the closest to the widest: this exercise, this part, this lesson, the theme, My grooves, all lessons.
  2. Search all sources at once.
  3. A click on a thumbnail selects it and plays it; a double-click takes it right away.
  4. Start from this groove: the new exercise (or variation) starts with this groove, ready to edit.

#Creating with the workshop

From the editor, Create with the workshop opens the chosen tool, linked to the lesson: what you create goes straight into it.

  1. The banner reminds you of the target lesson. Its part menu chooses where the exercises go, or creates a ＋ New part…. Back to the lesson or Cancel at any time.
  2. The brushes: the sound placed by a click (normal, accent, ghost; flam, drag… in More).
  3. The grid: a click places a note, another click erases it.
  4. + Instrument, under the grid: adds a row (ride, bell, crash, toms, pad…).
  5. Add to “…”: the exercise joins the lesson and you are back in the editor.

Ostinato and Combinations produce a whole series: you stay in the workshop, and the Lesson row of the results has the same part menu. The workshop is described in detail in The workshop.

#Sharing lessons

  • On a lesson card, Export creates a .sklessons file. Export my lessons, in the ⋯ menu at the top of the page, exports all your own and imported lessons at once.
  • Send the file any way you like (message, email, USB stick). The student opens it with Import lessons, or with a double-click.
  • If the teacher sends a new version, importing it updates the imported lesson; when they differ, the import window asks what to keep (see Opening a file). Your own lessons are never overwritten: a file carrying the same lesson arrives as a copy.

On Android, Export opens the phone's "Save as" window: choose a folder (Downloads, Drive…), then send the file.

#Provided exercises stay in the app

The lessons that come with the app are meant to be practised here, not passed around outside it. In the app you do everything with them: play them, copy them, make variations, print them for yourself. Only exported files change.

  • In an exported file (lessons, full backup, student roster), a provided exercise, its copy, or a variation that keeps its essentials is sealed: another StoneKiller app opens it as is, a text editor reads nothing. Your own work stays readable.
  • "Its essentials" means the exercise copied (or nearly), or more than half of what makes it distinctive: its syncopations, its placed ghost notes, its fills. The material shared by all grooves (eighth notes on the hi-hat, snare on 2 and 4, bass drum on 1 and 3) belongs to nobody: a basic rock beat you write stays yours. Once your variation moves away from the original's figure, it's your creation: it's exported readable.
  • In the workshop, Text mode doesn't show the notation of such an exercise: edit it in the grid.
  • When printed, the bottom of the pages reads "© … — personal use only".

During a live class, the teacher can also project any exercise to the students, without a file.

Chapter 7Part III · Practising

The practice plan

The Practice plan answers one question every day: "what do I work on today, and at what tempo?". It gathers the exercises you are working on, remembers your tempo for each one and brings them back at the right time. The better an exercise goes, the further apart its reminders; a hard exercise comes back soon. This is spaced repetition: the method used to learn vocabulary, applied to drumsticks.

At a glance

What forknowing every day what to work on, and at which tempo, without forgetting anything.

Wherethe Practice plan page; + Plan under each exercise to add it.

Key pointsplay the top exercise, rate it, move on to the next one. The rating sets the next reminder and the next tempo.

#Why a practice plan?

Without a plan, you replay what you like and forget what is hard. The plan fixes both habits:

  • what you have learned fades out gradually: an exercise rated Good several times comes back less and less often, to check that it holds;
  • what resists comes back soon, a bit slower, until it works;
  • the tempo rises by itself: each Good brings it closer to the tempo you are aiming for, in small steps.

Fifteen minutes a day on the plan beat one hour on Sunday.

#Adding exercises

  1. + Practice plan: adds the exercise, with the tempos set by the lesson. The button becomes ✓ In plan; another click offers to remove it (its history is then lost).
  2. Add to a list: files it in a list in My grooves, without scheduling it.
  3. Print: a sheet with this exercise alone.

At the top of a lesson, Whole lesson to the plan adds all its exercises at once; at the top of a part, + Practice plan adds just that part's exercises. Whatever is already there isn't added twice. Homework given by the teacher during a live class arrives by itself.

#Today's plan

  1. The counters: to practice today, Coming up (scheduled for later), Mastered (no more reminders).
  2. The exercise's tempos: Start tempo, where you started; Current tempo, the one you work at today (the player starts at this tempo); Steady tempo and Target tempo, what you are aiming for (see below). You can change them here.
  3. How was it?: your rating, once you have played the exercise. It sets the next reminder and the next tempo. Under each button, the app shows what will happen ("tomorrow · 70").

Below the counters, the tempos and the exercise stack up in one column; the rating buttons go onto two rows, big enough for your thumb.

A session goes like this: play the top exercise, rate it, move on to the next one. When today's list is empty, you are done.

#What each rating does

Rating Next reminder Tempo next time
Bad tomorrow 10% slower (never below the start tempo)
OK same delay as last time unchanged
Good later: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 30 then 60 days about 5% faster, toward the tempo you aim for
Mastered no more reminders –

As long as the tempo is still rising, reminders stay close together (4 days at most). Once you have held the tempo you aim for for more than a week, the app offers to mark the exercise Mastered.

Tip

Rate honestly: that is what sets the reminders. An over-generous Good raises the tempo too fast and brings the exercise back too late.

To go further than these four buttons (rating tempo, precision, dynamics… separately), see Self-assessment and progress.

#Steady tempo and target tempo

Two tempos say where the exercise is going:

  • the steady tempo is the one to hold easily, without mistakes, for the exercise to count as learned. When you reach it, the app offers Mastered;
  • the target tempo, optional, goes further. If it is set, the working tempo keeps rising toward it with each Good.

They come from the lesson (or the teacher) and can be changed on today's exercise. Without them, the tempo stays at the start tempo: only the delay between reminders changes.

#Managing the list

A plan grows fast: a lesson here, a groove there, homework from your teacher… and one morning fifteen exercises are waiting. Practising five properly beats fifteen half-heartedly. Rather than deleting everything (and losing the history), pause what can wait: the exercise keeps its tempo and ratings, but stays out of today's list until you resume it.

One exercise at a time:

  • ⏸ (at the end of the row, or Pause under today's exercise) pauses it. It moves to the Paused panel at the bottom of the page.
  • ▶ Resume, in that panel, puts it back in the plan: it comes back today.
  • ✕ Remove from plan takes it out for good (its history is lost; pausing keeps it).
  • A mastered exercise comes back with ↺ Resume, for example before a gig.

Several at once, the way you sort your e-mail:

  1. Select, at the top of the page: a box appears in front of each exercise, and every list opens (today, coming up, paused, mastered).
  2. Tick the exercises, or Select all above a list.
  3. The bar at the bottom says how many are chosen and offers Pause, Resume or Remove from plan (with a confirmation).
  4. Done closes the selection.

Tip

Before a busy period, tick everything that isn't a priority and pause it in one go. When you have time again, open Paused, Select all, Resume.

The How it works panel sums up these rules in the app. My progress, in the ⋯ menu at the top of the page, shows what your ratings say over time (see My progress); a paused exercise doesn't count among the weak spots there.

#Homework from the teacher

During a live class, the teacher can give homework. At the end of the class, it arrives by itself in your practice plan, with the tempos the teacher chose, and their message appears under the score.

#Your teacher's sheets

Sometimes your teacher gives you a printed sheet rather than a live class. If it has a QR code at the top right, the QR code icon Scan a QR code (at the top of the practice plan) brings it into the app: its exercises join your practice plan, and the lesson your journal. Scanned twice, nothing is duplicated.

A sheet with boxes under each exercise (days practised, your tempo, your rating) is filled in with a pen during the week. Then My boxes (photo) (the practice plan's ⋯ menu): take a photo of the sheet, nice and flat; the app reads the ticked boxes and puts them in your practice plan, as if you had rated each exercise here. No internet, no artificial intelligence: the two small QR codes at the ends of each line tell where the boxes are, and the ink tells which one is ticked.

  1. The photo, with the boxes read: green, the ticked one; orange, a line to check (two boxes ticked, or only one of the two marks read).
  2. Each exercise's rating, to correct with a click if the reading was wrong; a line that wasn't found is rated here by hand.
  3. Your tempo, if you wrote it on the sheet.
  4. Save my ratings: nothing is recorded before.

#Sending your practice to your teacher

Your teacher doesn't see what you do at home unless you tell them. Send my practice to my teacher (the practice plan's ⋯ menu) gives them, in one go, what you practised and rated since you last sent it: the exercises, the tempo, your rating. They prepare the next lesson with it, and you talk about the same thing. Nothing else is sent: neither your grooves nor your settings.

  1. For: your linked teacher (see Linking your app to your teacher), or Another teacher (they'll recognise you by your name).
  2. Period: since you last sent it (the default), the last 7 or 30 days, or since the beginning.
  3. What is sent: how many rated sessions, for how many exercises.
  4. QR code: show it to your teacher at the lesson; they scan it from your file.
  5. Save the file: a .skreport file to send them by email or message.

Sent twice, nothing is counted twice on their side.

Chapter 8Part III · Practising

Self-assessment and progress

After each exercise in the practice plan, you say how it went. This self-assessment does two jobs: it drives the practice plan (when the exercise comes back, at what tempo), and over time it shows where you are progressing and what is holding you back. This chapter explains the simple rating, the details per criterion, rating a whole series and the My progress dashboard.

At a glance

What forrating right after each exercise, and seeing over time where you are making progress.

Whereafter each exercise of the practice plan; My progress, on the Practice plan page.

Key pointsan overall rating (Bad to Mastered) drives the practice plan; the detail per criterion shows your real weak spot.

In this chapter

  1. The simple rating00
  2. Details per criterion00
  3. Rating a whole series00
  4. My progress00

#The simple rating

Four buttons, once you have played: Bad, OK, Good, Mastered. This is the overall rating: it alone sets the reminders and the tempo for next time (see What each rating does). To rate quickly and fairly, ask yourself just one question: could I play it again right now, at the same tempo, without mistakes?

  • no, far from it: Bad;
  • almost, with a few slips: OK;
  • yes: Good;
  • yes, easily, even at the tempo I am aiming for: Mastered.

If you rate from reading mode, the question comes when you move to the next exercise: see Reading mode.

#Details per criterion

An overall rating says "it works" or "it doesn't", but not why. The details let you rate separately what makes a good performance: tempo, precision, dynamics, endurance… After a few weeks, they show your real weak point: often not the one you think.

  1. The overall rating, as usual. Choosing it is what saves everything.
  2. + Details (tempo, precision…) opens the details; − Hide the details closes them. They are optional: open them only when you have time.
  3. A criterion, rated on three levels: Bad, OK or Good. A criterion left empty is not rated. Mastered does not exist here: it is an overall rating.
  4. The last steady tempo: the fastest tempo you played easily, without mistakes. −5 and +5 adjust it in one click. It is an objective measure of your progress: it feeds the tempo curve in My progress.
  5. Choose the criteria… opens the settings (see below).

The details do not change the reminders: they are saved with the session and feed My progress.

The criteria offered:

Criterion Question to ask yourself
Tempo did I hold the tempo, without rushing or dragging?
Precision do the strokes land exactly, hands and feet together?
Dynamics are accents, ghost notes and normal strokes clearly distinct?
Endurance did I last to the end without tensing up or fading?
Clean repetitions how many times in a row without a mistake?
Coordination, Sound, Relaxation, Reading, By heart to switch on depending on what you are working on

#Choosing your criteria

In Settings › Self-assessment:

  • Open the details per criterion by default: the details are open every time you rate, without going through + Details;
  • Criteria offered: tick the ones to rate. A few well-chosen criteria beat ten: three or four are enough;
  • + Add a criterion creates a criterion of your own (for example "Even rimshots"); ✕ removes it, sessions already rated keep their rating.

#Rating a whole series

After a run-through of 20 exercises, rating each one would be tedious. ★ Rate, in the bar of a run-through's board (Run through in a lesson, Practice in a list), rates them all at once:

  1. Whole series: one rating for everything, played at the tempo shown at the top.
  2. Each exercise follows the series' rating (Same as the series). Change only the ones that differ: another rating, or No rating for an exercise you did not really play.
  3. Exercises not yet in the practice plan are added to it, unless you untick the box.
  4. Save: the button says how many exercises will be rated.

#My progress

My progress (at the top of the Practice plan, or in Settings › Self-assessment) gathers your ratings to answer three questions: am I practising regularly, what is holding me back, and are my tempos going up?

  1. The figures for the period: rated sessions, days played, exercises worked on and average rating, with the change compared with the previous period. Period: 4 weeks, 3 months or 12 months.
  2. Sessions per week, colored by rating: regularity at a glance. An empty week stands out immediately.
  3. By skill: you progress less on an exercise than on a skill. Each criterion's rating counts for its family (rhythm: tempo, precision; sound and dynamics; coordination and body; reading and memory; and your teacher's categories). For each: how your ratings are spread, its level and how it changed, its curve week by week, and the exercises moving it forward (their ratings go up) or stalling (three ratings or more, no progress). An exercise your teacher linked to a skill counts too, through its overall rating.
  4. By criterion: how your ratings are spread for each criterion of the details. The weakest one is marked weak point: that is where your practice will pay off most.

Further down:

  • To work on again: the exercises that get the most Bad and OK ratings. A click takes you there;
  • Exercises in this period: for each one, its sessions, the tempos played and a bar comparing the steady tempo reached with the tempo asked for.

Tip

The weak point tells you what to work on, not what to give up. If it is Dynamics, choose exercises with accents and ghost notes, and slow them down: the difference in volume is easier to control slowly.

Chapter 9Part III · Practising

The metronome

The Metronome page is a complete metronome, for everything that needs no score: practising a rudiment, a song, your timing, or a groove scribbled in two clicks. There is nothing to save: you set it up, you play. Your favorite settings can be kept as presets.

Why a separate metronome, when every exercise already has its own click? Because you also practise without a written exercise: a song on the radio, a fill you are making up, a hand technique. And because it has tools the player does not: automatic speed-up, presets, a sound for the subdivisions, a groove instead of the click, and three training modes (rhythm wheel, rhythm pyramid, polymeter) that work on what a click alone cannot.

At a glance

What forpractising without a score: a rudiment, a song, your timing, or a scribbled groove.

Wherethe Metronome page.

Key pointsset the tempo in the middle of the dial, then ▶. Time signature, sounds, count-in, duration and speed-up are set in the cards below the dial; ⚙ changes the look of the lights, the pendulum and the wheel. Above the dial, choose the mode: Click, Groove, Wheel, Pyramid or Polymeter.
