In a stable version its entries show anyway, with the badge; the first time, the app offers to turn it on (Turn on and continue), and you can turn it off again in Settings › Development › Experimental features (see The settings). Nightly versions always have it.

Import a score… (the ⋯ menu at the top of the study list), or a file dropped onto the app's window: Guitar Pro (.gp3, .gp4, .gp5, .gpx, .gp) or MusicXML (.musicxml, .mxl, .xml).

  • A file with several percussion tracks (a drum kit, a tambourine, a shaker): the app asks which one to import, or All together.
  • The track becomes a study without media: its title and artist, its tempo, its tempo and time signature changes, its sections (the file's markers, their kind guessed from their name: intro, verse, chorus…) and its score, one block per section. Repeats and alternate endings are unfolded in the order they're played; identical bars in a row become one bar ×N.
  • Accents, ghost notes and flams are kept; toms are spread over the app's toms. What the app doesn't play (a shaker, a cowbell) is left out, and the message at the end of the import says so.
  1. The imported study: its title; its Source (in Info) says where the score comes from ("Score imported from…: check the rights before sharing it").
  2. Its sections and blocks, ready to work on: with the visualizer (see A song without video: the visualizer), or with the music, once a source is added.

#Into an existing study

You already have your study, synced to the video, with its sections: only the score is missing, and it exists in Guitar Pro. Import a score into this study… (the study's ⋯ menu) lays it on your bars. A score and a video don't always match (a longer intro, an extra repeat, a bar of silence): you say where its bars land, with one or more sync points.

  1. Bar of the score: a bar of the file (next to it, its section).
  2. Bar of the study: where it lands in your study (next to it, your section). From one point to the next, bars follow each other; what would run over the next point is left out.
  3. + A sync point where the score and the song stop matching; Match the sections suggests one point per section of the same kind, in order (intro on intro, chorus on chorus): that's what's suggested on opening, when both have sections.
  4. The result, live: where the score lands, how many bars are left out, how many bars already written will be replaced.
  5. What you take: the score (it replaces yours on these bars only, the rest doesn't move), the file's sections, and for a study without media, the tempo and time signatures. Undo (Ctrl+Z) undoes the import in one go.

Lyrics and subtitles (.srt, .vtt, .lrc, .txt, YouTube subtitles…) are imported in the Lyrics tab (see Lyrics).

#To another program

The other way round, the study's ⋯ menu writes its score (the version shown) with its sections, tempos and time signatures; bars without a score become rests.

  1. Export the score to Guitar Pro (.gp), to MusicXML or to MIDI.
  2. Experimental: the badge of features still being tried out.

MusicXML opens in most notation programs (MuseScore, Sibelius, Finale, Dorico): it's the safest. Guitar Pro is written in the Guitar Pro 7 and 8 format; if it opens badly somewhere, let us know. MIDI (General MIDI drums, channel 10) goes into a DAW (Reaper, Cubase, GarageBand), to play it with your own sounds. A groove exports the same way (see To another program).

On Android, exporting to Guitar Pro and MIDI isn't possible yet (the app says so); MusicXML works.

Warning

A score found online belongs to its author. The study keeps its source: check the rights before sharing or exporting it.

#Exporting a video

A study that works deserves to be shown: to a student, a band, on social media. The export records the video (or the visualizer) with the notes on top, or the notes alone on a green background, to key in an editing program over a filmed video.

⋯ › Export a video…, or a song on the Video page of the menu (it lists the studies and the note themes):

  1. Picture: Video + notes (or Visualizer + notes for a song without video), Notes only on green (for keying), or the video (the visualizer) alone. The notes have the look of the chosen theme.
  2. On top: the notes' title, the synced lyrics, the whole song; each turns on or off with a click.
  3. Sound: the song and the score's drums, the song alone, the drums alone, or no sound.
  4. Passage: the whole song, the section playing, or the In–Out zone; then the size, 1080p or 720p.

The picture always comes from the study's file, even when the online video plays on screen (see Change the source, in Creating a study). The export plays the passage in its own player and records it in real time: the window says what is going on (preparing, reading the file, recording, writing the file), shows the recorded picture, the time elapsed and what is left. If playback doesn't start (the browser waits for a gesture), Start playback starts it again; Keep up to here stops and keeps what is already recorded; Stop keeps nothing. Keep the window visible until the end. At the end, the app asks where to save the file (WebM). ⋯ › Quick export does it again with the same settings, on the In–Out zone, otherwise the section playing.

Without a file (a YouTube, Vimeo or SoundCloud video), the export gives the notes alone on green: an online video cannot be recorded (neither technically, nor by the site's terms). It says at which point of the video the notes start: place them there in your editing program, over the video. With the score's drums, or no sound.

Note

On Android, export will come later.

To film your drums while the song plays, from several angles, then edit the video: Film and edit (Capture). The videos the app writes (the mirror, the export, Capture) end up in My videos.

#Three layouts on trial

Where to put the video and the score? Three answers are on trial, in Settings › Development › Song study: layout:

  • Stacked (default): the video, the lanes and the controls, then the score below;
  • Side by side: the video and the controls on the left, the score on the right;
  • Score on the video: the section's score laid at the bottom of the video (without a video, the study stays stacked). For just a few bars, prefer Display › Notes on the video.

Tell us which one you prefer: the others will go.

Chapter 12Part IV · Songs and video

The mirror

Your teacher sees what you can't feel: the seat too low, the back rounding, the shoulders creeping up, a bent wrist. On your own, a mirror helps; a camera does better: it shows you from several angles, and delayed, so you can watch once the sticks are down. The Mirror page (Video category) does just that. Nothing is recorded without you: the pictures stay in memory for a few seconds and vanish when you leave the page; Record keeps them, only if you ask.

In this chapter

  1. The mirror page00
  2. A phone as a camera00
  3. Watching yourself on delay00
  4. Freezing the picture and keeping it00
  5. Drawing guides00
  6. Recording00
  7. When your teacher gives you a camera00

What is there to watch? Your posture: the height of the seat, the back, the shoulders. Your hands: the wrists, the height of the sticks. Your foot: the leg, the heel on the pedal. So many things you don't feel while playing, and that the score doesn't tell you. And since you can't play and watch yourself at the same time, the mirror knows how to wait: the Delay shows you what you have just played, a few seconds later. You play first, then you watch yourself.

This chapter presents the mirror page, then each function: adding a phone as a camera (a second angle, from the side or behind you), watching yourself on delay, freezing the picture and keeping a passage, drawing guides, recording for real, and what happens when your teacher gives you a camera during a class. The recordings end up in My videos. To film a cover with the song, from several angles, that is the job of Capture.

#The mirror page

  1. Turn on the camera: this device's (the webcam, the tablet's camera). Another camera adds one (a second webcam); A phone as a camera… adds a phone (see A phone as a camera).
  2. Delay: Live, or the picture from 3, 5, 10 or 20 seconds ago.
  3. Guides: lines on the picture (the middle, the thirds) to judge a straight back, level shoulders.
  4. Freeze stops all views at the same moment; Keep as a video… turns it into a video; Resume goes back to live.
  5. Each view: ⇋ Mirror flips it like a mirror (on by default for the camera facing you), Other camera (a phone: front or back), ✕ removes it. A double-click puts it full screen, to see it from the kit.
  6. A line you drew, with its angle.

The first time, the device asks for permission to use the camera; once granted, it turns on by itself at each visit. If it is refused, the app says so and asks you to check the app's permission; if the device gives no access to a camera, the page says so.

#A phone as a camera

Why a phone: the computer's webcam sees you from the front, whereas the back and the arms are better judged from the side, and the shoulders from behind. A phone placed there gives you that angle, without a cable. This function is experimental (the small orange triangle ▲ on the button): in a stable version, the first click turns on the app's experimental functions (see Settings, sounds and data).

A phone as a camera… opens the mirror's room: on a phone (or another computer and its webcam) with the app, Become a camera (Video category) finds it by itself, or scan its QR code; the device becomes one more view, placed beside or behind you (same Wi-Fi; the picture goes straight from one device to the other, not through the internet).

On the phone, the Become a camera page lists the mirror it finds; Become its camera, and it's connected, without scanning anything. By scanning the code, the phone first asks you to confirm which mirror it will film for; Send the picture confirms.

On the phone, the camera page shows what it sends and says so (“Picture sent to …”): put it down, screen on, and play.

On this page, the phone keeps few controls: Other camera (the front or the back one) and Stop. The mirror can also ask for the other camera, with the view's Other camera button. A computer with several webcams chooses from a list the one that sends its picture. If the mirror closes, the phone says so.

In a browser (the .html file), the mirror does not go through the local network: it only receives the picture of another tab of the same browser, to try (a demonstration link is offered under the code). For real phones, use the Windows or Android app.

#Watching yourself on delay

Play a passage, then watch yourself play it back, without stopping.

The picture shown is the one from 3, 5, 10 or 20 seconds ago: play, let the delay pass, and you see yourself playing. The delay applies to all the views at the same time. For that, the app keeps the last 30 seconds of each view, in memory only (never on disk, never sent elsewhere) and in reduced pictures; they disappear when you leave the page. The delay setting is kept from one time to the next.

#Freezing the picture and keeping it

A posture fault is easier to see when still: by freezing the picture, you go back over what just happened, all the views together.

Freeze stops all views at the same moment; the slider then steps through the last 30 seconds, all views together. Keep as a video… turns those seconds into a video (the views side by side), saved where you want: only if you ask. Resume goes back to live.

Keep as a video… is only active once the picture is frozen. It makes a small video, without sound: 12 frames per second, each view in a 640 × 360 pixel cell, flipped as on screen, the cells in a grid of two columns. It is MP4 if the device can write it, otherwise WebM. In the desktop app, a window asks where to save the file; in a browser, it goes to Downloads. For a full-quality video, with sound, use Record (below).

On Android, Keep as a video… does not record yet: the app says so (“Video export comes later on Android.”).

#Drawing guides

A back that is “nearly straight”, a thigh “nearly horizontal”: by eye, you get it wrong. A line drawn once on the right posture gives you a reference, and its angle shows to put a number on the gap.

With the guides on, drag on a view to draw your own line (back, thigh, forearm): its angle shows (↕ from vertical, ↔ from horizontal), and it stays from one session to the next. Shift while drawing locks the angle at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° or 90° (by finger, the line snaps to these angles). A click on a line selects it: drag it to move it, drag one of its ends to redo it, Remove (or Delete) takes it away. Undo (Ctrl+Z) goes back one gesture at a time: one bad line doesn't mean starting over. Clear the lines removes them all.

The Guides switch must be on to draw. A view keeps twelve lines at most: beyond that, the oldest is erased.

#Recording

To show a passage to your teacher, or to compare your posture from one week to the next, you need a real video, in full quality and with sound: that is what Record does, whereas Keep as a video… only keeps the last seconds, small.

● Record films for real: each view (and the microphone's sound, set for drums: without the filters made for voice) becomes a video, written as it comes into the videos folder, under Miroir (in the desktop app; see My videos; in a browser, the folder you choose, once per launch), as long as you like, keeping nothing in memory. ■ Stop finishes the files. In a browser that doesn't give a folder, the videos are saved when you stop. A view added during the recording waits for the next one.

Each view gives a separate file, named after the time and the view's name; the microphone's sound goes with the first. The format is MP4 (H.264) if the device can write it, otherwise WebM. When you stop, the app says how many videos are recorded and where. To find them, play them or rename them: My videos.

On Android, the Record button does not appear yet: writing the videos as they come is not ready there.

#When your teacher gives you a camera

During a live class, your teacher can give you one of their cameras (the video feedback, see During the class). See myself then appears in the class bar and opens the mirror with that picture, as one view more: it has everything the other views can do (the delay, Freeze, the guides), and you can add your own camera to it. It is live feedback, not a recording.

Chapter 13Part IV · Songs and video

Film and edit (Capture)

This chapter is for you if you want to publish a drum cover: the song plays, several cameras film you, and you get an edited video, or a folder ready for an editing program. The common thread: the song serves as a shared clock for all the cameras, so nothing has to be lined up by hand.

In this chapter

  1. The idea: filming with the phones you have00
  2. From the menu: Film and edit00
  3. Filming: the master window and its cameras00
  4. The take that arrived, and its angle00
  5. An iPhone or iPad, without the app00
  6. A GoPro over Bluetooth00
  7. Sync sounds00
  8. Importing other cameras and the DAW sound00
  9. The montage00
  10. Framing: position and zoom00
  11. Keyframes: a zoom that moves00
  12. The preview: originals, 1/2, 1/400
  13. Exporting the mix00
  14. Finishing in DaVinci Resolve00
  15. The project and its sources00

In order, you will find: the idea and the Film and edit page, the Capture window for filming, how a take comes back lined up with the song, the cameras that don't have the app (an iPhone, a GoPro, a DAW: the software where you record and mix the drums), the sync sounds and the import that line them up all the same, then the editing, framing, preview, export and finishing in DaVinci Resolve. To watch yourself play without making a cover, the mirror is enough; the videos you produce end up in My videos.

#The idea: filming with the phones you have

A drum video is better watched from several angles: the feet, the snare, the hi-hat, the face. Usually it takes several cameras, then lining up each take by hand in an editing program. Capture uses the phones you have: each one films while the song plays, and each take comes back lined up with the song. It becomes an angle of the study, which follows playback.

Note

Capture is experimental (Pro): turn it on in Settings › Development, or accept when the app offers it. An app camera is StoneKiller on a phone: a browser refuses the camera to a page on the local network, except Safari on the desktop app's secure page (an iPhone: see An iPhone or iPad, without the app). Other cameras (a GoPro, a camera) and your DAW deliver their files, which you import. The videos stay on the device: they go neither into a study file nor into a backup (the project takes them along when you want).

#From the menu: Film and edit

Filming a cover and editing it is a journey of its own, a creative one: the Film and edit page (Video category, Pro and Experimental badges) leads straight there, with two shortcuts, Film and Edit a video.

  1. The menu entry.
  2. The four steps: film (the cameras start together, on the song), import the other cameras and the DAW sound, edit, prepare for DaVinci Resolve.
  3. Your studies, the ones already filmed first, with their takes and cameras: Film, Import files and Edit open the study with the right window. Capture, the import and the montage live in the study: the song is the common time of all the cameras.

Just film, at the top of the page: an exercise, an improvisation or a lesson can be filmed without a song too. Film without a song creates a filmed session (a study without music, named after its date) and opens Capture: the cameras start together as with a song, the session lasts as long as the takes you keep, and you find it in Songs to import other cameras, edit it and prepare it for DaVinci.

#Filming: the master window and its cameras

⋯ › Capture… opens the window of the master, the app that plays the song:

  1. Add a camera and its QR code. On each phone (or computer) with the app, on the same Wi-Fi: Become a camera (Video category). The master's session shows up there by itself; Become its camera, and it's linked, nothing to scan. Otherwise (a browser, another network), scan the code: Scan its QR code on the same page, or Scan a QR code. The code carries the master's address and a session secret.
  2. The cameras that joined: what they film (a thumbnail), their state, their battery and their free space.
  3. Record all: a countdown, then all the cameras start at the same moment, the start sync sound plays and the song starts. Stop ends the take: the song stops, the end sync sound plays, then the cameras stop a moment later.

Webcam adds a webcam of this device (a laptop's, a USB webcam): it films in the window itself, along with the phones, and its take syncs the same way; if there are several, the app asks which one, and ✕ on its card removes it. Why: one more camera without a phone to set up, for example facing the kit from the computer.

Another computer and its webcam become a camera just like a phone: the app on that computer, same Wi-Fi, Become a camera. If it has several webcams, the Webcam list on its camera page picks which one films. The principle is always the same: one master (the one that records and starts the takes) and cameras that send their picture and follow the master; they have nothing to set up.

Framing has each phone send four frames per second, in big: you set the framing of every camera without running from one to the other (during a take, one frame every two seconds, to spare the Wi-Fi).

On the phone, the camera page shows big what it films, and what matters when you set it down: who it films for, the state in one word (ready, countdown, filming), the time filmed. Before the take: the front or back camera, 720p or 1080p. Each phone keeps its video second by second, then sends it to the master in pieces, over its own connection: a dropout loses nothing, sending picks up where it stopped.

#The take that arrived, and its angle

A take that arrived is lined up with the song: by the sync sounds the phone heard (to the millisecond), otherwise by the clocks (each camera set its own to the master's) then by the sound, comparing the attacks heard by the phone's microphone with those of the song; the drift of a long take is corrected. Without usable sound, the clock alignment stays. Keep (1) makes it an angle of the study, and the camera deletes its copy; Discard deletes it.

Under the video, the angle (1) picks the song or a filmed take: it follows playback (pause, loops, jumps) without drifting. ⋯ › Filmed angles… renames or removes them (the video is deleted from the device).

#An iPhone or iPad, without the app

The iPhone doesn't have the app (no App Store for it); its camera still works in Safari, on one condition: a secure page (HTTPS). The desktop app serves one, on the local network, with its own certificate (made on the computer; no authority on the internet). In the Capture window, under the QR code, An iPhone or iPad (without the app):

  1. Once: the certificate. Scan the first code with the iPhone's Camera app, open in Safari and allow the profile. Then Settings › General › VPN & Device Management: install; and Settings › General › About › Certificate Trust Settings: turn on “StoneKiller (local)”. The iPhone then trusts this computer, even when its address changes.
  2. Each session: the camera. Scan the second code, open in Safari, allow the camera: the iPhone shows up among the cameras and films like a phone with the app (MP4 H.264, which Resolve reads as is). Keep the screen on and Safari in front.

#A GoPro over Bluetooth

In the desktop app, Add a GoPro links a GoPro (HERO9 and later) over Bluetooth: it starts and stops with the other cameras, takes the computer's clock (its files carry the right date) and a HiLight at the start of each take (visible in Quik), and its card shows its battery, the minutes left on the card and whether it's recording. Pair it once in the system (Windows: Settings › Bluetooth, the GoPro in pairing mode: Preferences › Connections › Connect Device). The Bluetooth shutter jitters by a few hundred milliseconds: the sync still comes from the sync sounds, and its files come in through the import (the card, the cable). A GoPro that stops answering says so on its card; the take goes on without it. On Android, the GoPro is still started by hand.

#Sync sounds

A camera the app doesn't start, and the DAW recording the drums (Cubase, Reaper…), don't have the master's clock. To sync them anyway, the master plays two sync sounds through its speaker: a rising sweep just before the song, a falling sweep just after you stop. Everything recording in the room hears them at the same moment; found in a file, they tell where it sits in the take, to the millisecond, and how much its clock drifts between start and end.

The Sync sounds switch in the Capture window sets them (they're on by default). With them, Record all works even without a phone camera: GoPros started by hand and the DAW are enough. Each take is kept with the study (the time of its sync sounds, what the song was playing): its files sync later, on import.

Tip

The sync sounds must be heard where you record. With headphones, the song and the sync sounds stay in the headphones: keep the device's output on the speaker during the countdown, or also route it into a DAW input (a separate track, muted in the mix).

#Importing other cameras and the DAW sound

⋯ › Import files… (or Import files in the Capture window) takes the videos of a camera started by hand (a GoPro, a camera, a phone's camera app) and your DAW's sound (a WAV):

  1. One camera per row: a GoPro's chapters (GH01…, GH02…) go together, end to end; give it any name you like.
  2. How it synced: by the start and end sync sounds of a take (its clock drift is corrected), by a single sync sound, or, without any, by the song's sound searched across the whole file; then pick the take (usually the other files' one). A camera that kept rolling through several takes gives one row per take.
  3. Keep: a video becomes an angle of the study, a sound becomes a possible sound for the montage.

A large file's sound is read in pieces, without loading the whole file (a GoPro video of several GB): the sound of an MP4 or a MOV (AAC, PCM, MP3), a WAV. Files stay where they are, like a study's media: the study keeps a link to them.

#The montage

A simple edit, inside the study: choose which camera shows at each moment, with fades. The split of roles is deliberate: StoneKiller does what an editing program can't do on its own (filming with several cameras, syncing each one to the song to the millisecond, laying the score and the lyrics on top) plus the first edit; effects, colour grading and titles happen in DaVinci Resolve, which is free and gets everything ready-made (see Finishing in DaVinci Resolve). ⋯ › Montage opens it:

  1. The montage bar: the take being edited (if there are several), the sound of the montage (the song, the DAW sound, or a camera's: the study's song is muted), Export the mix, Prepare for DaVinci…, Project…, Finish the montage.
  2. V1 · program: the clips, each one shows a camera (in its colour). V2 · overlay puts a clip on top, at its opacity.
  3. One track per camera, where it filmed (its files); a click on it makes the V1 clip at that moment show this camera. Below, the sound imported from the DAW.

The gestures are DaVinci Resolve's:

Gesture What it does
1 to 9 while playing cut at the playhead and show that camera (Resolve's multicam)
1 to 9 when stopped the clip under the playhead shows that camera
Shift+1 to 9 a clip of that camera on top (V2), half transparent
Ctrl+B cut the clip under the playhead (the blade)
drag an edge, the junction trim a clip, roll the cut between two clips
the handle at the top of an edge at a cut: a cross dissolve centred on the cut; elsewhere: a fade from or to black (V1), transparency (V2)
double-click a clip its camera, its opacity, its fades, its framing, its keyframes
K a keyframe on the selected clip, at the playhead (K again at the same moment: remove it)
Del remove the chosen clip (a gap in V1 shows the study's video)

On top of the montage, the study keeps what it shows: the notes, the lyrics, the cues.

#Framing: position and zoom

A wide view of the kit already holds close-ups: the snare, the hi-hat, the feet. Like DaVinci Resolve's inspector (Transform), each clip has its framing: a zoom and a position, starting from its camera's.

  1. Zoom, Position X, Position Y (in %, the position as a share of the picture's height). Faster: pick the clip on the track, then drag the picture in the player to move it, wheel or pinch to zoom (a coloured frame shows the picture can be moved).
  2. Camera's framing: the clip goes back to its camera's.
  3. For the whole camera: this framing becomes the camera's (a double-click on a camera's track sets it too), for all its clips that don't have their own.

The framing shows in the player, goes into the mix export and into the timeline for Resolve (adjust-transform, to open with Use Sizing Information). A clip's framing can also change during the clip: see keyframes, just below.

#Keyframes: a zoom that moves

Why: a clip that slowly tightens on the snare during a fill, or an overlay that appears then fades away, brings movement to a cover filmed with fixed cameras. Like the keyframes in Resolve's inspector, you set the framing and the opacity at two moments; in between, the picture glides from one to the other.

  1. The framing (and the opacity, above) at the playhead. With keyframes, what you set here, or on the picture in the player, goes into the keyframe under the playhead (one is added if needed).
  2. A keyframe: its time, zoom, position and opacity; on the montage track, a diamond shows it in the clip.
  3. Smooth: the move to the next keyframe starts and arrives gently (otherwise: at a constant speed).
  4. Go: the playhead goes to this keyframe, and the settings show it. ✕ removes it.
  5. ◆ Keyframe at …: adds one at the playhead, with the settings above. Faster: select the clip, place the playhead and press K (K again at the same moment removes it).

Cutting a clip keeps the movement on both sides; an overlay clip you move takes its keyframes along; switching a clip's camera removes them (they framed the other picture). Keyframes show in the player, go into the mix export and into the timeline for Resolve (as keyframeAnimation: position, zoom, opacity).

#The preview: originals, 1/2, 1/4

Why: four 4K cameras means a lot of pictures to decode at once; a laptop or a tablet can't always keep up, and playback stutters. Like Resolve's "Timeline Proxy Resolution", Preview in the montage bar plays proxies: a light copy of each video, at half or a quarter of its height.

  • Preview: 1/2 or 1/4: the proxies are made once, in the background (the bar shows how far along they are); meanwhile the original plays, then the proxy takes its place without stopping anything. They stay on the device for next time.
  • Preview: originals: the videos as they are.
  • Clear the proxies (at the bottom of the list, with the space they take): they are made again when needed.

The mix export and the folder for Resolve always use the originals: the preview only changes what you see while editing.

#Exporting the mix

Export the mix opens the study's video export: the picture comes from the montage (its cuts, its fades, the overlay), the sound is the montage's, the notes and lyrics go on top as usual. It's the finished video in one step, to share as it is.

#Finishing in DaVinci Resolve

Why Resolve: it's a professional editor (films and series are cut on it), and its free version is enough for everything that follows: effects, colour grading, titles, fine cuts, export for YouTube. Rebuilding those tools in StoneKiller would give a weaker version of what already exists; instead, StoneKiller does what Resolve doesn't do on its own, syncing each camera to the song, and prepares the ground so there's nothing to set up.

Prepare for DaVinci…:

  1. What the folder holds:
    • the videos and the sound: the cameras' files as they are; the takes filmed by the app converted to MP4 on the way (Resolve doesn't read the browser's recording format): video as H.264 at a constant frame rate, sound as AAC (or PCM, in a .mov), at the same timestamps;
    • the timeline (.fcpxml), in your cameras' format: V1 with its cuts and cross dissolves, V2 at its opacity, each whole camera synced on its own track (disabled: take another shot from it), the montage's sound, the song, and the study's sections as markers;
    • the lyrics (.srt), one subtitle per timed line; the study (.sksong): the folder is also the project, it reopens in StoneKiller (see The project and its sources); a how-to (Read me.txt).
  2. Then, in Resolve: File › Import › Timeline…, then the folder's .fcpxml: everything is in place, to the frame. The lyrics: import the .srt into the Media Pool and drag it to the start of the timeline (a subtitle track, to style in Resolve). The notes: Export the notes (green background)… renders a Notes only video; put it on the top track and key out the green (3D Keyer effect).
  3. Prepare the folder… chooses the folder, converts and copies (the window shows how far it's got); The .fcpxml only saves just the timeline.

In the desktop app, the timeline knows each file's path: nothing to relink. Chrome and Edge prepare the folder too, but don't say where it is: Resolve shows the videos as offline, and Relink media then the folder finds them. Firefox and Safari don't give a folder: the .fcpxml only.

Note

To the frame: a camera's clock drift over a long clip (a few milliseconds), which the app corrects, isn't corrected in Resolve. V2's fades don't carry over (its opacity does).

#The project and its sources

Project… › Save the project… (or the folder prepared for DaVinci, which is one too) chooses a folder and puts the whole montage in it: a copy of each file (the song, the camera videos, the DAW sound) and the whole study (a .sksong with its angles, takes and montage). Keep it, copy it to another computer. To reopen it: import the folder's .sksong, open the study, then Montage › Project… › Relink files… and choose the folder: each file is found by its name (and its fingerprint). In the desktop app, Chrome and Edge; elsewhere, the app can't write to a folder.

Chapter 14Part IV · Songs and video

My videos

The videos the app writes used to be scattered: one folder for the mirror, another for an export. My videos (Video category, in the Windows and Android app) gathers them: the mirror's recordings, exported videos and Capture takes, grouped by folder, newest first.

In this chapter

  1. What the page shows00
  2. The videos folder00
  3. Play, rename, delete00

Every video feature of StoneKiller writes files: the mirror when you record yourself, the export when you make a video of a study, Capture when you film with several cameras. Without a common place, you look for your videos in three folders. This page shows them together, with what you need to play them, rename them, find them in their folder or delete them, without leaving the app. This chapter says what the page shows, where the files are, and what you can do with a video. The features that write to it: the mirror, the video export and Capture.

#What the page shows

The files are sorted into groups: Capture takes, one group per takes folder; Exported videos and others, what sits at the root of the videos folder; and one group per subfolder, such as Mirror for the mirror's recordings. Each group says how much room it takes, and at the top of the list the app gives the number of files and the total size. Each row shows the thumbnail, the name, the date and the size.

At the top, Editing projects: the studies filmed with Capture (Pro, experimental), with their takes, cameras and edit; Open leads to the song, on the edit when it has videos, otherwise on Capture.

In a browser, the page only shows the editing projects: a browser has no access to the computer's folders, and the page says so.

#The videos folder

The videos folder: Videos › StoneKiller on a computer (the ⋯ menu chooses another one, or goes back to it), the app's own folder on Android. The mirror records into it, under Miroir, without asking for a folder again; the save box of a video export opens there.

Open the folder opens the videos folder in the file explorer. Back in the app, the list reloads.

On Android, the folder is the app's own: it cannot be changed, and the page does not open the file manager (no Open the folder, nor Show in folder).

#Play, rename, delete

A video's thumbnail (a frame near the first second) plays it in the app; a sound file only shows its icon. A video's ⋯ menu renames it, shows it in its folder (the file explorer opens with the video selected) or deletes it (after confirmation: the file is erased from the disk).

A click on the thumbnail opens the video in a window, with its playback controls. Rename… asks for the new name, without the file's extension; if a file already has that name, the app says so (“This name is already taken.”).

Chapter 15Part V · Creating

The workshop

The Workshop is where you build your own exercises: a groove heard in a song, a variation of a lesson exercise, a whole series of coordination exercises, or what you have just played on your kit. What you create then goes wherever you want: a lesson, My grooves, the practice plan, a printed sheet.

At a glance

What forbuilding your own exercises: a groove, a variant, a series of coordination exercises, what you play.

Wherethe Workshop page.

Key pointsone tool per need (see the table below); they all use the grid editor, and what you create goes into a lesson or My grooves.

In this chapter

  1. Which tool?00
  2. Groove editor: writing in the grid00
  3. Pro workshop: composing from all the grooves00
  4. Ostinato and Combinations: making series00
  5. Record: you play, the app writes00

#Which tool?

You want to… Tool
write a groove note by note Groove editor
assemble a groove from pieces of other grooves the Pro workshop and its building blocks
a series of independence exercises (varied hands over fixed feet) Ostinato and Combinations
write down what you play on your kit Record
cross-rhythms (3 against 2…) Polyrhythms and polymeters
  1. The tools: Groove editor, Ostinato, Combinations and Record. The building blocks are in the pro workshop.
  2. Each tool moves forward in numbered steps, from top to bottom.

#Groove editor: writing in the grid

The Groove editor is the simplest tool: an empty grid (or a starting exercise) and the full editor. You place the notes, you hear them, the score is written under the grid. Everything the grid does (brushes, subdivisions per beat, repeats, selection, text notation) is explained in The grid editor.

At the top, a single bar, like a document's: the groove's name, Grid / Text, ⋯ and the main button: ★ Save…, or Save and close when you edit a groove that is already saved. The rest waits in ⋯: the other ways to save, New, Description…, Start from an exercise…, ⊞ Pro workshop, the text syntax and Cancel.

What the Groove editor adds to the editor:

  • Start from an exercise or chain several (in ⋯): loads an existing exercise as a starting point, or puts several exercises end to end.
  • New (in ⋯) starts again from an empty grid.
  • Description… adds a description to the groove: it is shown with it in your lists and lessons.
  • Your work in progress is kept automatically: it comes back when you reopen the Groove editor, even after closing the app.

#Saving your groove

★ Save… opens the Save as window: give it a name, then choose where: My grooves (and a list, or + New list…) or A lesson (one of your lessons and its part, or + New lesson… / + New part…). The last place chosen is offered next time. After that, Save changes updates the groove, and Save as… (in ⋯) makes a copy elsewhere.

When you edit an existing groove (or a variation), you finish as in a window: Save and close goes back to the previous page; ⋯ › Cancel forgets the changes (after confirmation). Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Shift+S opens Save as.

#Pro workshop: composing from all the grooves

The pro workshop is a large working window for composing with precise excerpts: you choose a model groove, take exactly the piece you are interested in (one beat, the snare part alone), and place it in your composition. ⊞ Pro workshop, in the ⋯ menu of the Groove editor, opens it.

The window has two columns: on the left, what you need to find a groove; on the right, the work, from top to bottom: the model, the tray, the composition. Each setting sits next to what it affects.

  1. Search all grooves: by name, lesson, sticking (rlrr finds the grooves containing this sticking) or time signature (6/8).
  2. Three ways to browse: Tree (themes › lessons › parts › exercises), List (with a preview of each groove) and Blocks (see Building blocks).
  3. The model: the chosen groove, in large. Open ↗ goes to the original; ▶ Listen, or ⟳ Loop the selection.
  4. Take a piece from the model's score: a click takes the beat touched, a double-click the whole bar, drag for a range, Shift+click extends.
  5. The piece bar: its size and sticking; its instruments, one click removes one (for example to take only the snare); then Copy (C), Place (Enter), To tray (B), or ⠿ Drag onto the composition. Also in ×N lists the other grooves that contain the same piece: choosing one opens it as the model.
  6. The tray keeps pieces for later. ▾ folds the model and the tray to make room for the composition.
  7. The composition: your grid, with all its tools, and its score, where a click chooses where to place. Place as: Overlay keeps what the other instruments play at that spot, Replace clears it first.

If the piece and what is already there need two different grids (sextuplets over sixteenths), the app asks what to do: keep both (finer grid), replace, or cancel.

Shortcuts: Space plays the composition, Shift+Space the model, / goes to the search, Esc deselects then closes. Closing the window loses nothing; ★ Save… is also at the top of the window.

On a narrow screen (900 pixels or less), the window takes the whole screen and the three areas become tabs: Search, Model, Composition. Touch a group of notes, then Place or To tray.

The left panel (Tree, List, Blocks) widens by dragging its right edge (double-click: its default width) and folds against the edge with ‹; a thin strip opens it again. Its list scrolls on its own, under its tabs.

#Building blocks

Many grooves look alike: the same snare beat, the same bass drum figure. The Blocks tab of the pro workshop cuts every groove in the app (exercises, variations, your grooves) into pieces of one beat, two beats or one bar, ready to drag into your composition. It is a quick way to explore: "what if I put this bass drum under my hi-hat?".

  1. The size: 1 beat, 2 beats or 1 bar.
  2. Filter by subdivision (eighths, sixteenths, triplets…), or by the name of the source groove.
  3. A block: a click plays it. ×N says how many grooves it appears in; ✓ marks the ones already in your groove.
  4. Drag a block onto a beat in the grid: it lands there. +, a double-click or Enter places it next. With a finger: long press, then drag. The grid adapts by itself (triplets in a sixteenth grid) and grows if needed.

Then the whole editor is at hand: shift, change instrument, undo…

#Ostinato and Combinations: making series

Independence (the hands do one thing, the feet another) is practised with series: a fixed part that keeps turning (the ostinato, for example bass drum and hi-hat foot), and on top, every possible combination of a few small figures. Writing these dozens of exercises by hand would take ages; these two tools generate them, from the simplest to the hardest.

The vocabulary: a cell is a small one-beat figure, named by a letter (A, B, C…). A combination is written with these letters: ABAB plays A, B, A, B, one cell per beat. Ostinato places the combinations over a fixed part; Combinations starts from a kit of cells, with no fixed part at first. Five steps:

  1. Cells (the building blocks): a kit of cells (sixteenths, triplets, flams…), cells generated on one beat, or your own patterns. The generator produces every way of placing notes in one beat: in sixteenths, the rest first, then 1, e, &, a, then 1 e, e &… up to 1 e & a. Tick the ones to combine, or a whole group at once (1 note, 2 notes…).
  2. Fixed part (ostinato): what does not change, for example the feet or the hi-hat; six models are offered. ▶ Listen to the ostinato plays it alone.
  3. Combinations: Compose (click the letters), Text (type ACAC, BABA…) or Generate: from the simplest to the finest, first a single cell over the whole bar (AAAA), then by half bars (AABB), then beat by beat (AAAB). Settings: Length, Changes, Different cells, Filters ("never the same letter twice in a row"…) and Order. The list stops at 300 combinations: tick fewer cells or add a filter.
  4. Instruments (collapsible): replace one instrument with another (snare → bell…).
  5. Result: a grid of mini-scores to listen to, save, add to a lesson or practise as a run-through. ☑ Pick and arrange… keeps only some exercises, in the order you choose, then saves them in a new list or adds them to the lesson.

Tip

To work on a generated series, use Practice: each combination plays 4 times, then the next, without touching the app. Start with 1 note per cell, at a slow tempo: combinations with 2 or 3 notes will come later.

#Record: you play, the app writes

You found a groove while playing, or you want to check that you play what is written? Record listens to your kit (electronic, microphone or pad) and writes the score: ghost notes, accents, placement in time.

  1. The source: Electronic kit (MIDI), MIDI file, Audio (mic, interface) or Practice pad.
  2. Play along with: the click alone, or a chosen groove as accompaniment.
  3. My takes: the last 40 takes, kept on the device. Open transcribes one again; ✕ deletes it.

Step by step:

  1. Choose the source and the length of the groove (in bars).
  2. Record: one bar of count-in, then play the same groove 4 to 8 times in a row. Stop when you are done.
  3. The app keeps what comes back on each pass and writes the score.
  4. Correct it in the grid if needed. Your corrections stay when you change the settings (threshold, tempo ×2 or ÷2, shifting the "1").
  5. Give it a name, then ★ Save….

When you Play along with a groove, the result is compared with it: "18/20 notes of the groove (90%) · 2 missed · 1 extra", and the score colors what differs. It is a real reading check: on every exercise, ● Record yourself opens Record directly with this exercise as the model.

Tip

In audio, Calibrate my kit… (a few hits on each piece) greatly improves recognition, and Measure latency realigns the timing. On the pad, Calibrate my dynamics… learns your ghost notes, normal strokes and accents in 15 seconds.

Note

MIDI works in the Windows app and in Chrome, Edge or Firefox, not in the Android app or in Safari. MIDI and the microphone are also missing on the page opened by a class QR code.

Chapter 16Part V · Creating

Polyrhythms and polymeters

Polyrhythms and polymeters layer two ways of dividing time. They give the "rolling" feel of African music, jazz, progressive rock and many modern fills. They are hard because the brain wants to merge the two voices into one. StoneKiller shows them (a strip and a circle synchronized with playback), lets you hear them voice by voice, and offers a method to get them in place.

At a glance

What forunderstanding, hearing and playing cross-rhythms (3 against 2, 5 against 4…) and figures that slide over the bar.

Wherethe Polyrhythms, Polymeters and Learning path pages.

Key pointslook at the strip and the circle, listen to each voice alone, then play them together, slowly; the Learning path gives the order.

In this chapter

  1. Two notions not to confuse00
  2. Polyrhythms00
  3. Polymeters00
  4. The learning path00
  5. Keeping a polyrhythm00

#Two notions not to confuse

  • A polyrhythm layers two regular pulses over the same duration. In 3 against 2 (written 3:2), one voice plays 3 even strokes while the other plays 2. Both voices start together again at each cycle.
  • A polymeter repeats a figure whose length does not fit the bar. A figure of 3 sixteenth notes played over a bar of 16 starts at a different place each time, and only lands back on the "1" after 3 bars. The pulse itself does not change.

In short: a polyrhythm changes the speed of one voice relative to the other; a polymeter keeps the same speed but shifts the figure on each turn.

#Polyrhythms

The Polyrhythms page is an explorer: you choose the voices, the app plays them, draws them and explains them.

  1. The voices: for each one, the number of strokes in the cycle (2 to 9) and the instrument. + Voice adds one (up to 4, for example 3:4:5), × removes it, ⇄ swaps A and B. pulse marks the voice that gives the beats of the bar: in 3:2 with the pulse on B (bass drum), the bar has 2 beats and the ride plays 3 even strokes over it.
  2. The strip: the cycle laid out on a common grid of ticks, numbered at the top. Each row is a voice, each circle a stroke. The column where all voices play together is highlighted. During playback, the tick that sounds lights up.
  3. The circle: the same cycle, seen as a clock. Each voice is a polygon: 3 strokes make a triangle, 2 a line, 4 a square. A hand turns during playback and passes over each stroke. Where two corners meet, the voices play together.
  4. The explanation: the size of the common grid and the spacing between each voice's strokes, then the resultant rhythm (see below).
  5. Listen: All the voices, or one voice alone (A, B…) to hear it as a model.
  6. sound the common grid (ticks): a small click on each tick of the grid.

Under these settings, the player plays the polyrhythm in a loop, with the score: each voice has its color, the same as on the strip and the circle.

#Reading the common grid

To play 3 against 2 accurately, you need a unit common to both voices: the smallest number divisible by 3 and by 2, that is 6. On a grid of 6 ticks, voice A (3 strokes) plays every 2 ticks (1, 3, 5) and voice B (2 strokes) every 3 ticks (1, 4). Counting the 6 ticks out loud means hearing exactly where each stroke falls.

The bigger the numbers, the finer the grid: 4:3 gives 12 ticks, 5:4 gives 20. That is what makes 5:4 much harder than 3:2.

#The resultant rhythm

When the two voices play together, you hear a single rhythm: the sequence of gaps between all the strokes. In 3:2, it is 2 1 1 2 (in ticks). This is the key to playing a polyrhythm: rather than thinking of two separate voices, you learn this single rhythm, then split it between the hands (or between hand and foot). A short phrase spoken on this rhythm helps a lot.

If the numbers share a common divisor (4:2, 6:4), the app says so: 6:4 amounts to playing 3:2 twice in a row. Start with the simple version.

#The memory phrase and the metronome wheel

Under the explanation, Memory phrases › Show the syllables adds under the strip a phrase whose syllables each fall on a hit of the resultant rhythm: "nice cup of tea" in 3:2, "pass the golden butter" in 4:3. During playback, the syllable of the hit that sounds lights up. For the other ratios, count the grid or write your own phrase in ✎ Phrases…, where each syllable is shown in the place of its interval. In the colors of the lights gives each syllable the color of the voice that plays. The details of the phrases, and where they come from: Memory phrases.

Do you also practise with the metronome's rhythm wheel? In Metronome look (the metronome's ⚙ button, or Settings › Metronome), tick Also on the Polyrhythms page: the circle becomes the same wheel, with the same LEDs, the same turning light and the same shapes. Only one drawing to learn. With Sober balls, the pulse takes the metronome's beat color.

  1. The wheel: the pulse on the outside, one ball per hit, the turning light.
  2. The memory phrase, the current syllable lit.
  3. Memory phrases: show them, choose the phrase, color it.

#The method

The app's How to learn them panel sums up how to get a polyrhythm in place. In detail, for 3:2:

  1. Set 3 on A (ride), 2 on B (bass drum), pulse on B. Lower the player's tempo to 40.
  2. Tick the ticks and count the 6 ticks out loud, without playing.
  3. Listen to B alone and play it with your foot while counting (ticks 1 and 4). Then A alone, with your hand (ticks 1, 3, 5).
  4. Play the resultant rhythm 2 1 1 2 with one hand, on one instrument. Then split it: A's strokes on the right hand, B's on the foot.
  5. Listen to All and play along with the app. Watch the circle: the hand shows the next stroke.
  6. Untick the ticks, raise the tempo in steps, then change instruments (cross-stick against hi-hat foot…).

With 3 or 4 voices, master each pair first (A:B, A:C, B:C), then add one voice at a time.

#All pairs

All pairs (2 to 9), under the explorer, gives an overview: the darker the cell, the harder the pair. Framed pairs have no common divisor: they are the "true" polyrhythms; the others reduce to a simpler pair. A click on a cell loads it into the explorer.

Further down, the Exercises by level (beginner to expert) are cards like in the lessons: to play, add to the practice plan, print.

#Polymeters

The Polymeters page presents figures that "cross the bar line". For a drummer, they are above all the basis of displaced fills: a group of 3, 5 or 7 sixteenth notes repeated until it lands back on the 1.

  1. The example, chosen from the list (sorted by level).
  2. The strip: at the top, the repeated Figure (here 16 times), each block being one figure; at the bottom, the Bar (here 3 times). You see the figures slide against the bars, then the two strips meet again at the end of the cycle. During playback, the cell that sounds lights up.
  3. The explanation: the length of the figure and of the bar, the length of the full cycle (here 48 cells, that is 3 bars and 16 figures), then the Figure starts: where each repetition begins, as bar and beat ("m2 1&" = bar 2, on the "and" of 1).

The player plays the whole cycle; above the score, a colored band marks each figure.

#The method

  1. Play the figure alone, in a loop and without a click, until you feel it as a pattern of its own.
  2. Add the metronome and count the bar out loud ("1 e & a 2 e & a…"): the figure starts at a different place each time.
  3. Spot the starts (the list and the strip) and say out loud where each figure begins.
  4. Play the full cycle until it comes back to the 1, then finish with a crash on the 1, or go into a groove: that is how it is used as a fill.

To write your own polymeter, use Polymeter in the grid editor: a figure of N cells is repeated along the whole row.

#The learning path

The Learning path page mixes polyrhythms and polymeters in their most useful versions, from the simplest to the hardest: 3:2 and the hemiola to begin with, up to 9:8 and 7/8 over 4/4. Each step says why it is useful and has its strip, synchronized with playback.

Follow it in order: each step prepares the next. Put the current step in your practice plan, and move on when the plan offers Mastered.

Each exercise of the path also has its Wheel button: it opens it in a window, with its player and its rhythm wheel, turning with playback, to see where the hits of both voices fall.

The full screen button (at the top of polyrhythms and polymeters, and on each exercise of the Learning path page) makes the strip, the wheel and the player cover the screen: something to play along with, nothing else. The same button, or Escape, leaves it.

#Keeping a polyrhythm

Like any exercise, a polyrhythm or a polymeter can be kept: ★ Save… files it in My grooves or in a lesson, with its explanation. When you create for a lesson, the Add to “…” button puts it there directly.

Chapter 17Part V · Creating

My grooves, backup and printing

My grooves is your personal collection: everything you have created or set aside, sorted into lists (a gig set list, the grooves of a style, the exercises of the week). This chapter also explains how to back up your data, move it to another device, and print exercise sheets.

At a glance

What forkeeping your grooves in lists, backing up your data, printing exercise sheets.

Wherethe My grooves and Print pages.

Key pointsmake a Full backup from time to time: nothing is kept anywhere but on your device.

In this chapter

  1. My grooves00
  2. Backing up and switching devices00
  3. Printing00

#My grooves

  1. The lists: All my grooves, Favorites and your own lists (for example a concert repertoire). Type a name to create one.
  2. A groove: it can be played, edited, added to the plan or to printing like a lesson exercise. In a list, ↑ ↓ change the order.
  3. Full backup and Restore: see below.

The lists move above the grooves: touch a list, then scroll through its grooves.

A list is not only for storage: it can be worked in a chained Practice run: each exercise is played several times (or for a set time) before moving on to the next (for example the first one 4 times, then the second one 4 times…), whole or bar by bar, with or without a rest between them: the same settings as Run through in a lesson. Print all adds its exercises to the print queue; then open the Print page.

#Sharing a groove by QR code

A groove you wrote often fits in a QR code: no file or email needed to pass it to a friend, your teacher or the student next to you. In a groove's ⋯ menu, QR code… shows it big; the other person scans it with their app (Scan a QR code) and keeps it in their grooves, with your name as the author. Scan a QR code is in the menu's shortcuts and on the home screen: the phone's camera can't open the app (it shows the code as text, or opens the class in the browser).

  1. The QR code: the whole groove is inside (its score, its title, its author).
  2. What it contains, written underneath: you know what you're scanning.

Only what you made yourself is shared this way: an exercise from the lessons shipped with the app (or a groove that keeps its essence) can't be shared by QR code. A groove too long for a QR code is shared as a file (see Backing up and switching devices).

#The groove library

So you have something to play in every style right away, each StoneKiller version comes with a groove library: rock, pop, funk, shuffle, reggae, metal, nu metal, metalcore (and its breakdowns), disco, hip-hop, punk, jazz, bossa nova, soul and Motown, country, 6/8 and 12/8 ballads. Each style goes from the basic groove (level 1) to a variation (level 2) and to a groove made of several bars, with a fill or a response (level 3). These are grooves, not songs: 95 in all, in 16 styles. A newer version adds its new grooves to the style lists you already have.

It's in the app: Groove library…, at the side of My grooves.

  1. One style per line, with its number of grooves and its levels; those not yet in My grooves are ticked. A style already added says so (already in My grooves).
  2. Tick or untick all.
  3. Add: each ticked style becomes a list in My grooves (“Library · Rock”…), in the app's language. Just one style: its list opens.

Adding it again makes no duplicates: a library groove you changed stays yours, and a style list keeps the grooves you put in it; a newer version only adds what's missing.

The same library comes with every release's downloads as a file: StoneKiller-Grooves-EN-<version>.skgroove (also in French and German), to share it or open it in another app (double-click, drop it on the window, or Import).

#Sharing a list

Share, at the top of a list in My grooves, saves it with its grooves to a .skgroove file. Whoever opens it finds it as is in their grooves (lesson exercises stay links to the lessons).

#Backing up and switching devices

Everything stays on your device: nothing is sent over the internet, and there is no online account keeping a copy. Backing up is up to you, from time to time and before switching devices or uninstalling the app: one file that holds everything, to keep wherever you like.

  1. My grooves › Full backup: a .skbackup file with your grooves, your lists, your cell kits, your personal notes, your lessons (own and imported), your practice plan, your routines, your sounds, the class journal, your recorded takes, your microphone and pad calibrations, and your song studies (without their audio or video files, which stay on the device). The Teach edition also adds the student register, with the photos and documents of the lessons.
  2. Keep this file (USB stick, cloud, e-mail).
  3. On the new device: My grooves › Restore, then choose the file (or open it with a double-click, see below). The file is merged with what is already there: nothing is erased.

The device preferences (displayed name, class Wi-Fi, count-in, display) are not in the backup: set them again in Settings.

On Android, Full backup opens the “Save as” window: choose where to put the file (Downloads, Drive…). In a browser, it lands in Downloads.

At the bottom of the page, a line says where your data is kept and how much space it takes. If the browser refuses all storage (private window), a ⚠ warning says so: nothing will be kept when you close.

The app's files each have their own extension: .skbackup (full backup), .sklessons (lessons to share), .skroster (student register, Teach edition), .sksong (a song study, without the music). You can open any StoneKiller file with any import button: the app recognizes its type and files it in the right place. Older .json files still open. A file created by a newer version of the app is clearly flagged: update the app to open it.

#To another program

A groove worked on here sometimes deserves to go elsewhere: into the band's notation program, into a DAW to dress it with real sounds. In the workshop, a groove's ⋯ menu writes it to Guitar Pro (.gp), MusicXML or MIDI: its repeats unfolded, its accents, ghost notes and flams kept. It's an experimental feature (in a stable version, the entry shows with its badge and offers to turn the feature on the first time), like importing Guitar Pro and MusicXML scores, which become song studies or go into a study (see Scores from other software); a .gp or .musicxml file dropped onto the app's window goes there on its own.

#Opening a file: the import window

A StoneKiller file opens in several ways: with an import button (Restore, Import lessons, the register's Import), by dragging it onto the app's window, or from the system:

With the installed Windows app, double-clicking a .skbackup, .sklessons, .skroster or .sksong file opens it in StoneKiller. Each type has its own icon, to recognize it at a glance: an amber LEÇONS (lessons), blue ÉLÈVES (students), green SAUVEG. (backup) or pink ÉTUDE (study) band under the app logo. If the app is already open, the file goes to it. The portable version does not register itself: drag the file onto its window.

On Android, tap the file (Downloads, attachment, Drive), then Open with StoneKiller, or Share › StoneKiller from a messaging app.

Nothing changes until you confirm: the import window first shows the file's type and its date.

  1. For each category (grooves, lists, lessons, practice plan, routines, sounds, students…): what is new, identical or different from what you already have.
  2. When they differ: the rule for the different items (see the table below).
  3. Choose one by one: each difference, with the date of both versions.

New items are always added. For different items (the same groove or lesson, changed on one side or the other), pick the rule under When they differ:

Rule Effect
Keep the most recent the version changed last (the default)
Take the file's version the file's version replaces yours
Keep mine your version stays, the file's is ignored
Keep both (copy) the file's version arrives as a copy, marked “(imported)”, next to yours

Choose one by one lists the differences with the date of each version (the most recent in bold): you can change the choice for one item without touching the others. An import never deletes anything. After a full backup, the app restarts on the merged data.

#Printing

A printed sheet is still useful: on the music stand, in a student's folder, for a substitute teacher. Printing lays out the scores cleanly, with a title block and page numbers.

#Right away

  1. Print next to a part's title: a sheet with that part.

The same button exists everywhere: Print on an exercise, Print the lesson at the top of a lesson, Print the whole theme in the lesson book. The preview opens first, with its settings (layout, options): check it, then Print opens the print dialog.

A lesson often has more variations than exercises, and space counts on paper: the preview of an exercise, a part, a lesson or a theme lets you choose which ones to print.

  1. Variations: None (just the exercises), The lesson's, or The lesson's and mine (with your variations from My grooves, made from these exercises).
  2. Where variations go: After each exercise, or At the end of each part, under a “Variations” heading, to keep the exercises together.

Your choice is kept for the next print.

#Composing a sheet

To gather exercises from several places, add them to the Print queue (button under each exercise, or Print queue at the top of a lesson), then open the Print page.

  1. Title: adds a title (and Subtitle for one level below).
  2. Text: a free paragraph, in markdown (instructions, dates…).
  3. Page break: what follows starts on a new page.
  4. Print: the system print preview; choose the printer or “Save as PDF”.

On Android, printing goes through the phone's print service, which also offers “Save as PDF”.

The arrows ↑ ↓ arrange the items, ✎ edits a title or a text. The options set what is printed: sticking, descriptions and notes, legend, new page at each title. Titles by lesson arranges everything automatically, one title per lesson.

Bars per line sets how many bars each line of score holds (1 to 8): As space allows fits as many as there is room for, at least two; 1 or 2 give an airy score, for a beginner or to write on. A bar to repeat keeps its ×N just above its repeat barline, where the eye lands at the end of the bar.

Boxes for the student adds, under each exercise, a line to fill in by hand: the Days practised (seven boxes to tick), My tempo (the tempo reached) and a rating (Bad, OK, Good, Mastered). Why: a student who practises on paper keeps a record of the week, and the teacher sees it at the next lesson, or the student enters it in the app. With QR code for the student's app, the student's app even reads the ratings from a photo of the sheet (see The sheet's QR code).

The legend, at the end of the sheet, explains every note written on the sheet and only those: each instrument and each way of playing it (accent, ghost note, open hi-hat, accented tom…), and the sticking used. A sheet of hi-hat grooves has no line for the ride.

Preview chooses how you see the sheet on screen:

  • Continuous: the sheet in one piece, handy while you put it together;
  • Pages: the sheet split into A4 pages, with the same page breaks as the printout, the header and the page numbers. You see where each exercise falls before printing, without opening the print dialog.
  1. The bottom of each page: the date and “page n / N”.
  2. The top of the following pages: StoneKiller and the title of the sheet.

The sheet always prints on a white background, even in the dark theme.

Layout sets the density: Normal (airy), Compact (smaller scores, less space) or 2 columns (two exercises per row, never split across two pages). The first page has a plain title block (logo, StoneKiller, date, title); the following pages have a header with StoneKiller and the title, and at the bottom the date and “page n / N”. If the browser adds its own line as well (address, time), untick Headers and footers in its print window.

In the Teach app, your school's name and logo (see Your school) go into the title block, and the school's name at the top of the following pages: a sheet given to a student carries the school that gives it.

  1. The school's logo and name.

#The sheet's QR code

A printed sheet gets lost, is copied badly, and what's written on it never reaches the app. With QR code for the student's app, the sheet carries a QR code in its title block: the student scans it (Scan a QR code, the icon at the top of their practice plan), and its exercises join their practice plan, the lesson their journal. The lessons shipped with the app appear by name (the student already has them); your grooves, in full. A very full sheet keeps all the titles, and only the scores that fit.

With Boxes for the student as well, the rating line sits between two small QR codes: the student ticks the boxes with a pen during the week, then takes a photo of the sheet (My boxes (photo)); the app reads the boxes and puts the ratings in their practice plan (see Your teacher's sheets).

  1. The sheet's QR code: its exercises, its title, its date, the school.
  2. The left mark of a line: the sheet and the exercise number.
  3. The rating boxes, to tick with a pen.
  4. The right mark: together with the left one, it tells the app where the boxes are, even on a photo taken at an angle.

Chapter 18Part VI · Teacher and student

How teacher and student connect

The teacher and the student each have their own app, on their own device: no account to create, no server to install. Yet they have to find each other: the teacher wants to know who is there, to project an exercise and to give homework; the student wants to receive what is given and to show what they have practised. This chapter explains how the two apps talk to each other, so you know what to prepare depending on your room and your students, and how each thing travels.

They talk in three ways: you link once, you find each other on a shared Wi-Fi during the class, and between two classes you exchange files and QR codes. None of this needs the Internet. A student without the app or a room without Wi-Fi each have their own solution, below; and to do without the app altogether, see Paper or connection: the routes.

At a glance

What forunderstanding how the teacher's app and the student's app find each other, and choosing how to run the class together.

Wherethe Class page (the teacher starts, the student joins); Settings › My classes › My teachers (the teachers the student is linked to).

Key pointslink the student's app once; during the class, a shared Wi-Fi is enough, even without the Internet; between two classes, files and QR codes.

In this chapter

  1. Linking your app to your teacher00
  2. Ways to run a class together00
  3. A class without Wi-Fi00
  4. A student without the app00
  5. The school server00
  6. What travels during a class00
  7. What travels between two classes00
  8. What does not go over the internet00
  9. What travels by which route, in a table00

#Linking your app to your teacher

Your teacher recognises you at every class without you doing anything, even if you change your nickname or the app updates: you just link your app to them, once. They show you an invitation QR code from your file; in your app, Scan a QR code (Classes, Practice plan or My grooves page), aim at it, then Link. At the next live class, your app introduces itself on its own, and the link is confirmed.

On a device that allows it (the installed app, or a secure page), your app has its own key, StoneID: it signs your arrival at the class, and nobody can pretend to be you. The key never leaves the device; only its public part goes to your teacher. Your linked teachers are in Settings › My classes › My teachers.

Why link? Without a link, the first time, the teacher has to pick you out in the Class panel themselves (see The class panel). With the link, they know you before your first class. The link also serves to give you personal content: an exercise encrypted for your device, that only your app opens, and that you know comes from your teacher (see Personal content). On the teacher's side, the invitation is sent from the student's file (see Their devices): the QR code is valid for 24 hours, for a single scan.

#Ways to run a class together

For a live class, the devices only need one thing in common: the same Wi-Fi, without Internet access if need be. Depending on the room, it is the school's, a Wi-Fi that a phone creates for the occasion, or that of a small router. And a student doesn't even need the app.

  • The room's or the school's Wi-Fi. The simplest: the teacher starts the class, and the students' apps find it by themselves (▶ Join). It is enough for everyone to be on the same Wi-Fi; a “guest” Wi-Fi often isolates the devices from one another (see If a student cannot find the class).
  • The Teach app on Android creates the Wi-Fi. No Wi-Fi in the room? The teacher's phone creates one, without Internet (see A class without Wi-Fi).
  • A hotspot or a small router. The same thing with any phone (iPhone included) or a travel router, for a teacher on a computer as on a phone (see With a hotspot or a small router).
  • A student without the app. Their browser is enough: they scan the class's QR code (see A student without the app).

Two things do not work: mobile data (4G, 5G), because a phone on 4G cannot reach the teacher's device, and Bluetooth, which is too limited for a class (see Frequently asked questions).

#A class without Wi-Fi

The class does not need the internet, only a shared Wi-Fi. If there is none in the room, a phone creates one. Everyone connects to it, and the class traffic stays in the room, using no mobile data.

Everything is set in the 📶 Lesson Wi-Fi window: the button shows the Wi-Fi in use. There are two ways: This phone creates the Wi-Fi (the Teach app on Android), or An existing Wi-Fi (router, hotspot): you give its name and password. The Wi-Fi you enter is kept for the app: from one class to the next it is the same, and the students' phones reconnect by themselves, without scanning anything (the Wi-Fi created by the Android app gets a new name each time). Forget this Wi-Fi removes it (a new password, another room).

The students then scan two QR codes, one at a time so the camera doesn't pick the wrong one: the ① Wi-Fi step first, then the ② Class step. Under each QR code, what it does and what is left to do. After QR code ①, some phones only offer the network: then open the phone's Wi-Fi settings and pick the class Wi-Fi (the password is written under the QR code). A click on a QR code enlarges it on its own.

#The StoneKiller Teach app on Android creates the Wi-Fi

Only the Teach app on Android (Android 8 or newer) can create this Wi-Fi; otherwise the button does not appear.

  1. Start the class, tap 📶 Lesson Wi-Fi, then Create a Wi-Fi network with this phone (the This phone creates the Wi-Fi part).
  2. The first time, Android asks for a permission (Nearby devices, or Location up to Android 12): accept. Up to Android 12, the phone's location must also be turned on.
  3. The students scan QR code ①, agree to join the Wi-Fi, then scan QR code ②. With the StoneKiller app on Android, one scan is enough: Scan the QR code on the Class page, on QR code ①; the app joins the Wi-Fi (Android asks to confirm), then finds the class.
  1. The steps: ① Wi-Fi, then ② Class (already on the address of the new Wi-Fi).
  2. The QR code of the step shown; a tap enlarges it.
  3. 📶 Lesson Wi-Fi: the window, where the same button stops the Wi-Fi. It also stops when the class ends.

This Wi-Fi has no internet: it is only for the class.

Note

If the phone's hotspot is already on, Android does not create a second Wi-Fi. Use the hotspot instead, as described below.

#With a hotspot or a small router

This method works with a Windows computer as well as with a phone, and any phone can create the Wi-Fi, iPhone included.

  1. Turn on a phone's hotspot, or plug in a small travel Wi-Fi router.
  2. Connect the teacher's device to this Wi-Fi, then start the class.
  3. Tap 📶 Lesson Wi-Fi and enter the Wi-Fi name and its password (the An existing Wi-Fi (router, hotspot) part).
  1. The Wi-Fi name and its Password.
  2. They are kept for the app: the next classes use the same Wi-Fi.
  3. Forget this Wi-Fi.
  4. Save.
  1. 📶 Lesson Wi-Fi: the Wi-Fi in use.
  2. The steps: ① Wi-Fi, then ② Class.
  3. The QR code of the step; a click enlarges it.
  4. What it does, the password, and what is left to do on the phone.

A Windows computer without a connection cannot create a Wi-Fi itself: use a phone's hotspot.

Tip

If the class page does not open on a student's phone, turn off its mobile data for the duration of the class. Some Android phones switch to 4G when the Wi-Fi has no internet.

Note

A phone accepts only a limited number of devices on its Wi-Fi, often 5 to 10. For a large class, get a small travel router.

#A student without the app

A student who hasn't installed the app, or a parent who has come to watch the class, is not left out. Their phone is enough: they open the camera, aim it at the class's QR code and tap the link. The class page opens in the browser, with the code already filled in: nothing to install, no account. In a room without Wi-Fi, they first scan the QR code ① to join the class's Wi-Fi.

They see what the teacher projects, and can hear the drums on their phone (see With a phone, without the app). Two limits: the page has neither a microphone nor MIDI, and what it keeps stays in that phone's browser, tied to the teacher's address. The teacher sees them in the class under the name they typed, like the others. For sustained work, the app remains the right way.

#The school server

By default, there is nothing to install: the teacher's app hosts the class itself, on the room's network. Some schools prefer a StoneKiller server of their own, run by their administrator: it passes the class between the teacher and the students, which is mostly useful when they are not on the same network, or when the teacher only has a browser (the Teach edition cannot host a class there).

The teacher and the students then choose School server in Settings, under Connection, with the address their administrator gives them, then Test connection. The server hands each message to its recipient without keeping it, but, as on the local network, the exchanges are not encrypted end to end (see Privacy: what the app sends). If your school has no server, you don't need one.

#What travels during a class

During the class, the teacher sends neither their screen nor sound. They send the exercise, the tempo and the moment playback starts; each student's app shows it and plays it with its own sounds. A modest Wi-Fi is therefore enough.

  • From the teacher to the students: the projected exercise (its score, its title, its description), the tempo, the metronome, the start and stop of playback; a message, shown above the score, and the place in the setlist (“2/4”); the board, when the teacher composes live; the homework and the end of the class; and, if the teacher decides, a short video given to a student or a camera's picture (the video feedback, a feature in trial), which go directly from one device to the other.
  • From the students to the teacher: the student's name and what they do (they follow the projection, explore on their own, have paused, or are reconnecting), and what identifies them: their device's ID and, if they are linked, the signature of their arrival. Nothing else leaves: neither their practice plan, nor their grooves.
  • What stays with the teacher: the notes written in the Class panel are never projected.

#What travels between two classes

Outside the class, there is no shared Wi-Fi any more, and none is needed: what travels are files (by email, by message, on a USB stick) and QR codes (shown on screen, or printed on a sheet). The app of the one who receives always shows first what is arriving and from where: nothing comes in without a yes.

  • From the teacher to the student: a personal content (a .skpersonal file or a QR code, encrypted for the student's linked device; see Personal content); a printed sheet with its QR code, which the student scans (Scan a QR code) or whose boxes they photograph (My boxes (photo)) (see The sheet's QR code); a groove by QR code, a list of grooves or lessons by file; and a student's lessons, as an .ics file for their calendar (see The schedule in your calendar).
  • From the student to the teacher: their work, with Send my practice to my teacher: a QR code to show at the next class, or a .skreport file to send; the teacher receives it with Receive their practice…, from the student's file (see Sending your practice to your teacher). A groove the student has written travels the same way, by QR code or by file.

#What does not go over the internet

The app has no account or server of its own, and nothing above needs the Internet.

  • The class travels over the room's Wi-Fi, from one device to the other. (With a school server, it goes through that server: ask your administrator where it is hosted.)
  • A camera's picture (the mirror, the video feedback, Capture) goes from device to device, on the same network.
  • A QR code contains what it carries, and the camera reads it: no server is consulted. The boxes on a sheet are read in the app, without the Internet or artificial intelligence.
