  • The student's StoneID key never leaves their device: only its public part goes to the teacher.
  • The practice plan, the log and the grooves stay on the device: only what you send yourself leaves.

A file sent by email or by message, on the other hand, goes through that service: it is the sender's choice. A personal content stays unreadable for anyone but the student's device.

#What travels by which route, in a table

What travels By what When
The invitation to link the student's app a QR code once
The exercise, the tempo, playback, the homework the class's Wi-Fi (or the school's server) during the class
What the student does (follows, explores, is paused) the class's Wi-Fi during the class
A short video, a camera's picture the class's Wi-Fi, device to device during the class
A personal content a .skpersonal file or a QR code between two classes
A sheet of exercises paper, with a QR code and boxes read from a photo between two classes
A groove, a list, lessons a QR code, or a .skgroove or .sklessons file between two classes
The student's work a QR code or a .skreport file between two classes
A student's lessons, for their calendar an .ics file between two classes

Chapter 19Part VI · Teacher and student

Paper or connection: the routes

The app is optional. A student without a smartphone, a parent who prefers paper, a class where the Wi-Fi has dropped or the battery is empty: everything must be able to go on. That is why each piece of information exchanged between the teacher and the student has two routes: a route through the app, and a route on paper. This chapter sets them side by side, piece by piece, so you can choose, student by student, the one that suits, without anyone being left out.

The two routes often meet: a printed sheet carries a QR code that the student's app scans, and the boxes ticked with a pen are read from a photo. Each section starts with what you want to pass on, then gives the With the app. route and the On paper. route, each pointing to the chapter that explains it in detail. For how the devices find each other (linking, Wi-Fi, files), see How teacher and student connect.

At a glance

What forchoosing, for each piece of information, the route through the app or the route on paper.

Wherethis chapter is a map; the steps are in the chapters each section points to.

Key pointseverything the teacher gives or receives has a route on paper; the two mix (a QR code on a sheet, boxes read from a photo).

In this chapter

  1. Exercises to work on00
  2. The class homework00
  3. A sheet of exercises00
  4. Tick boxes and ratings00
  5. The student's work handed to the teacher00
  6. Personal content00
  7. The review and the register00
  8. The schedule00

#Exercises to work on

A student works better when they know what to practise, without having to ask.

With the app. In the student's file, the To work on list keeps its exercises from one lesson to the next; during a class, one click projects what each student present has to practise (see A student's file). Exercises reach the student's Practice plan through the class's homework, through a sheet they scan or through personal content (the following sections), or because they add them themselves (+ Plan).

On paper. Print, at the top of the file, prepares a Lessons sheet: what there is to practise, with the scores or as a list, to give to the student or their parents (see A student's file).

#The class homework

What is given at the end of a class must not depend on the student's memory.

With the app. During the class, Give as homework turns the projected exercise into a homework; at End the class, the homework goes out over the class's Wi-Fi and enters each student's Practice plan, with the tempos chosen (see Giving homework).

On paper. What you put in Given to work on for the lesson is printed with its report: Print, in the unfolded lesson, produces the report with the scores given to work on, for the student or their parents (see The lessons). A sheet prepared in advance does the job too (see the next section).

#A sheet of exercises

A printed sheet gets lost, is copied out wrong, and what is written on it never reaches the app: the QR code settles that, without forcing anyone to have the app.

With the app. On the Print page, tick QR code for the student's app: the sheet carries a QR code in its title block. The student scans it (the Scan a QR code icon, at the top of their Practice plan): the exercises join their practice plan, the lesson joins their journal. Scanned twice, nothing is doubled (see The sheet's QR code).

On paper. Without the QR code, the sheet is enough on its own: scores, fingerings, legend. It is composed on the Print page, then Print opens the system's print dialogue, or “Save as PDF” to send it (see Composing a sheet).

#Tick boxes and ratings

Noting what was practised sets the reminders and the tempo for next time: on paper as in the app, there has to be a place to do it.

With the app. The student notes each exercise played in their Practice plan: Bad, OK, Good or Mastered. The app sets the next reminder and the next tempo (see What each rating does).

On paper. With Boxes for the student (on the Print page), each exercise has its line to fill in with a pen: the Days practised (seven boxes), My tempo and the rating. The teacher sees it at the next class. If the sheet also carries the QR code, the student can photograph it with My boxes (photo) (the ⋯ menu of the Practice plan): the app reads the ticked boxes, they correct them if need be, and Save my ratings carries them over to their practice plan (see Your teacher's sheets).

#The student's work handed to the teacher

The teacher doesn't see what the student does at home, unless the student shows them: that is what they need to prepare the next class with what was really practised.

With the app. Send my practice to my teacher (the ⋯ menu of the Practice plan) gives, in one gesture, what the student has practised and rated since their last send: a QR code to show the teacher at class, or a .skreport file to send them. The teacher receives it with Receive their practice…, from the student's file; sent twice, nothing is counted twice (see Sending your practice to your teacher and, on the teacher's side, Their practice at home).

On paper. The student brings their filled-in sheet to class (days practised, tempo, rating of each exercise) and the teacher looks at it with them: nothing to scan, the sheet is the report (see The sheet's QR code).

#Personal content

An arrangement written for one student, a score that must not circulate: the teacher can give it to them alone.

With the app. In the student's file, Personal content encrypts exercises for the student's linked devices: only their app opens them, they know they come from their teacher, and the app respects what you allow (editing, printing, sharing again). They travel by QR code (for short content) or by a .skpersonal file. The student's app must be linked first (see Linking your app to your teacher and Personal content).

On paper. Print the exercise and hand it over in person (see Printing). Paper encrypts nothing: the sheet can be read by anyone who holds it. If the exercise must stay with the student alone, keep to the app route.

#The review and the register

What happened in class must leave a trace: for you, for the student, for their parents.

With the app. During the class, the Class panel notes who keeps up and who drops out; at End the class, the Review proposes, for each student, what they did and their rating, and Update the register applies what you ticked. The student keeps the class in their Class journal (see The lesson review and Students).

On paper. Print, at the top of a student's file, prepares their file, their lessons or the year overview; in the student list, Print turns the register into a table; a lesson's report also prints by itself. To give to the student or their parents, or to file away (see A student's file).

#The schedule

A student or their parents want to know when the next classes take place.

With the app. The schedule is in the Teach app (Schedule page). On a student's file, Calendar (.ics) draws from it a file with their upcoming classes, to send to them or to their parents: it opens in any calendar, without StoneKiller (see The schedule in your calendar).

On paper. In the schedule, Print prepares the days shown (one day, 5 days or the week), for a teacher or a room, with the school's header; the student's file, printed, also lists their classes (see Printing the schedule and A student's file).

Chapter 20Part VII · Teaching

Preparing a class

A lesson that runs smoothly is prepared beforehand. In front of the students, searching for an exercise loses the group; not knowing where each one stands forces you to ask everything again. Preparing means deciding in advance what to show, what to give and to whom, so that class time is spent playing.

This chapter is written for the teacher (Teach edition). It gathers what the app lets you prepare: the class setlist, the lesson in the schedule, a student's next lesson, personal content and a sheet to hand out. Each part sums up and points to the chapter that details it. When there is also a route without the app, two paragraphs say so side by side: With the app. and On paper.

At a glance

What forarriving at class with the exercises to show and what each student has to work on again, already sorted.

Wherethe Setlist page, the Schedule and each student's file (Teach edition).

Key pointssort the exercises into the class setlist; prepare the lesson in the schedule or in the student's file; in class, you project without searching.

In this chapter

  1. The class setlist00
  2. The session in the planner00
  3. A student's next lesson00
  4. Personal content00
  5. A sheet to hand out00

#The class setlist

With the app. Preparing a class often means choosing a sequence of exercises in advance. Put them in the Class setlist (see The Setlist): during the class, you move from one to the next without searching.

  1. The ticked exercises, in order: a click projects that one. On the students' side, the projection shows its place (“2/4”).
  2. Next ▶ projects the next exercise; ◀ Previous goes back.
  3. Open: the setlist page, to tick, reorder or set the tempos.
  4. Clear: the setlist starts again from scratch, for the next class (after confirming; nothing is deleted from the lessons or My grooves).

During a class, ▶ Project also exists on a part, a lesson or a theme: their exercises go into the class setlist and the first one is projected. If an exercise is playing, the app asks: Now (projected right away) or After this one (Next leads to it).

+ Setlist on an exercise asks where to add it: the Class setlist (to project during this class), The session (the next session in the planner, to prepare it) or My setlist (to practise yourself). Each choice says what it is for; during a class, the class setlist comes first.

This setlist exists before class: fill it the day before, it waits for you at startup and stays from one class to the next until you clear it.

On paper. No screen, or students without a device: Print, in the ⋯ menu of the setlist page, prints its ticked exercises in order, with their scores and their own settings, to play the setlist from the sheet or to give it to a student (see The Setlist).

#The session in the planner

A lesson in the schedule already has its student (or group), its day and its room: that is the right place to say what will be done in it. The preparation stays attached to that lesson, without mixing with another day's.

With the app. In the class window, + Prepare adds an exercise planned for that particular class, and a free note keeps what needs to be brought (see A lesson). The setlist The session gathers this planned work and its students' To work on list, without duplicates, ready to play or print; + The planned work pours it in (see The session setlist). On the day, for a particular class, ▶ Start lesson opens the session window with what is planned (see Running a lesson).

On paper. Print, in the schedule, prints the days shown; the option Planned for this lesson (With planned work) adds to each lesson what is planned for it (see Printing the schedule).

#A student's next lesson

From one week to the next, you quickly forget what you asked of each student. The register remembers: in the student's file, the To work on list is their next lesson, ready when they arrive.

With the app. + Add an exercise fills it from My grooves and the lessons, with the preview to listen to before choosing; → Student, everywhere in the app (an exercise, a song study, what you are projecting), adds what you have in front of you. For each exercise, you can say what it works on and why (see Preparing the next lesson and What the exercise works on). For a group class, → Send to the class puts its list in the queue of the Class page: during class, its exercises come first in the Project… choice.

On paper. Print, at the top of the file, prepares a Lessons sheet: what they have to work on, with the scores or as a list, to give to the student or their parents (see A student's file).

#Personal content

An arrangement written for a single student, a score that must not circulate: this is not for the class. Personal content, at the top of the student's file, encrypts it for their app: only they open it, they know it comes from you, and you choose what they can do with it (edit it, print it, share it again). It goes by QR code (short content) or by a .skpersonal file, to send by email or by message.

The student's app must be linked to yours (see Their devices); otherwise, the app offers to invite them. The details are in Personal content; what the student sees is in Content from your teacher.

#A sheet to hand out

Not every student has the app, or a device to hand during class. A sheet is prepared beforehand and handed over in person: it is used during class, and the student keeps it for the week.

With the app. What you want to give can also go straight into the student's app: the class's homework enters their Practice plan at the end of the class (see Giving homework), and personal content arrives encrypted for them (see above).

On paper. Gather the exercises from several places into the Print queue, then compose the sheet: title, instructions, scores (see Composing a sheet). Two options make it more than a sheet. QR code for the student's app: the student scans it with Scan a QR code, their exercises join their practice plan and the lesson their journal (without the app, the sheet is enough on its own). Boxes for the student: under each exercise, a line to fill in with a pen during the week (the days practised, their tempo, their rating), which you see at the next class. What the student does with it on their side is in Your teacher's sheets; the sheet and its QR code, in The sheet's QR code.

Chapter 21Part VII · Teaching

During the class

In a group class, everyone looks at the same exercise, at the same tempo, on their own screen. The teacher shows an exercise: the students see it on their screen, hear it at the right tempo and can play along. At the end, the homework goes straight into each student's practice plan: no more photocopies, no more "which exercise was it again?". The class runs over the room's Wi-Fi, or over a phone's Wi-Fi if there is none. The teacher's app (Windows or Android) hosts it itself: no server to install, no account to create.

This chapter follows a group class in the order you act: starting it, letting the students in, projecting, following the class, giving homework, then what the students see on their side. A one-to-one lesson is run differently: see Running a lesson. Before class, see Preparing a class; after, After the class. When an action also has a route without the app, two paragraphs say so side by side, With the app. and On paper.; all the routes are brought together in Paper or connection: the routes.

At a glance

What forgetting a group to work on the same exercise, at the same tempo, each on their own screen.

Wherethe Class page; running a class needs the Teach edition.

Key pointsthe teacher starts, the students join with the code or the QR code; at the end, the homework goes into their practice plan.

In this chapter

  1. Starting a class00
  2. Getting the students in00
  3. Projecting and controlling00
  4. The Class panel00
  5. Projecting on another screen00
  6. A short video for the students00
  7. Video feedback: each student watches themselves play00
  8. Giving homework00
  9. Student side00
  10. Running a lesson00
  11. If the connection drops00
  12. If a student cannot find the class00

In a browser or an .html file, the Teach edition cannot host a class: Start the class opens a demo there, to try with two tabs (a teacher, a student). For real students, install the Windows or Android app, or use the school server (Settings).

#Starting a class

As long as the class is not started, the students have nothing to join: everything starts from the Class page.

  1. Start the class. A 6-digit code and a QR code appear.

#Getting the students in

Students only need the code or the QR code: with the app, they join the class; without the app, a phone opens it in its browser. What each one sees is described below, in Student side.

  1. The Class code and the class link, to hand out if needed.
  2. The class QR code: a phone that scans it opens the class in its browser, with nothing to install. A click enlarges it on its own in a window, to show the whole class.
  3. 📶 Lesson Wi-Fi: for a room without Wi-Fi (see A class without Wi-Fi).
  4. The connected students.
  5. That day's schedule: today's lessons in the planner (Teach edition), to find each student's session.
  6. End the class.

The app finds its own address on the network. If the computer has several (Wi-Fi, cable, virtual machine…), choose the one on the students' Wi-Fi under the QR code.

Important

The first time, Windows asks you to allow StoneKiller Teach on the network: accept for private networks. Without this, the students cannot find the class.

#Projecting and controlling

With the app. Before showing an exercise to the whole class, it is better to see and hear it yourself first. ▶ Project… opens a choice window:

  1. Search for an exercise.
  2. The list: at the top, what the students present have to work on (and the class queue), then My grooves and the lessons, folded by lesson. Create in the workshop writes a groove for the occasion.
  3. The preview of the exercise clicked, to listen to: nothing is sent to the students yet. The tempo set in the preview is the one projected.
  4. Project, or Cancel.

On a phone, the list takes the screen; touching an exercise opens its preview, ← List goes back.

When students present have planned work, a panel, To work on, students present, shows it above the player:

  1. For each student present, what they have to work on: a click projects it. The students sent to the class from their file are there too, even if absent from the class, with Remove from the queue.
  1. ▶ Project…: change the exercise. During the class, every exercise in the app also has a ▶ Project button.
  2. Compose live: a grid appears, and the students see the groove being built note by note. Give the board a name if you like; + New board starts another one.
  3. 📺 Projection screen: the score in large on another screen (see Projecting on another screen).
  4. Message: an instruction shown above the score on the students' screens.
  5. This player drives the students: play, stop and tempo are followed on their side.
  6. → Student: what is projected goes into a student's To work on list, for their next lesson (see The student register).
  1. The students line: who is here, who is reconnecting, and who has paused the projection. An exercise projected while a student is paused is marked Not done for them in the class journal.

Your class goes on while you go elsewhere in the app (a lesson, the register): a pill at the top of every page reminds you and takes you back in one click. If the app closes during the class, it offers to Resume it with the same code when you come back: students reconnect by themselves. If the Android app had created the class Wi-Fi, create it again; students scan QR code ① again (see A class without Wi-Fi).

On paper. No screen, or students without a device: print the class setlist (Print, in the ⋯ menu of its page) and hand it out. Its ticked exercises come out in order, with their scores and their own settings: each one plays from their own sheet (see The Setlist and A sheet to hand out).

#The Class panel

During a class, you need to see at a glance who is following and who has dropped off, and to jot down a remark without leaving the projection. The Class panel gives one line per student.

During the projection, the app notes by itself what it knows: the time spent on each projected exercise and the tempo played. You only note what it can't know, with one gesture.

  1. Tick one or more students: to write them a note, or to give them a quick mark.
  2. What they are doing: following the projection, exploring on their own, paused, or reconnecting (their connection dropped; they come back by themselves).
  3. ✓ Got it: they got the projected exercise (click again to undo). Receiving an exercise does not mean playing it: you are the one who marks it.
  4. ↺ Again: not yet; the review will offer to put it back for next lesson.
  5. Who they are. A device already linked to a student of the register is recognised by itself: ✓ and their name, which opens their file. An unknown device waits for your decision: That's Léa when a student of the register has that name, + New student, Link to… another student, or Guest for a one-off student (nothing goes into the register). Once linked, the device is recognised at every class, even under another nickname.
  6. The quick marks, without leaving the projection: ✓ Got it and ↺ Again in big, for the ticked students (or the only student in the class), or on the keyboard, + and −. The review picks them up for you to confirm.
  7. The note, for all ticked students.
  8. Add the note (or Ctrl+Enter). Your notes stay with you: they are never projected. You find them again in the lesson review.

#Projecting on another screen

In a classroom, not every student has a device, and a score reads better in large. Two ways, which combine with each other and with the connected students:

  • 📺 Projection screen opens a second window: the score in large, with no buttons, following playback. With a second screen plugged in (projector, TV, extended screen), the app places it there, in full screen; otherwise, drag it where you want. Your system's screen mirroring (Miracast, AirPlay, Cast) sends this window to a TV without a cable.
  • Another device as a screen: under Project to another device, a link and a QR code. The classroom PC, a tablet or the smart TV that opens it becomes a screen of the class, without counting as a student.

The screen makes no sound: the sound comes from your device, or from the students'. The number of screens connected shows next to the students.

#A short video for the students

A movement is easier to show than to explain, and by next week the student will have forgotten it. Short video…, above the projected exercise, records a demonstration to watch again at home: one camera, your device's sound, no editing.

  1. The camera's picture, as in a mirror: your device's camera (another webcam can be picked on the right, if there is one).
  2. ● Record, then ■ Stop: three minutes at most.

The recorded video takes the camera's place:

  1. The part to keep: drag the two handles.
  2. Or while it plays: Start here, End here; Replay the part plays it again. The title is the projected exercise's, to change if you like.
  3. Who for: the connected students you tick.
  4. Give to …: the video goes over the class connection, device to device, without the internet, and lands in their journal (Your videos).
  5. Share…: WhatsApp, email, Messages… (your device's share sheet). Save the file… keeps it on your side; Redo starts again.

The part becomes an MP4 that messaging apps play (a WebM if the device can't make MP4: the app says so). With no sharing on the device (Linux, macOS), save the file, then send it. Nothing is kept unless you ask: closing the window forgets the video. Someone other than you in the picture? Ask for their consent before sharing.

#Video feedback: each student watches themselves play

Why: in a room with several drum kits, you can't stand behind every student. A camera pointed at their kit shows them what to fix (their hands, their back), on their own device, while they play. It's a mirror, not a recording. A feature on trial: see Experimental features in Settings.

  1. One live thumbnail per webcam on your device. Show my cameras opens them the first time; in the next lessons, they open on their own.
  2. The students receiving this camera: a green dot means the picture arrives, orange that it's on its way, grey that the student isn't there (it goes as soon as they connect). ✕ takes it back.
  3. Give to…: the single gesture; or drag the thumbnail onto the student, in the class. A camera can go to several students, a student can receive several.
  4. In the class, the student's row shows their cameras.

The assignment stays from one lesson to the next: Léa finds her camera again as soon as she connects. If she changes kits, move the camera: there's nothing else to set.

On the student's side, See myself appears in the lesson bar. It opens the mirror with your camera's picture, and everything the mirror can do: the delay (seeing yourself right after playing), Freeze, the guides, and their own camera as well.

  1. Your camera's picture.
  2. Delay: live, or a few seconds later.

The picture goes straight from your cameras to the students' devices, on the room's network, without going through the Internet, and stays nowhere.

#Giving homework

With the app. An exercise shown in class only sinks in if it is worked on at home: the homework sends it to the student, with its tempos, without any photocopying.

  1. The start tempo and the target tempo, then Give as homework: the projected exercise becomes homework.
  2. The homework of the class.

When you End the class, the homework goes to the students and enters their Practice plan (without homework, the app asks for confirmation). The Review opens next (see The lesson review). Everything that was shown is kept in the Class journal, for the teacher as for each student: one item per exercise, folded, with its name (the template's, or the one given in the workshop or on the board), where it comes from (the lesson, My grooves, the song study; “after” the exercise the board started from) and a small ▶ to hear it again. A click unfolds it; Expand all opens them all. The board counts as a single item, in its latest version.

On the teacher's side, each class in the journal also leads further: the file of each recognised student, and That day's schedule. From the class to the file and the planner, without searching.

On paper. A printed sheet can stand in for homework: the exercises to work on, their scores, some instructions. With QR code for the student's app, a student who has the app scans it (Scan a QR code) and their exercises join their practice plan; with Boxes for the student, they tick off their week with a pen, and you see it at the next class. Without the app, the sheet is enough on its own (see A sheet to hand out and The sheet's QR code).

#Student side

To guide the students, you need to know what they see. A student joins in one of two ways: with the StoneKiller app, or without the app, in their phone's browser.

#With the StoneKiller app

  1. The teacher's class appears by itself: tap ▶ Join. This works on the same computer as the teacher or on another device on the same Wi-Fi.

Only the Windows and Android apps find the class by themselves. In a browser or an .html file, type the Teacher's address, or paste the class link.

  1. Your name, as the teacher will see it.
  2. Teacher's address, if the class does not appear: the one shown under the teacher's QR code, for example 192.168.1.23:8787.

Scan the QR code opens the device's camera: point it at the teacher's QR code. QR code ② (the class) lets you in right away. In a room without Wi-Fi, the Android app joins the Wi-Fi of QR code ① by itself, then finds the class (see A class without Wi-Fi).

Joining a class opens the app full screen, and what the teacher projects shows in large: just the score, following the teacher. Your hands stay free to play, without touching anything.

  1. Sound on this device: off at first, because in the same room the sound comes from the teacher's device (otherwise, echo). Turn it on to hear the drums on your device, in sync with the teacher's: remotely, or with headphones.
  2. ■: you take over to explore on your own (tempo, playback…); ↺ Back to the teacher puts you back on what the teacher shows.
  3. ✕: leaving full screen pauses the projection, right away. Esc, the phone's back button or a gesture that leaves full screen do the same: nothing is lost, you pick up again in one tap.
  4. Leave: the only button that takes you out of the class (the app asks you to confirm).

While paused, the teacher sees it, and the exercise is marked Interrupted in your journal (Not done in the teacher's). Receiving an exercise doesn't mean you played it: this way the teacher knows what to go over with you.

  1. ▶ Back to the projection: back to full screen, on what the teacher shows now.
  2. Sound on this device (see above).
  3. Leave the class. The app asks you to confirm.

The class goes on while you go elsewhere in the app; changing page also pauses it. A pill at the top of every page reminds you:

  1. ↺ Back to the lesson: back to the projection, full screen, in one tap.

Without sound, the playhead follows the teacher's on the score, even if the device has never played a sound. If the connection drops (Wi-Fi lost for a moment, phone asleep), the app reconnects by itself and picks up what the teacher shows; on the teacher's side, you appear as “reconnecting” in the meantime. If the app closes (by mistake, or closed by the phone while asleep), it offers to Resume the class when you come back, for 3 hours: you return under the same name, and your journal carries on.

#With a phone, without the app

Open the camera and point it at the teacher's QR code, then tap the link. The class page opens in the browser, with the code already filled in.

  1. Your name.
  2. Join.

Tip

To hear the drums on the phone, tap Sound on this device. On iPhone, also turn off silent mode. The browser shows “Not Secure”: this is normal on a local network.

This phone page has no microphone or MIDI (insecure address). What it keeps (plan, journal) stays in the phone's browser, tied to the teacher's address: if it changes (another Wi-Fi), the page starts from scratch. For continued work, install the app, or make a Full backup.

#Running a lesson

With the app. During a private lesson, there is no time to go from one page to another. ▶ Start the lesson opens a window for this student alone: everything you note in it comes back to their file, with no risk of picking the wrong student.

  1. To work on: a click opens the exercise in the middle. + Add an exercise adds one during the lesson; → Give to work on gives one for next time.
  2. The current exercise, with its score and its player. The tempo you play it at becomes the ♩ reached; an exercise without a score can be written on the spot (✎ Write it).
  3. Its status, its tempos, Again next time, a remark, and the assessment (see Assessing).
  4. The report of the lesson, in formatted text, with its attachments and the lesson's assessment.
  5. Projection screen: the score in large on another screen (see Projecting on another screen).
  6. Invite the student: a code and a QR code so they follow on their device.
  7. End the lesson: the lesson enters the table, with what was opened or noted. The To work on list keeps what was not seen, what is marked Again next time and what was given; a Mastered exercise leaves it.

Closing the window without ending asks for confirmation, so nothing is lost. The clock, at the top, counts the length of the lesson.

On a phone, the three columns become three tabs: Exercises, Current and Report.

On paper. A student without the app leaves with a sheet: Print, at the top of their file, prepares Lessons (what they have to work on, with the scores, and their lessons), and a lesson's report prints by itself (see A student's file).

#If the connection drops

A Wi-Fi that drops out, a phone going to sleep, a relay restarting: the class doesn't stop for all that. The app reconnects on its own; a break of a few seconds goes unnoticed. Beyond that, a banner says so, on every page: Connection to the class lost: retrying, with Retry now. On the teacher's side, it reminds you that students no longer see what you project; on the student's side, that you can keep playing alone. When it comes back, Back in the class., and everyone picks up where the teacher is. If nothing comes back, see the list below.

#If a student cannot find the class

If the class doesn't appear for a student, check in this order:

  1. Are the teacher and the students on the same Wi-Fi? A “guest” Wi-Fi often isolates devices from one another.
  2. On Windows, is the teacher's app allowed on private networks? (Windows Settings › Firewall › Allow an app through firewall.)
  3. Does the teacher's computer have several addresses? Choose the one on the students' Wi-Fi under the QR code.
  4. Type the teacher's address into Teacher's address.
  5. In the Settings, the connection must be set to Local network (automatic).
  6. For the school's IT person: the class uses port 8787 (TCP) and, to be found automatically, port 8786 (UDP), on the local network.
  7. No Wi-Fi in the room? See A class without Wi-Fi.

Chapter 22Part VII · Teaching

After the class

When the class ends, its trace has to be kept. For the teacher, what happened must reach the register without copying everything out; for the student, what they have to work on again must be found. Without that, at the next class you start again from memory.

This chapter follows both sides. First the teacher's: the class review, then the follow-up that comes after (the register, the work the student sends back, the next lesson). Then the student's: what they find on their device and what their teacher can give them on top; these last parts are written for them. When there is also a route without the app, two paragraphs say so side by side: With the app. and On paper.

At a glance

What forputting what happened in class into the register, and knowing what is left for the student.

Wherethe Review opens at End the class (Class page) and stays in the class journal; for the student, the Practice plan and the Class journal.

Key pointsnothing goes into the register unless you ticked it; the homework arrives in the student's practice plan by itself.

In this chapter

  1. The lesson review00
  2. What comes next00
  3. On the student's side00
  4. What stays in the journal00
  5. Content from your teacher00

#The lesson review

What happened in class should reach the register, without copying everything and without the app deciding for you. When you End the class, the Review opens:

  1. The tempo reached: the last one played during the class, to correct if needed. Next to it, the time spent on the exercise.
  2. For each student and each exercise: seen, done or interrupted. The app starts from what it knows (Got it marked, a pause during the exercise); you correct it.
  3. The rating, proposed from the class: Good for an exercise they got, OK for an “again”. Change it, or pick — to give none.
  4. Their notes, editable; + Note adds one, ✕ removes one (a note written for several students is only removed for this one).
  5. The proposed updates to their register, to tick: keep the lesson in their file, with its notes, tempos and ratings; put an interrupted exercise to work on next lesson; remove a done exercise from To work on; add a student who is not yet in the register.
  6. Later: the review waits for you in the class journal, Review button.
  7. Update the register applies what is ticked, and nothing else. The ratings then count in their progress by skill (their file, and My progress on their side).

A confirmed review can still be changed: ✓ Review, in the journal, reopens it.

#What comes next

A class doesn't stop at its review: what you noted prepares the next one, and what the student does at home comes back to you. Three things follow one another.

#The register, up to date

At the next class, you start from the student's file rather than from memory.

With the app. Once the review is confirmed with Update the register, the lesson is in the student's file, among their lessons (see The lessons), and their assessments count towards their progress (see Their progress). After a one-to-one lesson run in the session window, End the lesson files it in their table (see Running a lesson).

On paper. A lesson's report prints by itself, with the scores given to work on, for the student or their parents (see A student's file).

#The work the student sends back

What the student does between two classes matters as much as the class: did they practise, at what tempo, what got stuck? With that, you prepare the lesson instead of asking everything again.

With the app. The student chooses Send my practice to my teacher in the ⋯ menu of their practice plan (see Sending your practice to your teacher): a QR code to show you at class, or a .skreport file to send you by email or by message. In their file, Receive their practice… reads it; you confirm before anything is added (see Their practice at home).

On paper. A sheet given with Boxes for the student is filled in with a pen during the week: the days practised, the tempo, the rating. The student brings it to the next class and you see their week at a glance; with the app, they can also photograph it (My boxes (photo)) and their ratings go into their practice plan (see Your teacher's sheets and The sheet's QR code).

#The next lesson

The student's To work on list keeps what was not seen, what is to be taken up again and what was given; an exercise that is mastered leaves it (see Preparing the next lesson). The setlist The session shows that the lesson has passed: Switch to the next session starts again from the work planned for the next one (see The session setlist). To prepare everything, see Preparing a class.

#On the student's side

This part and the two that follow are written for the student: it is what they see on their device.

With the app. The homework you received is in your Practice plan, and the class is in your Class journal, at the bottom of the Class page: each exercise that was shown can be replayed, kept in My grooves or added to the plan.

A video your teacher gave you (a short demonstration) is in that class in the journal, under Your videos: one click opens it.

  1. The video.
  2. Play or Pause, the position, the speed (50 % or 75 %: the movement in slow motion).

It stays on your device; deleting the class from the journal deletes it too.

On paper. If your teacher gave you a sheet with a QR code, scan it with Scan a QR code: its exercises join your practice plan and the lesson your journal. Without scanning, the sheet is enough: fill in its boxes with a pen during the week, and show it to your teacher at the next class (see Your teacher's sheets).

#What stays in the journal

By default, everything the teacher projects or gives you on paper stays in your Class journal. On a shared device (the family one, the classroom PC), untick Keep in my class journal what the teacher projects or gives on paper in the settings (see The settings): nothing is kept there.

#Content from your teacher

Your teacher can give you exercises for you alone: a .skpersonal file (by email, by message) or a QR code. They are encrypted for your linked device: only your app opens them. Open the file, or scan the QR code; the app shows who it comes from and what you may do with it.

  1. Who it comes from: verified when it is signed by your linked teacher's app.
  2. What your teacher allows: edit it (copy it into a lesson), print it, share it on.
  3. Its exercises can join your practice plan; Keep puts it in your journal.

The app respects these choices: without the right to print, the print sheet doesn't show the exercise; without the right to share it on, a copy only leaves the app sealed, and can't be shared by QR code. What you see and play stays visible: it's a nuisance, not a protection.

Chapter 23Part VII · Teaching

Students

With ten or twenty students, you quickly forget who is working on what and where each one stands. The Teach edition keeps a register of your students: one file per student, what they have to work on, and each of their lessons, with what was worked on, at which tempo, what you think of it, and the photos or documents of the lesson. At the next lesson, you pick up exactly where you left off.

This chapter follows a student from start to finish: the list, their properties, their file, their lessons, your assessment, their progress and their year. Their classes and their dates are in The schedule and the calendar; the school, the teachers and the credits in The school, teachers and credits; the live class in During the class.

At a glance

What forfollowing each student from one lesson to the next: what they worked on, at which tempo, what comes next.

Wherethe Students page (Teach edition).

Key pointsone file per student, with their To work on list. ▶ Start the lesson runs it in a window, for this student alone; End the lesson files everything in the table of their lessons. The live classes they attended are added automatically.

#The student list

The list is a table: one row per student, with what you need to know before a lesson, to see at a glance who hasn't come for a long time or who has a lesson to prepare.

  1. New student: creates a file.
  2. Seen in class, not in the register yet: the students who joined one of your live classes; one click adds them.
  3. A student: a click on their name (or on the row) opens their window; File › opens their full file.
  4. The columns: Level, number of Lessons, Last lesson ("4 days ago"), exercises planned for the Next lesson, exercises Working on and Mastered. A click on a heading sorts the table; a second click reverses the order.

On a phone, the table keeps the student, their last lesson and the next one; the rest is in their window, one tap on the row away.

Schedule (at the top) opens the week's lessons (see The schedule); the Next lesson column gives the date of each student's next lesson.

My school (at the top) describes the school: its places and rooms, its teachers, its logo (see Your school).

Search students filters the list. Archived students are filed apart, under Archived; Restore puts them back in the list.

With the app. In the ⋯ menu at the top of the page, Export and Import export or import the register on its own (a .skroster file, which only opens in the Teach edition), with the photos and documents of the lessons. It is also included in the full backup.

On paper. Print, in the same ⋯ menu, turns the register into a table: one row per active student, with their level, their number of lessons, their last lesson, their last assessment, the number of exercises to work on and their goals.

#A student's properties

To make someone work well, you need to know what they like to play, what they aim for and where they get stuck. A student's window keeps it at hand.

  1. Their figures: lessons, last lesson, next lesson, exercises in progress and mastered.
  2. The student: name, level, their instruments (a click on a chip, + An instrument to add one), contact, parent contact, lesson pace, and Billing (who pays, the address, a reference: free text, the app calculates nothing). A new student gets the school's default instrument.
  3. Their music: the music styles they play (a click on a chip; + Other style to add one), then the target styles and techniques and their gear.
  4. Strengths and points to work on.
  5. For you: their goals and your notes. The Names used in class (the nicknames they join live classes with) are folded at the bottom.
  6. Archive: the student leaves the list without anything being lost. Delete erases their file, all their lessons and their attachments (after confirmation).
  7. Open the file ›.
  8. Save keeps your changes; Cancel forgets them.

A file is often filled in while talking with the student or their parents: a typo in a name slips in quickly. So nothing is saved before Save. Cancel, Esc or ✕ close the window; if you changed something, the app asks first: Save, Don't save, or go back to the window. What is filled in also shows at the top of their file, under their name.

A renamed student keeps their former name among the Names used in class: earlier live classes still find them. And once a class review is confirmed, each student recognised by name stays linked to it through their file, whatever happens to their name later.

#Their availability

Finding a slot for a student starts with knowing when they can come: after school, not on Wednesdays, preferably on Tuesdays. Written down once, it helps every time you look for a time for them (see Suggesting slots). Under Availability (folded at the bottom of their window), paint their typical week:

  1. The brush: Preferred, Possible, Not possible, or Erase.
  2. Press, then drag: the whole block of days and hours takes the brush's colour ("Monday to Friday, 5 pm to 7 pm").
  3. Not possible: no slot will be suggested there.
  4. The summary, in words; it also shows on the folded line.

What isn't painted stays unknown: a slot may fall there, and the suggestion says so. With the keyboard, each cell is a button (arrows to move, Enter to paint). Like the rest of the file, availability is saved with Save.

#Their devices

A student joins classes with their phone, a tablet or the room's PC. Each device linked to their file (in the Class panel, during a class) gets them recognised by itself, whatever nickname they type. At the bottom of their window, Devices lists them, with the name given when linking and its date.

  1. Remove a device that was lost, lent or sold: at the next class, it becomes an unknown device again.

For a student to be recognised even before joining a class, whatever nickname they type, link their app once and for all: Link their app (QR code)…, under Devices. The student scans the QR code with their app (Scan a QR code) and accepts; at the next live class, their app introduces itself and joins their file.

  1. The invitation QR code, for that student.
  2. It is valid for 24 hours, once.

A device linked this way has its StoneID key (the StoneID key label in the list): it signs its arrival at the class, and no other device can take its place. That key is also used to encrypt personal content for them.

#A student's file

At the top, what applies to the whole student: name, level, instruments, goals. The rest is mostly looked at course by course: a student who takes drums and a workshop doesn't have the same dates or the same credits. The file has three tabs: Next lessons (one card per course, see A student's lessons, then what they have to work on), History (their year, then their sessions, by course or in order) and Skills (their progress skill by skill, then exercise by exercise). The chosen tab stays from one visit to the next.

  1. ✎ Properties: the student's window.
  2. 📊 Progress: their dashboard (see Their progress).
  3. ▶ Start the lesson: run the lesson in a window (see Running a lesson).
  4. The next lesson: their To work on list. An exercise, with a link to its score.
  5. Its status: To do, Working on or Mastered.
  6. ♩ reached and ♩ target: the tempo reached and the goal. Next to them, a free remark.
  7. → Send to the class: the student's list waits in the Class screen, for a group class (see Projecting and controlling).
  8. ✓ Lesson done: the planned lesson moves into the table of lessons, dated today, as it is. It is grouped with the same day's live class, if there was one with this student.

A click on an exercise in the list doesn't open the editor: a window offers to See the exercise on its page (the lesson, My grooves, the song study…) or See the original of a variation, and only as an option to Edit in the workshop. The file's scores are Compact (more bars per line, depending on the room, with the playhead) or Large, as you prefer (Score size).

On paper. Print (at the top of the file) prepares a sheet to hand out or file away, and follows the open tab. In the preview, Document switches between them:

  • Student sheet: who they are (level, instruments, goals, styles, contact details, parent contact, billing), and their courses as a table (when, teacher and room, lessons given this year, credits left). The sheet for the folder, or for the front desk.
  • Lessons (from Next lessons): what there is to practise (with the scores, or as a list) and their sessions (all, the last 5 or the last one), course by course with a page break between two courses; Course keeps only one. The sheet to give the student or their parents.
  • Year overview (from History): see Their year.

A lesson report also prints on its own, with the scores given to practise, for the student or their parents.

#Preparing the next lesson

+ Add an exercise opens a choice window: the list on the left (what the student already has to work on, My grooves, the lessons), the preview of the exercise clicked on the right, to listen to before choosing. + Free exercise (text)… adds work with no score (reading, a song, technique), Create in the workshop a groove written for the occasion.

You also add to the list from the rest of the app: the → Student menu of an exercise, of a song study, or of what is projected during a class.

  1. → Student.
  2. Pick the student, or + New student.

An exercise already in the list is not added twice.

#What the exercise works on

An exercise isn't an end in itself: you give it to work on a skill (tempo, coordination, reading) or for a reason that motivates the student (learning this song, preparing the concert). Saying so when you give it helps the student understand, and you follow up: Skill, on an exercise to work on (in their file, or during the lesson).

  1. The skills, sorted by family: your assessment criteria (see Assessing).
  2. A chosen skill.
  3. Motivation: why you give it, in a few words (ideas are suggested).

The exercise then shows its skills and motivation. When you rate it (★ Assess), its rating counts for those skills in the Skills tab (see Skill by skill), except for a criterion you rated separately; given and not yet rated, it appears there as to work on.

#Personal content

Sometimes an exercise is for one student only: an arrangement written for them, a score you don't want to see circulating. Personal content (at the top of their file) encrypts it for their app: only they open it, they know it comes from you, and their app respects what you allow.

  1. For which devices: the student's devices linked by QR code (see Their devices). With no linked device, the app offers to invite them.
  2. The exercises: + Add an exercise (a lesson shipped with the app goes by its name: the student already has it).
  3. What they may do with it: Edit it (copy it into a lesson), Print it, Share it on (QR code, file).
  4. QR code: short content, to scan right away.
  5. Save the file: a .skpersonal file to send them by email or message.

It's a nuisance, not a protection: what the student sees and plays stays visible; their app doesn't print it or let it out unless you allow it.

#The lessons

  1. The table: #, the date and the start of the report, on one line. The live classes the student attended show up by themselves (● Live class), with everything that was shown; they are found through the name they gave when joining.
  2. What is attached to the lesson, as small chips: attachments, exercises worked on (♪), exercises given (→) and the assessment.
  3. Unfolded: the report, in formatted text (bold, italic, highlight, heading, lists). Pasted text arrives without its formatting.
  4. The attachments: photos (as thumbnails), PDFs, sounds, videos. Attach a file, or drop them on the area; on a tablet or phone, Take a photo (an annotated score, the position of the hands). Photos are reduced, other files kept up to 10 MB. A click opens one in large.
  5. Exercises worked on: what was done during the lesson, to annotate like the next lesson.
  6. Given to work on: what the student takes home; + Give to work on also adds it to their To work on list.
  7. Assessment: your view of the lesson.

Expand all opens all the lessons; + New lesson adds one done outside the app (private lesson, exam…).

  1. By course: each course's sessions under its name, numbered within the course; those on a day without a course go under Other sessions. In order: all of them, newest first.
  2. The course, above its sessions.

#Skill by skill

Progress is about skills more than single exercises: rhythm, dynamics, coordination, reading. Each criterion rated in an assessment (of the session, or of an exercise) counts for its skill: the Skills tab gathers them.

  1. Criteria…: the ones you offer when assessing, and yours (see Assessing).
  2. A skill family: Rhythm, Sound and dynamics, Coordination and body, Reading and memory, and your categories.
  3. Their latest marks, as dots, oldest to newest; on hover, the date and the exercise.
  4. The trend: ↗ improving, ↘ slipping (the last three marks against the three before), → steady.
  5. How many marks, and the exercises that worked on it.

#Exercise by exercise

  1. Each exercise worked on: its latest status, its best tempo, and, unfolded, what was noted at each lesson.

#Their practice at home

What the student does between lessons matters as much as the lesson: whether they practised every day or not at all, you don't prepare the session the same way. Their app sends it to you (see Sending your practice to your teacher); the Skills tab of their file shows it.

  1. Receive their practice…: scan the QR code their app shows, or open the .skreport file they sent you (opened directly, the app recognises the student).
  2. How many rated sessions, over how many days, the last one, and when you received it.
  3. Each exercise: how many times, its tempo (from the first to the last), its last rating.
  4. Dashboard: the same as in their app: sessions per week, criteria, tempos.

The student is recognised by their linked app, otherwise by name; you confirm before anything is added. A session received twice counts once.

#Assessing

The student already assesses themselves in their practice plan; your view uses the same words, so you both talk about the same thing. ★ Assess, on an exercise worked on, or Assessment, on a lesson:

  • an overall rating: Bad, OK, Good or Mastered;
  • + Detail by criterion, if you want to go further: tempo, precision, dynamics, coordination, sound… Criteria… chooses the ones you offer, among those of the self-assessment, and adds your own.

In Criteria…, the criteria are filed by skill. A new criterion picks its own, or a New category… of yours (Style, Improvisation, Playing in a band…); ✕ removes a category (its criteria go to Other, the marks stay).

The overall rating shows in the table of lessons, in colour.

#Their progress

📊 Progress opens the student's dashboard, the same as the one of their self-assessment: their regularity, their criteria, their weak points and their tempos, based on their lessons with you. For each exercise worked on, your assessment counts, otherwise its status (Mastered counts as mastered, Working on as OK).

Their progress also reads by skill (rhythm, sound and dynamics, coordination, reading, and your own categories): its level, its curve, the exercises that move it forward or stall. The ratings from a live class review (see The lesson review) count as soon as the register is updated. A student who takes several courses (drums and a workshop): Course shows the progress in one, or All their courses.

#Their year

At the end of term, for a report or a meeting with the parents, you want to see a student's year at a glance: were they there, how many lessons, how many are left.

With the app. At the top of the History tab, Their year shows it month by month.

  1. The school's reference year (School year, Financial year or Custom year: see The year and the calendar; a school year from September otherwise), or Calendar year (January to December). If the reference year is the calendar year, there's nothing to choose.
  2. ‹ and ›: the year before, the year after.
  3. Their figures: lessons done, attendance, hours given, absences, cancelled lessons, upcoming lessons and credits left.
  4. One dot per lesson, month by month, in the colour of its state (done, absent, cancelled, to confirm, upcoming). Click a dot to open the lesson.
  5. All their courses, or just one: the figures and dots then show only that one.

On paper. For the folder, for the parents, or to compare with the office's list: Print, from the History tab, prepares the Year overview, one table per course, one line per date of the course over the period, like the list a teacher keeps by hand.

  1. Document: the student sheet, the lessons, or the year overview.
  2. Course: all their courses (a page break between two), or just one.
  3. Year: this year, or the previous one.
  4. Page: portrait or landscape.
  5. CSV and XLSX: the same table for a spreadsheet (one sheet per course in the XLSX file; the CSV uses the language's separator). For the school's accounts or a report, without copying.
  6. A closed date (holidays, a public holiday), in grey, with its name: the line is there, without a number.
  7. The totals: done (of planned), absences, cancelled, to confirm, to come, hours given, and the credits (bought, used, left).

Each line: the session no. (neither closed days nor cancelled lessons take a number), the date and time, the actual duration, the teacher, who came instead if there was a substitute (a parent taking their daughter's lesson every other week), the state, the reason, whether it was moved and from when, and the credits used.

Chapter 24Part VII · Teaching

The schedule and the calendar

A week of classes is never quite like the one before: a student absent, a make-up lesson, a teacher covering for another, a holiday. This chapter is the year's schedule, kept in the same place as your students. You see what is planned there, you note what took place, and the app works out the counts from it: the lessons given, the absences, the credits left.

We start with the week, then with one lesson: marking it present or absent, moving it, adding a new one. Next come each student's lessons and the group lessons, then the lesson given by another teacher. The rest is used less often: a day off (a concert, a bridge day), printing, your calendar, the slots offered, the planning of the whole school, the year and its calendar.

At a glance

What forseeing the week's lessons, noting what happened, placing and moving lessons.

Wherethe Schedule page (Teach edition), which the Schedule button at the top of the Students page also opens.

Key pointsa click on a lesson opens it (present, absent, move…). The lessons that come back every week are set in the student's file. The school calendar greys out the lessons on closed days.
