#The schedule

Many teachers keep their timetable in a spreadsheet next to the app: who comes when, who was absent, how many lessons are left on the package. The schedule does it in the same place as the register, without ever mixing up two things: what was planned and what really happened. If Alice is absent and another student takes her slot, her absence stays recorded, and what was worked on goes into the file of the student who was there.

Note

StoneKiller records what happened; it does not force reality to fit the plan. Every default (duration, regular lesson, credits) can be changed lesson by lesson.

  1. ‹ Today ›: the week shown.
  2. A planned lesson: the drawing of its instrument, the student, the time, the room and the teacher, and what is planned. Click to open it.
  3. A lesson done (green).
  4. An absence (orange); "Inès → Max": Max took the slot.
  5. A cancelled lesson (struck through).
  6. A closed day (holidays, public holiday, blocked day): that day's regular lessons are greyed out. Clicking a day's name opens it (see A day).
  7. School calendar…: the year's holidays, public holidays, blocked days and events (see The year and the calendar).
  8. + Lesson: a lesson added by hand; clicking an empty spot of the grid adds one at that time.
  9. Day, 5 days, Week: one day in full, the working week (Monday to Friday) or the whole week. The app remembers your choice.
  10. Calendar (.ics): the schedule to your calendar, or events from your calendar to the schedule (see The schedule in your calendar).
  11. Print: the days shown, on paper (see Printing the schedule).
  12. An event (a concert): shown at the top of the day, without hiding anything.
  13. Outside teaching hours, the grid is greyed out (see Teaching hours); when Show picks a teacher, it's their hours. The grid shows those hours; ▲ and ▼, in its corners, open it two hours earlier or later (a lesson at 7 am, a rehearsal at 10 pm), ↺ goes back to the teaching hours. Lessons outside them always stay visible.

On a phone, the week becomes a list, day by day.

Once the school is filled in (see Your school), the schedule takes it into account:

  1. A group lesson: a single block, with the course name and its students, each in the colour of their state (present, absent…). Click to open the group's session (see Group lessons).
  2. ⚠: the room is taken at that time (with the reason), or too small for the group (“4 students for 2 places”). The lesson is still possible: it's a warning, not a ban.
  3. Show: all lessons, those of one teacher or those of one room. Handy in a school with several teachers; the app remembers your choice.

Lessons that come back every week are regular lessons: they are set in the student's file (see A student's lessons), and the schedule repeats them by itself.

#A lesson

It's the everyday gesture: a click on a lesson in the schedule opens it. You start it, or note what happened (the lesson took place, the student was absent, the lesson is cancelled), and you prepare what comes next.

  1. Its state, duration, room, teacher, and whether it comes from the student's regular lesson or was added.
  2. What is planned: for this particular lesson (+ Prepare), and, for the student's next lesson, their To work on list. A free note below (what to bring, why it was moved…).
  3. ▶ Start lesson: the usual lesson window (see Running a lesson), with what is planned. At the end, the lesson is marked done, with its actual duration.
  4. ✓ Present: the lesson took place; it goes into the student's history without details, to complete later if you want. A lesson done keeps its actual duration, to correct in its window (30 minutes of a 90-minute lesson): with a credit worth a time, that is what counts.
  5. Absent: the absence is recorded, with its reason (see below). Then Replace with… starts another student's lesson in this slot.
  6. Move…: another date, time or duration, for this lesson only.
  7. Other teacher…: this lesson is given by another teacher of the school (see A lesson given by another teacher).
  8. + Prepare: an exercise planned for this particular lesson.

A past lesson that was neither started nor marked Present, Absent or Cancelled is to confirm (dotted). If there was a lesson with this student that day (a live class, a lesson run from their file), it counts as done on its own.

The student's name (in a group lesson, each student's) opens their card: their lessons, their credits, what they're working on, without going through the menu. On Android, a time (Move…, the regular lesson, a room's unavailability) is picked in two lists, hours and minutes, or on the dial (the button beside them): the hours (1 to 12 outside, 13 to 00 inside), then the minutes; picking the minutes sets the time and closes the dial.

Cancel lesson… asks who cancels it (the student, the teacher, the school, other), then strikes it through; Restore sets any lesson back to "planned". A changed regular lesson (moved, prepared, cancelled) becomes an exception: Back to the regular lesson removes it. On a closed day, Lesson anyway keeps the lesson.

An absence or a cancellation keeps its reason (The student, The teacher, The school, Other) and a word ("traffic jam", "ill"). The reason says what happened, never what suits: whether it counts is a separate decision. A student stuck in traffic stays recorded absent, reason The student; you may choose not to charge the lesson (Credits counted: Doesn't count), with a word to remember why. The year report and the printed overview then tell the truth, and the package stays right.

A lesson added by hand on a closed day, or outside teaching hours, is allowed: its window flags it, without blocking anything.

#Adding and moving a lesson

A new student, a make-up lesson: the simplest is to put the lesson where it will go, by drawing it. When you hover over the grid, a dashed frame already shows the lesson a click would add, to the nearest quarter of an hour and with your students' usual length. Press, then drag from the start time to the end time: the lesson follows the pointer, with its times and length, and turns orange if it overlaps another one. When you let go, the lesson's window opens, already filled in: all that's left is to choose the student (or the group) and, if they take several courses, which one. Esc cancels the drawing.

  1. The lesson being drawn, with its times and length, while you drag.

On a tablet, press and hold (it vibrates) before dragging; without a long press, the page scrolls as usual.

A student changes their time, a lesson falls on a public holiday: a planned lesson moves the way it is drawn. Grab it and drag it to another time or another day; pull its bottom edge to change its length. The frame shows where it goes, with its times, and turns orange if it overlaps another one: that is allowed, the two lessons then share the column. When you let go, for a regular lesson, the app asks:

  • This lesson only: an exception; the other weeks keep their time;
  • The series from here: this lesson and the next ones move to the new day and time; past weeks never move. For a lesson already past, only that lesson moves.
  1. The lesson you are moving, faded.
  2. Where it goes, with its times and length.

A lesson done, marked absent or cancelled does not move: it is what happened. Esc cancels the move; a simple click still opens the lesson.

#A student's lessons

A student often takes more than one course: drums on Tuesday, piano on Monday, a group workshop. Each has its time, its room, its teacher and its package; putting everything into a single rule would get the credits wrong. The Next lessons tab of their file keeps them apart, under Their courses: one card per course, with everything about it.

  1. A course: its instrument, its name, its regular lessons (day, time, frequency), its teacher and its room.
  2. A group lesson, with the other students (see Group lessons).
  3. The course…: its settings.
  4. Credits…: its package (see Credits).
  5. Its year: lessons done ("12 of 36 planned", when the course says how many it plans), absences, cancelled lessons, and credits left. On hover, since when it counts.
  6. To confirm: past lessons with nothing recorded (not present, not absent, not cancelled, and no session that day). A click opens the schedule of their week, to mark them.
  7. Its next three dates, with what is planned; click one to open it.
  8. + Regular course: a new course for them, alone or in a group, that comes back every week.
  9. + One-off lesson: an extra date, outside their regular lessons (a make-up lesson); these dates have their own card, One-off lessons.
  10. Calendar (.ics): their upcoming lessons, as a file for their calendar or their parents'.

Under the cards, one line counts all their courses together.

  1. The course name (“Drums”, “Groove workshop”); without a name, the course takes its instrument's.
  2. The instrument: its drawing goes with the course on the file and in the schedule.
  3. The type: Individual lesson or Group lesson, and its students.
  4. The normal duration, the usual teacher and room (the school's are offered).
  5. A regular lesson: day, time, its duration if it isn't the normal one, the frequency (every week, every 2 weeks…), and the period (from… to…). A course can have several (Tuesday and Thursday).
  6. + Regular lesson. A new regular lesson runs from the chosen day to the end of the period (the school year, or the teacher's period).
  7. Lessons planned in the period: how many lessons the period should count (36 in the year); next to it, how many the regular lessons really give, holidays and closed days removed, in red if some are missing. Suggested slots and the year overview use it.
  8. The availability of its students, as a reminder: it is set in one place only, each student's window; the link leads there.
  9. Count lessons in credits: for a package. Without the box, the app counts nothing: lessons take place, that's all. With it, each lesson done uses credits, and what is left shows everywhere (the file, the schedule, the overview).
  10. For a package: whether a student's absence counts a credit (an absence announced too late, for example), and what a credit is worth for this course (otherwise the teacher's or the school's).

Changing the day or time of a regular lesson doesn't rewrite the past: the old schedule ends the day before, the new one applies from today. At the bottom of the window, Stop this course ends its regular lessons yesterday (past lessons stay in the history); Delete this course removes it.

A register from before version 0.21 loses nothing: each student's regular lessons become their first course, with its credits.

#Group lessons

A workshop, a lesson for several students: it is a single course, but each student has their attendance, their credits and their history. In the course settings, choose Group lesson, then add its students.

  1. Group lesson.
  2. Its students: + Add a student, ✕ to remove one. A student who joins during the year only counts from today; one who leaves keeps their past lessons.
  3. The room: its capacity is compared with the number of students.

In the schedule, the group's session is a single block. Click to open it:

  1. ⚠: the room is taken, or too small for the group.
  2. Present or Absent, student by student: each gets the session in their file, and their credits.
  3. ✓ All present: the whole group in one click.
  4. ▶ Live class: the Class page, to teach the group live (project, follow each student; see Live classes).
  5. The course…: its settings.

Cancel lesson cancels the session for the whole group; Move… moves the whole session, and dragging it in the schedule moves the series from there.

#A lesson given by another teacher

A course is a student (or a group) and their teacher, all year long. But one day Claire is ill and Julian stands in; another day, Julian takes the lesson because he knows the piece better. The course doesn't change teacher for all that: only that one lesson is given by someone else.

Other teacher… (in the window of a lesson, or of a group lesson) picks a teacher of the school (My school › Teachers, see Teachers). If the school has no other teacher, the Add a teacher window opens (see Adding a teacher): the teacher you add gives this lesson.

  1. The school's teachers, with their instruments; The course's teacher gives it back.
  1. The lesson says who gives it, and whom they replace; the schedule marks it ↔ (a filter on a teacher shows the lessons they really give).

It's an exception for that day: the following weeks keep the course's teacher, and nothing in the past changes. During the lesson too, the Start lesson window has a Teacher choice (when the school has several): the session keeps who gave it, and the schedule shows it.

#A day

A concert on Friday, a teacher's training day, a bridge day: clicking a day's name, at the top of its column, opens it.

  1. The lessons planned that day, and how many are hidden by what is recorded.
  2. What already marks this day (here, an event): its kind, its dates, its name, who it's for; ✕ removes it.
  3. Mark this day: Event, Blocked day, Holidays, Public holiday or School closed. Under the buttons, what it changes.
  4. Its name ("School concert"), until which day, and For: the whole school, or one teacher.
  5. Add.
  6. The year's calendar…: the whole year (see The year and the calendar).

A blocked day never gets a lesson on its own: regular lessons don't land on it, and suggested slots skip it. But you can always add a lesson there by hand (a make-up lesson, an exam), without unblocking anything. An event hides nothing: it shows at the top of the day, and goes into the exported calendar.

#Printing the schedule

On paper. A sheet on the staff-room wall, the schedule to hand to a substitute: Print (in the schedule) prepares the days shown, with the chosen filter (a teacher, a room), with the school's header. Everything the view shows is printed, lessons on a closed day included (in grey, with the name of the closure).

  1. View: Day, 5 days or Week.
  2. Layout: Graphic (as on screen) (the grid of hours: each lesson in its place and at its height, side by side when they overlap), Day by day (one table per day: the time, the student, the room, the state) or One column per day (a list per day).
  3. Page: Depends on the view (the grid in landscape, a single day in portrait), Portrait or Landscape.
  4. Planned for this lesson: with or without the work planned for each lesson.
  5. What marks a day (an event, holidays); a closed day is hatched.
  6. A lesson: the time, the student (or the group lesson and its students), the room and the teacher, and its state.

A group lesson fits in one block, with its students. Print then opens the usual print dialog: on paper, or as a PDF (see Printing).

#The schedule in your calendar

Your calendar (Outlook, Google, Apple) goes everywhere with you, and your students or their parents have theirs. Calendar (.ics) moves the lessons from one to the other through a file: no account, no sync.

  • Export the planning: an .ics file with the lessons and the calendar (holidays, public holidays, blocked days, events) of the next 26 weeks, as the schedule shows them (moved lessons and closed days included). Open it in your calendar. Exported again after changes, it updates the lessons instead of doubling them.
  • On a student's file, Calendar (.ics) makes the same file with their lessons only: to send to them, or to their parents.
  • Import an .ics file: the upcoming events of your calendar, each with what it will become.
  1. An event whose title contains a student's name: a lesson for that student.
  2. An unrelated event: nothing is imported.
  3. A whole day: Holidays, a Public holiday, a Blocked day or an Event (the app guesses from the title; change it if needed). It goes into the school calendar.
  4. Import: what is chosen goes into the schedule.

Change whatever you like before importing. An event already imported is flagged, and does not go in twice. The file does not link the two: what changes later in your calendar only comes back into the schedule with a new import.

#Suggesting slots

Finding a time for a new student, or for a group of four, means cross-checking a lot: the teacher's hours, everyone's availability, free and equipped rooms, the lessons already set. In a course's window, Suggest slots does that work and offers two or three slots; you choose.

  1. Suggest slots, under the regular lessons.
  2. A slot in a typical week: the day, the times, the room.
  3. Why this one: preferred or possible for whom, the room equipped with the course's instrument, right after another of the teacher's lessons, closed weeks.
  4. Choose: the slot becomes a regular lesson (from next week), with its room. Nothing is saved before Save.

The rules are simple, and you can always override them:

  • never outside the teacher's hours (or the school's); never when a student said Not possible;
  • never when the teacher or a student already has a lesson, nor in a room that is taken or too small;
  • preferred hours first, then possible ones, and different days; a room equipped with the instrument comes first;
  • the next four weeks are checked: a week when that day is closed (holidays, blocked day) doesn't count, and the suggestion says so.

No slot? Widen the hours, or add the lesson by hand: everything is still allowed.

#Planning the school

At the start of the year, or when everything changes (one more teacher, one room less), placing lessons one by one takes long, and the order matters: the first one placed takes the best slot. Plan the school… (at the top of the schedule) places all regular lessons at once, one teacher's or the whole school's, with the same rules as Suggesting slots. It's a proposal: nothing changes until you adopt, lesson by lesson.

  1. Priority: who goes first, and so chooses their slot: Long-standing students first, Order of enrolment, or Least available first (whoever has only one possible slot keeps it).
  2. Keep current times when possible: a lesson that still fits where it is stays there; only the others move.
  3. The proposed slot, with its room: blue, a lesson that changes; red, No place.
  4. Why: its turn (the number), what put it there (kept in place, long-standing student, enrolled early, few possible times), then what makes the slot good.
  5. Adopt: the lesson moves to this time from the chosen date; earlier weeks don't change.
  6. Don't move: this lesson stays where it is when you run Propose again.

A lesson without a place is never forced: widen the hours, free a room or pin other lessons, then run it again.

#The year and the calendar

Holidays and public holidays change every year, and don't fall the same way for everyone: a music school follows the school year, an association its financial year, a studio the calendar year. The reference year divides up the calendar and each student's year; the calendar records, year by year, the days when regular lessons don't take place. Once recorded, each week's lessons take it into account on their own: no regular lesson falls during the holidays.

  1. Reference year: School year (from the start of term to the summer), Calendar (January to December), Financial (from a chosen day: 6 April, 1 July) or Custom (each year's dates: 24 August to 3 July; + A year adds one, and between two, the app falls back to the school year).
  2. The month term starts (school year), or the day and month it starts (financial).
  3. The current year, its dates and what is in the calendar.
  4. School calendar…: the year's holidays, public holidays, blocked days and events.
  5. The school's teaching hours (see Teaching hours).

Public holidays are calculated (Easter, Ascension and Whit Monday move every year): no need to look them up. In the calendar, Public holidays… offers them for the year:

  1. The country: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Germany, Austria, the United Kingdom, the United States or Canada. The app remembers your choice.
  2. A public holiday, ticked: untick those that don't concern you.
  3. A regional day (St Andrew's Day in Scotland, Good Friday in Alsace-Moselle, a holiday of a single canton, state or province) isn't ticked: tick it if it concerns you. Those already in the calendar are greyed out.
  4. Add the ticked days.

School holidays, on the other hand, are decided each year (by the ministry, the region, the canton): add them, copy last year's, or import the official .ics file.

  1. ‹ and ›: the year before, the year after; Reference year… leads to its setting.
  2. The year's summary: its dates, its holidays, its public holidays, its blocked days and its events.
  3. Public holidays….
  4. + Holidays, + Blocked day, + Event: one more line, to date.
  5. Copy last year: the previous year's holidays and blocked days, 52 weeks later (the same weekdays). Official dates change from one year to the next: check them.
  6. Import a calendar (.ics)…: official holidays are often published in this format (see The schedule in your calendar).
  7. A line: its kind, its dates (from… to…), its name, and For: The whole school, or one teacher (a training course, leave); it then only affects their lessons.

The kinds of days:

  • Holidays, Public holiday, School closed: no regular lessons.
  • Blocked day: no regular lessons, and suggested slots skip it; a lesson added by hand is still allowed (a make-up lesson, an exam).
  • Event (a concert, a meeting): shown in the schedule and in the exported calendar, without hiding anything.

Nothing is deleted: a regular lesson on a closed day is greyed out in the schedule, and Lesson anyway keeps it. A day can also be marked from the schedule, by clicking its name (see A day).

Chapter 25Part VII · Teaching

The school, teachers and credits

A course is given somewhere, with someone, and often for a package. This chapter describes that setting: the school, its rooms, its teachers, its teaching hours and the credits. Filled in once, it is offered everywhere, in the classes, the schedule and the printouts, and the app can warn you when a room is taken or a class falls outside the hours. This is the Teach edition, whether you teach alone or in a school with several teachers.

We start with your school (its name, its places and its rooms), then its teachers: adding one, and saying who gives a class or a session. Next come the teaching hours, which frame the schedule, and the credits, which count the packages. The last topic is sharing the school with another teacher, by a file.

At a glance

What fordescribing the school once (places, rooms, teachers, teaching hours) and counting the packages, so that the classes and the schedule offer it everywhere.

Wherethe My school page, button at the top of the Students page (Teach edition); the credits, in the student's file (Credits…).

Key pointsadd your places, your rooms and your teachers; the Teacher list and the Room or place of a class then offer them. Another teacher receives the school by a .skroster file.

In this chapter

  1. Your school00
  2. Teachers00
  3. Teaching hours00
  4. Credits00
  5. Sharing the school with another teacher00

#Your school

In a music school, the same things come back at every lesson: the room, the teacher, the instrument. Typing them every time means “Room 2” here and “room2” there, and not seeing that a room is already taken by the choir. My school (at the top of the student list) describes them once; courses and the schedule then offer them everywhere.

  1. The school: its name, its address and its logo, at the top of every printout (see Printing); the default instrument, offered for a new student and their first course. The year and the calendar have their own part (see The year and the calendar).
  2. Places and rooms: a place (the conservatory, an annex), its address, then its rooms. + A place, + A room. A place that isn't open during the school's hours (an annex on Saturday mornings) has its own Opening hours.
  3. A room's capacity: how many students it holds. The schedule flags a group lesson too large for it.
  4. Its equipment: instruments (a drum kit, a piano) and the rest (Other…: an amp, a whiteboard).
  5. Availability…: when the room isn't free.
  6. Teachers: their name, their contact (phone, email) and their instruments (see Teachers).

In a class, Room or place offers these rooms when you type. Write it as in the school, with the name of the place if there are several (“Conservatoire · Room 2”): that is how the schedule recognises the room, flags it as taken or too small, and how suggested slots choose it. Other text is allowed, but without a warning.

A room that is taken is often taken every week, at the same time, with exceptions: the choir every Tuesday, except on concert day. Availability… describes it like a calendar series.

  1. The reason (“taken by the choir”, “building work”): the schedule shows it on a lesson planned in that room at that time.
  2. The series: the day, the times (or all day), the frequency, and the period (from… to…).
  3. Free on this day: a date when the room is free anyway; the rest of the series doesn't move. ✕ puts the date back into the series.
  4. + Every week (a series) or + Once (building work, from… to…).

The school is saved with the register and goes into its backup (.skroster). Imported on another device, it joins the school already there: places, rooms and teachers merge by identifier, without duplicates.

#Teachers

A class says who gives it: in the schedule, in the student's file, on the printouts. So the school keeps the list of its teachers, so that their name is always written the same way and the app knows each one's hours and rules. This list is in My school, section Teachers: one line per teacher.

Their names are offered in courses and the schedule. A renamed teacher is renamed everywhere: their courses, sessions and blocked days follow.

On a teacher's line:

  • their name and their contact (phone, email); the contact stays in this list;
  • their instruments (+ Instrument adds one, ✕ removes one): they show when you choose another teacher for a session;
  • their Teaching hours: without hours of their own, these are the school's (see Teaching hours);
  • A credit is worth and Their lesson period: only if they differ from the school's (see Credits). Empty, the period is the school's year; filled in, their new regular lessons take these dates (the lessons start later, end earlier);
  • ✕ (Remove the teacher) takes them off the list. The lessons and sessions that carry their name keep it, but the app no longer finds their hours, their period or their credit.

Teaches at (on a teacher's line, when the school has several places): the places where they teach. Slots suggested for their lessons only look for a room there.

#Adding a teacher

A teacher adds a teacher in a window (their name, their contact); in a lesson or a session, the Teacher list offers the school's teachers and + Add a teacher…, the same window, without leaving the lesson.

The Add a teacher window asks for their Teacher's name and their Contact. OK adds them to the list; Cancel, Esc or ✕ close the window without adding anything. In a class, the added teacher is chosen straight away. Their instruments, places and hours are then set in My school.

#A course's teacher

Each class has its usual teacher. You choose them from the Teacher list, among the school's; No teacher leaves the box empty. The list is in the class's setting (The course…, from the student's file), and also in the window that adds a class by hand or moves it. For a new class, it starts from the name you gave in the Settings (Your name).

This choice matters: it is the teacher's name that links the class to its line in My school. Their teaching hours, their period and what a credit is worth for them apply to the classes that carry their name, and the suggested slots keep to them.

#A substitute

One day, a class's teacher is ill or held up: another teacher at the school can give that session, without the class changing teacher. Other teacher…, in the class window, chooses them from the teachers on the list (see A lesson given by another teacher); if the school has no other, the Add a teacher window opens in its place.

When the teacher themselves is away for several days (a training course, leave), note it in the school calendar: the line has a For choice, which can be that teacher alone; only their classes are then affected (see The year and the calendar).

#Teaching hours

A school doesn't teach at all hours: 2 pm to 8 pm on weekdays, Saturday mornings; each teacher has their days. Teaching hours grey out the rest of the schedule and frame the suggested slots. They forbid nothing: a lesson can always be added by hand outside them, and its window only flags it ("Outside that day's teaching hours: allowed, your call").

They're set at three levels, from the broadest to the most precise: the school (Teaching hours, in Year and calendar), a place (Opening hours, if it has its own), a teacher (on their line). With no hours written, nothing is greyed out.

  1. A painted cell: the teacher teaches at that time. Press, then drag to paint a block (Monday to Thursday, 3 pm to 8 pm); a block started on a painted cell erases it.
  2. In the background, the school's hours: the teacher's fit within them.
  3. The summary, in words ("Mon–Tue 15:00–20:00 · …").
  4. Remove these hours: the teacher goes back to the school's.

#Credits

Many students pay a package rather than each class: ten classes in advance, for example. Credits tell you what is left for them, without a spreadsheet alongside. They are switched on class by class (see A student's lessons).

Credits are deliberately simple: you record purchases (+10 for a ten-lesson package); each lesson done uses some, and so does each absence (unless you unticked A student's absence counts a credit). No invoices or payments: only what is left. Each course has its own package: drum credits don't pay for piano.

What a credit is worth. By default, a credit = a lesson. But a student sometimes comes for 30 minutes of a 90-minute lesson, or two lessons don't last the same: a credit can then be worth a time (10, 15, 30… minutes). It is set at three levels: the school (My school, Lessons part), the teacher (on their line), then the course (in its settings, A credit is worth); the most precise wins. A lesson done then counts its actual duration: 45 minutes at 15 minutes per credit is 3 credits.

In the Credits… window:

  • the summary: bought, used, left, and what that makes in lessons;
  • the ledger: each line with its kind (Purchase, Correction, Carry-over), its date and its word; ✕ removes one, after confirmation;
  • Note the purchase: credits paid for;
  • Correct: +x or −y at any time, with a mandatory reason (a lesson offered, a mistake): everything stays recorded;
  • Carry over: credits left to another package course of the student (the next year, another instrument). Nothing is lost: the same course from one year to the next simply keeps its balance.

A lesson's count can also be changed in its window (Credits counted: Doesn't count, 1, 2…): a student absent for a reason you don't want to charge, without touching the reason.

#Sharing the school with another teacher

In a school with several teachers, each has their own app, and nobody wants to copy everything again: the rooms, the calendar, the students. Without a server, the school is shared by file: one teacher exports it, the others import it, and everything merges by identifier, without duplicates.

  1. Export the school: a .skroster file with the school (places, rooms, teachers, hours, year), the calendar, the students (name, instruments, availability, contact) and their lessons, with moved or cancelled lessons.
  2. Import a teacher's school: another teacher's file. The import window shows what is new, identical or different; a conflict is settled there.

What belongs to each teacher doesn't go: sessions, reports, your notes and goals for each student, credits, linked devices. An imported student keeps, at the other teacher's, what was already there. Exchange again when the school changes (a teacher, a room, a student, a time); automatic sync will come with StoneKiller Academy.

Chapter 26Part VIII · Step by step

Step by step

Complete examples, from the first click to the result. Each one fits in a few steps and points to the chapter that describes each screen in detail.

In this chapter

  1. My 15-minute session00
  2. Raising the tempo of a hard groove00
  3. Learning a groove limb by limb00
  4. Preparing a lesson for my students00
  5. Giving a live class00
  6. Following a student from week to week00
  7. Writing down a groove heard in a song00
  8. Building a series of independence exercises00
  9. Preparing an exercise sheet00
  10. Switching devices without losing anything00

#My 15-minute session

The goal: work every day on what matters, without wondering what to do.

  1. Open the Practice plan page. Today's exercise is at the top, at the tempo where you left off.
  2. To frame the work, open Session in the player, choose 3 minutes, then Start the session.
  3. Play. Too fast? − lowers it by 5 BPM, right away: better slow and clean.
  4. Rate honestly: Bad, OK, Good or Mastered. The next reminder and the next tempo are worked out for you.
  5. Move on to the next exercise. When today's list is empty, you are done.

Further reading: The practice plan, Self-assessment and progress.

#Raising the tempo of a hard groove

The goal: go from 70 to 100 BPM on a groove without losing cleanliness.

  1. Add the groove to your plan (+ Practice plan). On today's exercise, set the Steady tempo to 100: that is the goal.
  2. Every day, play it at the Current tempo offered and rate it. Each Good raises the tempo by about 5%; a Bad brings it down a little.
  3. For an extra push, open the Metronome in Groove mode, write the groove in Edit the groove, then tick Speed up or slow down: +2 BPM every 4 bars, from your current tempo up to 100. Stop at the first slip: the tempo shown is your limit for the day.
  4. Open + Details when you rate, and give your last steady tempo: My progress turns it into a curve.
  5. When you hold 100 without mistakes, the app offers Mastered.

Further reading: Speeding up or slowing down, Steady tempo and target tempo.

#Learning a groove limb by limb

The goal: get a groove in place when the coordination resists.

  1. Open the exercise and lower the tempo by 20 BPM.
  2. Instruments: mute the bass drum. The app plays the hands, you play the foot alone, listening to where it falls against the snare.
  3. Unmute the bass drum and mute the hi-hat: you play the hi-hat over the rest.
  4. Unmute everything and play the whole exercise with the app, then switch Drums off to play it with the click alone.
  5. If only one passage is stuck, start a Session with Each bar ×4: each bar loops four times before the next.

Further reading: Muting instruments, Sessions.

#Preparing a lesson for my students

The goal: a lesson ready to play, with its tempos, to give to the students.

  1. Lessons › New lesson, then give it a title.
  2. Add a Part ("Warm-up"), then Exercises: write them in the grid, start from an existing groove (Start from an existing groove…), or go through ✦ Create with the workshop….
  3. In ☰ Outline, give each exercise its Steady tempo (and a Target if you want to push). Whole section sets every exercise of a part at once.
  4. View lesson and play it: this is what the students will see.
  5. To hand it out: Export creates a .sklessons file to send; or project it during a live class. For a specific student, → Student adds an exercise to their next lesson.

Further reading: Creating a lesson, Sharing lessons.

#Giving a live class

The goal: the whole class on the same exercise, at the same tempo, each on their own screen.

  1. In StoneKiller Teach, installed on Windows or Android: Class › Start the class.
  2. The students join: the student app finds the class by itself; a phone scans the QR code.
  3. Project an exercise: it appears for everyone. Your player drives theirs: play, stop and tempo.
  4. Give as homework the projected exercise, with its tempos.
  5. End the class: the homework goes into each student's Practice plan, and everything shown into their journal.

No Wi-Fi in the room? The Teach app on Android creates one. Further reading: Live classes.

#Following a student from week to week

The goal: know at each lesson where every student stands.

  1. After the class, open Students: the class appears in the file of every student who attended.
  2. For each exercise, choose To do, Working on or Mastered, the tempo reached and a remark.
  3. Prepare the Next lesson: add the exercises for the following week.
  4. At the next lesson, the file shows what was planned: one click projects these exercises.

Further reading: The student register.

#Writing down a groove heard in a song

The goal: work out a groove by ear, keep it and practise it.

  1. Workshop › Groove editor. Set the tempo with the metronome's Tap if you don't know it.
  2. Start with the skeleton: bass drum and snare. Click in the grid, listen, compare with the song.
  3. Add the hi-hat or the ride, then the details: ghost notes (Ghost brush), hi-hat openings (Open brush).
  4. ★ Save…: give it a name (the song title) and file it in My grooves, in a "Repertoire" list.
  5. From its card: + Practice plan to work on it, Print for the music stand.

Do you have an electronic kit? Play it and let Record write it down. Further reading: The grid editor, The workshop.

#Building a series of independence exercises

The goal: 20 hand exercises over a foot ostinato, from the simplest to the hardest, in a few clicks.

  1. Workshop › Ostinato.
  2. Cells: tick the generated cells with 1 note (the four positions of one note in a beat).
  3. Fixed part: choose a model, for example "Bass drum on the beats + hi-hat foot on 2 and 4". ▶ Listen to the ostinato.
  4. Combinations › Generate, length one bar, progressive order: the list goes from AAAA to the most varied combinations.
  5. ☑ Pick and arrange…: keep the first 20, then ★ Save as a new list.
  6. Open the list in My grooves and start Practice: each exercise plays 4 times, then the next. ★ Rate rates the series at the end.

Further reading: Ostinato and Combinations, Rating a whole series.

#Preparing an exercise sheet

The goal: a clean sheet, with a title and instructions, for the music stand or the students.

  1. Under each exercise you want, click Print queue (or Print queue at the top of a lesson to take everything).
  2. Open the Print page: the exercises are in the queue.
  3. Add a Title, an instruction Text, and reorder with ↑ ↓.
  4. Layout: Compact or 2 columns to fit on one page.
  5. Print: choose the printer, or "Save as PDF" to send it.

Further reading: Printing.

#Switching devices without losing anything

The goal: get your lessons, grooves, practice plan and sounds back on a new computer or phone.

  1. On the old device: My grooves › Full backup. A .skbackup file is created.
  2. Send it to the new device (USB stick, email, cloud).
  3. Install StoneKiller on the new device, then My grooves › Restore and choose the file.
  4. Set the device preferences again (name, display, count-in) in Settings: they do not travel.

Further reading: Backing up and switching devices.

Chapter 27Part IX · Reference

Settings, sounds and data

The Settings adapt the app to your device and to the way you work: the page that opens at launch, your name for classes, how scores are displayed, the count-in, the self-assessment and the drum sounds. This chapter also explains where your data is kept.

At a glance

What foradapting the app to your device and to the way you work, and knowing where your data is.

WhereSettings, at the bottom of the menu (on a phone, in More).

Key pointsyour name for classes, the score engraving, the count-in and the sounds; your data stays on the device.

In this chapter

  1. The settings00
  2. Drum sounds00
  3. Bluetooth: the sound delay00
  4. Language and theme00
  5. Where is my data?00
  6. About00

#The settings

  1. Mode: Simple (the “I want to…” home, the categories in the menu, the essential settings) or Full (every page and every setting; see Simple or full). The change is immediate.
  2. Start screen: the page the app opens at launch. By default the Home page in simple mode, the Metronome in full mode, to start playing right away; otherwise any page of the menu (Lessons, Songs, Practice plan…), or The last page opened, to pick up where you left off. With the metronome, also choose its mode (or The one used last time) and whether it opens full screen.
  3. Menu and home…: the page that sets the categories (order, colour), the home tiles and the menu pages, with a preview (see At startup).
  4. Interface: New (the menu on the side, at the bottom on a phone) or Classic (the tabs at the top, as before version 0.10). Both lead to the same pages, only the way there changes; the app reloads to switch from one to the other.
  5. Connection for live classes:
    • Local network (automatic): the default setting, nothing to configure;
    • School server: for schools that have installed a StoneKiller server; ask the administrator for the address, then Test connection;
    • Demo in this browser (tabs): to try class mode on your own, with two browser tabs, a teacher and a student;
    • None: in the student edition, the Class page disappears; the Teach edition keeps it.

Between the interface and the connection, Language: the choice of language (its flag and its name), and Languages… to add one or correct a translation (see Language and theme).

Further down:

  • Your name: the one the teacher sees during classes. The connection and the name apply with Save;
  • My classes: Keep in my class journal what the teacher projects or gives on paper (ticked by default): each class and each scanned sheet stays on the device, with its exercises to play again. On a shared device (the family one, the classroom PC), untick it: nothing is kept there. Below, My teachers: the teachers your app is linked to (see Linking your app to your teacher), with Remove to forget a link;
  • Display: the score engraving (standard drum key, or GrooveScribe's conventions) and, on a phone, opening reading mode as soon as an exercise starts, the number of bars per line in reading mode, in portrait and in landscape, and the dots on repeats (which pass of a ×N bar is playing);
  • Count-in: none, 1 or 2 bars of click before a session or a run-through, and optionally before every ▶ playback. As many clicks as there are beats in the bar: 4 in 4/4, 3 in 3/4, 2 in 2/4;
  • Metronome: the look of the lights, the pendulum and the rhythm wheel, the wheel on the Polyrhythms page, and full screen on a phone (see Look: lights and pendulum);
  • Online services: YouTube, Vimeo and SoundCloud, on or off for song studies; nothing goes to a service until it is on, and unticking it stops its player at once (see Creating a study and “Privacy” below). The Privacy button gives the summary;
  • Self-assessment: the details per criterion and the criteria offered (see Choosing your criteria);
  • the app edition (StoneKiller or Teach).

The other settings apply right away. In simple mode, everything after Display (the connection, the count-in, the metronome, song studies, assessment, the edition) is folded into More settings, at the bottom of the page.

At the very bottom, Development gathers what is still being tried out. In a stable version, Experimental features opens the features marked Experimental: today, scores from other software (Guitar Pro, MusicXML, MIDI; see Scores from other software). They work, but may still change: you try them knowingly. Reload the page (or reopen the app) to see the change. Their entries show even when the box is unticked (with the Experimental badge): the first time, the app offers to tick it for you. Nightly versions always have them. Features marked dev only exist on the development server (for the app's developers): they're in no released version.

#The profile

At the top of Startup, the Profile sets in one go what you see without unfolding anything: the mode, the menu order and its folded pages, the bottom bar, the order of the spaces and the start screen (see At startup: what you're here for).

  1. The current profile, or set by hand (not saved yet) when your layout matches none.
  2. Choose a profile… reopens the startup window.
  3. Save as a profile… keeps the current layout under a name. Your profiles are offered at startup (My profiles) and listed here, with Apply and ✕; saving under an existing name replaces it.
  4. Ask me again next time I start: the question comes back at every launch while it's checked.

#Drum sounds

Every drum kit sounds different, and phone speakers do not sound like headphones. The sounds page lets you choose, stroke by stroke, the sound that suits you: a drier snare, a brighter ride, or your own recording. Settings › Configure sounds opens it.

  1. Preset: a preset changes everything at once ("All Salamander", for example). An All … preset ticks a source for each stroke: the kit's, otherwise the first one in the fallback order that has it; you see what will sound, nothing is guessed during playback. You can save your own mix under a name: it joins My presets, and is erased with Delete preset.
  2. The circle chooses the sound for the stroke, among the sources offered: the banks you have installed, the app's free kits (CrocellKit, the starting one, Aasimonster, Salamander, AVL…) and, for the metronome, the clicks the app makes itself. The chosen box turns blue.
  3. ▶ listens without changing anything, so you can compare before choosing.
  4. Import adds your own sound to the stroke (audio file up to 5 MB). It stays on your device.
  5. If missing: what plays when the chosen bank has no such sound: the next source (in the fallback order set at the top), another stroke of the same instrument (the normal stroke instead of the ghost note, for example), or nothing.
  6. Volume: the volume of the stroke in the mix.

Instruments are grouped by category (feet, snare, hi-hat, cymbals, toms, percussion, metronome); click a name to expand it. At the start of each row, the note as it is written in the score. The What plays column shows the sound actually played; an orange frame marks a fallback sound, and the ≈ sign a simulated sound (a flam, drag or buzz built from single strokes). ▶ Play a groove plays a short groove that goes through almost every instrument.

Each stroke also has its own Volume in the mix (from −12 to +12 dB, ↺ to go back to the default), under its name. Why per stroke: the second bass drum, crash 2 or the open hi-hat don't sit at the same level as their neighbours; each one is set on its own, without touching the others. The categories (feet, cymbals…) are only there to sort. The bass drum starts at +6 dB: without it, on laptop or phone speakers, a snare played at the same moment almost completely covers it. A volume set for a whole instrument in an earlier version stays the volume of its strokes until you change one.

#Sound banks

A sound bank is a whole drum kit in a .skaudio file: a kit recorded by someone else, your school's kit, or sounds your teacher has prepared. It adds to the free kits without waiting for a new version of the app, and is removed just as easily.

To install one, open the file (double-click, drag it onto the window, or Import) or click + Import a bank (.skaudio) at the top of the sounds page. Before installing, the app shows what the bank contains and who published it:

  1. Who made the sounds, under which licence, and what the bank brings: the number of strokes and the size.
  2. Who published it: "Verified: published by StoneKiller" when the bank is signed by StoneKiller and has not changed since. A bank that is not signed, or signed by an unknown publisher, installs too, with a warning: only install it if you know where it comes from. A bank that claims to be signed by StoneKiller but was changed afterwards is refused.
  3. Play the whole kit with …: ticked, the bank becomes the current setting; unticked, it joins the sources, and you choose its sounds stroke by stroke.
  1. The installed bank: its version, author, licence and who published it. Remove deletes it from the device; the strokes that used it move on to the next sources.
  2. Its preset, All …, joins the list of presets.
  3. Its place in the fallback order: at the top when it plays the whole kit; otherwise right after the chosen kit, or at the end if you had changed your setting. A stroke it does not have moves on to the next source.

A bank with the same identifier as an installed bank replaces it (the window shows the version it replaces). It stays on the device: the full backup does not include it, so keep the file to install it elsewhere. An installed bank plays, but cannot be edited or exported again in the app: its sounds belong to whoever made them. Only the bank-making tool (separate) builds one, from its own sounds.

Note

Banks are made from a folder of sounds, with a development-only tool: see Drum sounds.

#Bluetooth: the sound delay

Bluetooth delivers the sound late, often by 0.15 to 0.3 s depending on the headphones or speaker, and the device does not always report it to the app. The playhead, the metronome lights and, in class, following the teacher then look ahead of what you hear: confusing when you play while reading.

Settings › Sound delay (Bluetooth) lines all of this up again:

  1. Connect your headphones or speaker, then Calibrate….
  2. Start: the app plays 16 regular clicks. Tap the big button (or the space bar) together with each click, by ear, without watching the screen.
  3. The measured delay is shown. If your taps were regular, Apply; otherwise, Start again.

The slider also sets the delay by hand. Then check with the metronome: the lights and the pendulum should land with the click. The setting applies to the device: set it back to 0 when you go back to a cable or the built-in speaker, and calibrate again when you change headphones.

Note

This setting does not make the sound arrive sooner: it lines up what you see with what you hear (and, in class, the moment your device plays). To record with a microphone, the measurement to make is still Measure latency, in the Record tool.

#Language and theme

You choose the language at the bottom of the menu (on a phone, in More), in the welcome window, or in Settings › Language: French, English or German. Each language has its flag: you find yours at a glance, even in an app shown in a language you don't read.

  1. The current language, its flag and its name: a click opens the list.
  2. A language: one click, and the whole app switches to it.
  3. + Add a language…: a language pack (see Adding or correcting a language).
  4. Languages…: the built-in languages and the installed packs.

Where space is short (the menu on a narrow screen, a phone, the welcome window), only the flag remains; the language's name shows on hover. A language whose country has no drawn flag (a pack's) shows its letters (ES, PT).

Everything follows this choice: menus, messages, dates and numbers, the app's windows. In the Windows app, even the web engine's own messages (a microphone permission, for example) use the app's language from the next launch, no longer Windows' language. The app follows your device's light or dark theme, scores included: the dark theme is easier on the eyes in the evening, in the rehearsal room.

#Adding or correcting a language

A school abroad, a student who reads their own language better, a drum term you say differently where you live: a language pack adds a language to the app, or corrects a built-in one, without waiting for a new version. You fill it in with a spreadsheet app (Excel, LibreOffice, Google Sheets), it is checked when you add it, and it stays on the device.

  1. Settings › Language › Languages…, then Translate into a new language…: the language code (es, it, pt-BR…), its name in that language (Español) and the language you translate from. The app saves a spreadsheet with all its texts, in French, English and German, and an empty column for the new language.
  2. Fill in the last column in your spreadsheet app. An empty cell keeps the text of the source language: you can translate step by step, starting with what you see most. Keep words in braces ({n}, {name}…) as they are: the app puts a number or a name there.
  3. Save as CSV, then Add a language (CSV or .sklang)…. The app checks every text and sums up: how many are translated, and what it skips, with the reason (an unknown key, a variable in braces that doesn't exist, an HTML tag). A skipped text shows in the source language: nothing invalid gets in.
  4. Install and use: the app restarts in the new language.

For an installed language:

  • Spreadsheet (CSV): the same spreadsheet, already filled in. After an app update, new texts are empty cells there; fill them in and add the spreadsheet again;
  • Share (.sklang): a file to send; on the other device, add it with Languages…;
  • Remove: the language disappears from this device.

To correct French, English or German: that language's Spreadsheet (CSV), change what doesn't suit you, then add the spreadsheet. Only the changed texts are kept: later versions' improvements keep coming for the rest. Remove the corrections goes back to the original texts.

Note

Language packs are not in the full backup: keep the spreadsheet or the .sklang file. The guide stays in French, English or German (in the pack's source language).

#Where is my data?

Your working data is saved on the device, in the app (or in the browser for the .html version): your own lessons, grooves, lists, practice plan, sounds, class journal, recorded takes, calibrations and, for teachers, the student register. There is no account, and StoneKiller receives nothing from you. Preferences are kept in the app's local storage (localStorage), documents in its local database (IndexedDB): these are not cookies.

Consequences:

  • this data belongs to this installation (or this browser): it syncs with no other device;
  • on Android, it is excluded from Google backups and from transfer to a new phone: it also holds this device's keys, which must not end up on another one;
  • uninstalling the app can erase it: make a Full backup first (My grooves page);
  • to switch devices, make a Full backup, then Restore on the new device (see Switching devices without losing anything); the file goes wherever you put it.

The backup takes all of this with it; only the device preferences (name, class Wi-Fi, display, count-in) have to be set again.

#Privacy: what the app sends

The app has no usage statistics, sends no error reports, shows no ads, and loads no font or script from elsewhere to work. It only contacts what you choose:

  • YouTube, Vimeo, SoundCloud, for a study on online media: nothing goes to the service until you turn it on (Turn on YouTube in the study, for this time or remembering your choice, or Settings › Online services). Once on, it is contacted for the title, the thumbnail and the player: it receives your IP address and the media link, and applies its own rules, cookies included. Turning it off stops its player, and nothing more goes to it; a script of the service already loaded goes when the app restarts;
  • the live class: the exchanges include the chosen name, device, connection and pairing identifiers, what the student is doing (following, exploring, paused), the exercises, the tempo, the messages, the homework and the videos given. They go through the teacher's app on the local network, or through the school's server set in the settings (ask its administrator where it is hosted). The relay hands each message to its recipient without keeping it: a student never receives what goes to another. These exchanges are not end-to-end encrypted; on the local network they travel in clear (HTTP), except through the teacher app's HTTPS address. During a class, the teacher's app announces its name and the class code on the local network, so students can find it;
  • the local network for Capture, the mirror and video feedback: pictures go from device to device, with no server on the internet;
  • an internet address you give a study (an online audio file): that server receives the request; a share goes to the app or destination you choose.

Privacy (in About, and Settings › Online services) gives the summary in the app, even offline; the full policy is a web page, opened only if you click. The app's libraries and their licences are in licenses/THIRD-PARTY.md.

#About

The About link, at the bottom of the app (and in the Settings), shows the version, the edition, the device and the credits (sounds, music font, licences). Copy the details puts them on the clipboard: paste them into your message to report a problem.

Installation and devices

This reference chapter gathers everything that depends on your device: the editions, installing and updating, the features that change from one device to another, and the keyboard shortcuts.

In this chapter

  1. The editions00
  2. Installation00

#The editions

The editions stack up: each one does everything the previous one does and adds its own tools.

Edition Who it's for What it adds
StoneKiller the student, the drummer who works alone lessons, player, practice plan, editor, printing, Setlist, joining your teacher's classes
Pro the drummer who goes further the pro workshop (composer, tracks), playing along with a video; Pro badge
StoneKiller Teach the teacher start live classes, project, Class panel and review, give homework, keep the student register and schedule; Teach badge
Academy (coming) the school the same work, shared between several teachers: sync, rooms, shared calendar

Why editions? The student does not need the teacher's tools, and the teacher keeps their data (register, classes) separate. A Pro or Teach feature is recognised by its badge. There are two apps to install: StoneKiller, which also contains the Pro edition, and StoneKiller Teach. During the trial, everything your app contains is open. Once installed (Windows, Mac, Android), the two apps live side by side, each with its own data. Two .html files opened in the same browser, on the other hand, can share the same data; the student register only appears in Teach.

The Teach app was called StoneKiller Prof up to 0.19. On Windows, the first StoneKiller Teach installer removes the old app by itself and keeps its data: nothing to uninstall, and above all do not tick “delete the data” if you uninstall it yourself, because Teach uses the same data. At the first class, Windows asks again for network permission. On Android, Teach replaces the installed app; on a Mac, move the old StoneKiller Prof to the bin after opening Teach once.

#Installation

Device File
Windows 10 or 11 StoneKiller_<version>_x64-setup.exe (installer) or StoneKiller-<version>-portable.exe (no installation)
Mac (macOS 11 or later, Apple Silicon or Intel) StoneKiller_<version>_universal.dmg
Android 7 or newer StoneKiller-<version>.apk
Any computer StoneKiller-<version>.html: a single file, to open in Chrome, Edge or Firefox
Web server (school, website) StoneKiller-web-<version>.zip: to upload to a server; does not open from the disk

For the Teach edition, the file names start with StoneKiller-Teach.

#Windows

  1. Run StoneKiller_<version>_x64-setup.exe. It installs for your account only and does not ask for an administrator password.
  2. If Windows shows “Windows protected your PC”, click More info, then Run anyway.
  3. StoneKiller appears in the Start menu.

The portable version starts directly, with no installation, for example from a USB stick. Your data stays on the computer, not on the stick: to take it with you, make a Full backup (My grooves page).

#Mac

  1. Open StoneKiller_<version>_universal.dmg and drag StoneKiller into the Applications folder. The same file works on Apple Silicon (M1 and later) and Intel Macs, with macOS 11 (Big Sur) or later.
  2. The first time, the Mac refuses to open the app: it does not come from the App Store and is not notarized by Apple. Open System Settings › Privacy & Security, scroll down to the message about StoneKiller, click Open Anyway and confirm. It won't ask again. (Up to macOS 14, right-clicking the app and choosing Open also works.)
  3. The Mac asks for your permission the first time you record with the microphone, and the first time you join or start a live class (local network): accept.

#Android

  1. Copy the APK to the phone or tablet, then open it.
  2. Android asks you to allow installation from this source: accept.
  3. StoneKiller appears with your other apps. While the app is open, the screen does not go to sleep.

#Browser

Double-click the .html file. It works without the internet. Your data is kept by this browser, on this computer: if you change browser or computer, it does not follow. Make a Full backup to take it with you.

#Updating

  • Windows: run the new setup.exe; it replaces the old version and keeps your data.
  • Mac: open the new .dmg and drag the app into Applications, replacing the old one; your data stays.
  • Android: install the new APK over the old one; your data stays.
  • .html file: replace the old file with the new one, in the same place, and open it in the same browser.

A yellow banner warns you if your data comes from a newer version than the app that is open: update the app before changing anything.

The width of the window matters more than the device: a tablet in portrait or a narrow window on a computer have the same layout as a phone (menu at the bottom, compact bars, pro workshop in tabs).

Shortcuts need a keyboard. A Bluetooth page-turner pedal behaves like a keyboard: it also works on phones and tablets, in reading mode.

Frequently asked questions

The most common problems with their solution.

In this chapter

  1. I can't hear anything00
  2. The playhead is ahead of the sound00
  3. My electronic kit is not recognized00
  4. The students cannot find the class00

  9. How do I raise the tempo little by little?00

  11. Which version of the app do I have?00
  12. I changed phones. How do I get my data back?00
  13. I have an old .json file: does it still work?00
  14. How do I update the app?00
  15. A yellow banner mentions a newer version00
  16. The phone screen turns off while I play00
  17. Can the student and the teacher use the same computer?00

A word from the app or from the drums escapes you? The Glossary explains it in one sentence.

#I can't hear anything

  • Tap the screen or click once: browsers only allow sound after a gesture.
  • Check the Volume at the bottom of the menu (on a phone, in More), and the device volume.
  • Sound status should be green. If it is not, wait for loading to finish.
  • On iPhone, turn off silent mode.
  • In the player, Drums must be on, and no instrument muted in Instruments.
  • During a class, on a student's phone: tap Sound on this device (off at first, to avoid an echo in the room).

#The playhead is ahead of the sound

It is almost always Bluetooth headphones or a Bluetooth speaker: the sound arrives late. Measure this delay once with Settings › Sound delay (Bluetooth) › Calibrate… (see Bluetooth: the sound delay).

#My electronic kit is not recognized

MIDI works in the Windows app and in Chrome, Edge or Firefox, not in the Android app or in Safari. Plug the kit in by USB before opening Workshop › Record, then Enable MIDI, and hit a pad to check.

#The students cannot find the class

See If a student cannot find the class.

#There is no Wi-Fi in the room

The class does not need the internet, only a shared Wi-Fi network. Without Wi-Fi, create one. See A class without Wi-Fi.

#Can students join with mobile data (4G, 5G)?

Not directly: a phone on 4G cannot reach the teacher's computer, because the carrier and the router block incoming connections. A server on the internet would be needed. With a phone's Wi-Fi, however, everyone is on the same local network: the class traffic stays in the room and uses no mobile data. The StoneKiller Teach app on Android creates this Wi-Fi in one tap, and a QR code gets the students onto it. See A class without Wi-Fi.

#What about Bluetooth?

No. Browsers on iPhone have no access to Bluetooth, and a device only accepts a few Bluetooth connections at a time (4 to 7), too few for a class. Local Wi-Fi does better, with nothing to install on the student's side.

#How do I play a part myself while the app plays the rest?

In the player, Instruments: mute the instrument you want to play (the bass drum, for example). The app plays everything else. See Muting instruments.

#How do I raise the tempo little by little?

Day by day, the practice plan raises the tempo with each Good. During a session, the metronome does it bar after bar. Full example: Raising the tempo of a hard groove.

#I have to rate twenty exercises after a run-through

Not one by one: ★ Rate rates the whole series at once, and you only change the exceptions. See Rating a whole series.

#Which version of the app do I have?

The About link, at the bottom of the app, shows the version, the edition and the device. Copy the details puts them on the clipboard, to report a problem.

#I changed phones. How do I get my data back?

On the old device: My grooves › Full backup. On the new one: My grooves › Restore. See Backing up and switching devices.

#I have an old .json file: does it still work?

Yes. Backups, lessons and registers from versions 0.4 and earlier open with the same buttons. New files are named .skbackup, .sklessons and .skroster.

#How do I update the app?

Install the new version over the old one (Windows: the new setup.exe; Android: the new APK), or replace the .html file. Your data stays. See Updating.

#A yellow banner mentions a newer version

Your data was saved by a newer version of the app (for example a backup restored from another device). Update the app before changing anything, so you lose nothing.

#The phone screen turns off while I play

The Android app keeps the screen on as long as it is displayed. In a browser (.html file, class page opened by QR code), set the phone's sleep timeout to a longer time while you play.

#Can the student and the teacher use the same computer?

Yes: install both editions. The student app finds the class of the StoneKiller Teach app on the same computer, exactly as it would on the network.

Chapter 31Part IX · Reference

Glossary

This glossary gives, in one sentence, the meaning of the words of the app and of the drums that a beginner may not know: rhythm and drums, lessons and practice, songs and video, creating, the teacher's class, the app itself and its files. Each word points to the chapter that covers it. The terms are sorted by theme, then alphabetically.

In this chapter

  1. Rhythm and drums00
  2. Practising00
  3. Songs and video00
  4. Creating00
  5. Teaching00
  6. The app00
  7. Files00

#Rhythm and drums

  • Accent: a stroke played louder. → The grid editor
  • BPM: beats per minute: the tempo. → Playing an exercise
  • Buzz: a pressed stroke that bounces into a roll. → The grid editor
  • Snare drum: the drum with the dry sound set in front of the drummer, played with sticks. → The drum key
  • Hi-hat: two cymbals stacked on a stand, closed or opened with the pedal. → The drum key
  • Drum key: on the score, the place of each instrument on the staff and the shape of its note. → The drum key
  • Click: the short sound of the metronome, one per beat. → The metronome
  • Cymbal: a metal disc struck with a stick; the crash marks an accent, the ride holds the pulse. → The drum key
  • Sticking: which hand or foot plays each note: R (right), L (left). → The drum key
  • Drag: two quick small notes before the main note. → The grid editor
  • Fill: a short drum phrase, often on the toms, that links two parts of a piece. → Studying a song
  • Flam: two strokes almost together, a small note right before the main one. → The grid editor
  • Ghost note: a very light stroke, almost silent. → The grid editor
  • Bass drum: the big drum played with the foot, on the pedal, which gives the low end of the groove. → The drum key
  • Bar: a group of beats between two barlines (in 4/4: four beats). → The metronome
  • Ostinato: a repeated figure that does not change while the rest varies. → The workshop
  • Practice pad: a rubber surface to work on your sticking in silence. → The drum key
  • Paradiddle: rudiment R L R R · L R L L. → The lesson book
  • Polymeter: a figure whose length does not line up with the bar, so it shifts at each repetition. → Polyrhythms and polymeters
  • Polyrhythm: two rhythms that share the same duration (3 against 2…). → Polyrhythms and polymeters
  • Repeat ×N: a bar played N times before the next one. → The grid editor
  • Rudiment: a basic stick pattern (paradiddle, flam, drag…). → The lesson book
  • Subdivision: how a beat is divided: eighths (2), triplets (3), sixteenths (4, “1 e & a”), sextuplets (6). → The metronome
  • Tempo: the speed of the music, measured in beats per minute (BPM). → Playing an exercise
  • Beat: the pulse, the one you count “1, 2, 3, 4”. → The metronome
  • Tom: one of the drums mounted or standing on the floor, higher or lower than the snare drum; often used in fills. → The drum key

#Practising

  • Lesson: a group of exercises on one subject, filed under a theme and split into parts. → The lesson book
  • Mastered: the rating that removes an exercise from the practice plan's reminders, because it is mastered. → The practice plan
  • Reading mode: the score alone, large, full screen: the phone on the music stand, at the kit. → Playing an exercise
  • Practice plan: the list of what you work on, with the tempo and the next reminder of each exercise: it tells you each day what to play. → The practice plan
  • Spaced repetition: going back over an exercise later and later once it is mastered, and sooner when it is hard. → The practice plan
  • Session (practice): a time of work set on an exercise, by duration or by number of repetitions. → Playing an exercise
  • Setlist: the basket of exercises you gather to play them in one go, in order. → Playing an exercise
  • Steady tempo and target tempo: the tempo to hold easily, without mistakes, for an exercise to be mastered, and the faster one you aim for next. → The practice plan
  • Theme (lessons): a “shelf” of the lesson book, which files neighbouring lessons together. → The lesson book

#Songs and video

  • Angle: a take filmed, which has become a view of the study: you choose it under the video, and it follows the song's playback. → Film and edit (Capture)
  • Align: to put the score, or a camera's take, exactly against the music. → Studying a song
  • Capture: the feature that films with several cameras while the song plays, each take lining back up with the song. → Film and edit (Capture)
  • Delay: in the mirror, the picture from a few seconds ago: you play first, then you watch yourself. → The mirror
  • Study: a song (its video or audio, its sections, its score, its exercises) that you work on in the Songs page. → Studying a song
  • Master and camera: in Capture, the master is the device that plays the song and starts the takes; the cameras are the other devices, which film and send it their picture. → Film and edit (Capture)
  • Mirror: the page where you watch yourself play, from several angles, live or on delay, to correct your posture. → The mirror
  • Play mode: the stripped-down study for playing: the video and the score, without the aligning and writing tools. → Studying a song
  • Montage: choosing which camera is seen at each moment, with crossfades, to make a video from the takes. → Film and edit (Capture)
  • Take (Capture): what a camera films between Record all and Stop; lined up with the song, it is kept as an angle or set aside. → Film and edit (Capture)
  • Sync sound: a sound the master plays just before and just after the song, to line up the cameras the app does not start, and the DAW. → Film and edit (Capture)
  • Section: a part of a song (intro, verse, chorus, bridge…), set against the music. → Studying a song
  • DAW: digital audio workstation: the software where you record and mix, such as Cubase or Reaper. → Film and edit (Capture)
  • Theme (video notes): a setting for how the notes look on the video (frame, movement, colours) and in the visualizer, which can be kept in a file. → Studying a song
  • Visualizer: the animated drawing that shows a song's music and drums when there is no video. → Studying a song
  • In–Out zone: the part of the song bounded by an entry point (In) and an exit point (Out), which you work on and loop. → Studying a song

#Creating

  • Workshop: the page where you make your own exercises: a groove, a variation, a coordination series, what you play. → The workshop
  • Building block: a piece of an existing groove (one beat, two beats, a bar), reusable in the workshop. → The workshop
  • Cell: a small one-beat pattern, named by a letter, that you combine in Ostinato and Combinations. → The workshop
  • Groove: the drum pattern, a few bars long, that repeats and drives a piece along. → The grid editor
  • My grooves: your personal collection of grooves and exercises, sorted into lists. → My grooves, backup and printing
  • Variant: a modified copy of an exercise (an extra bass drum, another sticking…), shown under the original exercise. → Playing an exercise

#Teaching

  • Review: at the end of a live class, the window where you see what each student did, with your notes, and where you confirm the update of the register. → After the class
  • Live class: a class where the teacher shows the exercises on each student's screen, at the same tempo, over the room's Wi-Fi. → During the class
  • Credit: a class bought in advance: each class given uses one. → The school, teachers and credits
  • Homework: an exercise the teacher gives at the end of a class: it arrives in the student's practice plan. → During the class
  • Package: a batch of classes bought in advance (for example ten), whose remaining credits the app counts. → The school, teachers and credits
  • Class panel: during a class, one line per student: what they are doing, whether they have finished, who they are. → During the class
  • Register: in the Teach edition, the list of your students, with their file and the history of their lessons. → Students
  • Link: connect a student's app once to their file, with a QR code, so the teacher recognises it at every class. → How teacher and student connect
  • Lesson (in the register): a class given to a student, recorded in their file: what was worked on, at what tempo, what the teacher thinks of it. → Students

#The app

  • Shortcut: a menu entry that leads straight to a function you often look for (writing a groove, recording what I play…). → Finding your way around the app
  • Home: the start page of simple mode: “I want to…” tiles that lead to the right page. → Finding your way around the app
  • Category: one of the six groupings of pages in the menu, each with its own colour: Tempo and rhythm, Exercises, Songs, Video, Create, Classes. → Finding your way around the app
  • Edition: the version of the app for the use: StoneKiller (the base, for students), Pro, Teach (for teachers); each adds tools to the previous one. → Installation and devices
  • Experimental: a function that works but may still change; it carries a small orange triangle ▲. → Settings, sounds and data
  • Simple and full mode: two ways of showing the same pages: simple mode starts from the home page and the categories, full mode puts every page in the menu. → Finding your way around the app
  • Profile: the choice made at opening (I practise, I learn on my own, I make covers (music and video), I teach), which sets the mode, the menu and the start page in one go. → Finding your way around the app

#Files

  • .sk… file: all the app's files have an extension that begins with .sk; any import button recognises their type and files them in the right place. → My grooves, backup and printing
  • .skaudio: a drum sound bank to install. → Settings, sounds and data
  • .skbackup: the full backup of your data. → My grooves, backup and printing
  • .skgroove: a list of grooves to share. → My grooves, backup and printing
  • .sklessons: lessons to share, for example from a teacher to their students. → The lesson book
  • .skroster: the student register, for the Teach edition. → Students
  • .sksong: a song study, without the music. → Studying a song
  • .sktheme: a display theme for the notes, to share. → Studying a song

Benutzerhandbuch

StoneKiller

Version 0.41.024. Oktober 2026

StoneKiller ist ein Schlagzeug-Lehrbuch, das spielt. Jede Übung erscheint als Noten und wird in dem Tempo gespielt, das du wählst, mit oder ohne Metronom. Ein Übungsplan sagt dir jeden Tag, woran du arbeiten solltest, und verfolgt deinen Fortschritt. In der Werkstatt schreibst du deine eigenen Grooves, und der Lehrer kann seinen Live-Unterricht im WLAN des Raums geben.

#Kurz gesagt

  • ÜbenLektionen nach Themen, ein einstellbarer Player, Übungssessions mit Timer und ein vollständiges Metronom.
  • Erstelleneinen Groove in ein Raster schreiben, Zellen kombinieren, aufnehmen, was du spielst.
  • Unterrichteneine Übung bei allen Schülern projizieren, Hausaufgaben geben, jeden Schüler begleiten.
  • Ohne InternetAlles funktioniert offline, auch der Live-Unterricht.
  • Deine Daten bleiben bei dirkein Konto, nichts wird ins Internet geschickt.
  • ÜberallWindows, Android oder einfach eine Datei, die du im Browser öffnest.

#Wo anfangen?

  • Du lernst StoneKiller gerade kennen: Schnellstart, zehn Minuten, um deine erste Übung zu spielen und auf den Übungsplan zu setzen, dann Sich in der App zurechtfinden.
  • Du übst allein: Eine Übung spielen, dann Der Übungsplan und Das Metronom. Um einen Song zu lernen: Einen Song studieren.
  • Du unterrichtest: Das Lehrbuch, Wie Lehrkraft und Schüler verbunden sind, Während der Stunde und Die Schüler.
  • Du filmst dein Schlagzeugspiel: Der Spiegel, Filmen und schneiden und Meine Videos.
  • Du willst eigene Übungen schreiben: Der Raster-Editor, dann Die Werkstatt.
  • Du suchst, wie etwas geht: Schritt für Schritt oder die Häufigen Fragen. Ein Wort, das du nicht kennst: das Glossar.
